In the impact the linear momentum of the bullet is taken up by the
bullet + block system.  If the block is at rest before the impact

$$m_{b}v_{0}=(M+m_{b})v_{i}$$

is the (horizontal) momentum just after the impact, $v_{i}$ being the
common velocity of the bullet–block system immediately after the
embedding.  The kinetic energy which remains after the perfectly
inelastic impact is then converted into gravitational potential energy
in the swing

$$\frac12\,(M+m_{b})v_{i}^{2}=(M+m_{b})gh ,$$

so that the velocity immediately after the impact is the velocity
which will carry the system to the height $h$,

$$v_{i}=\sqrt{2gh}$$

independently of the masses.  Hence

$$v_{0}=\frac{M+m_{b}}{m_{b}}\,v_{i}
      =\frac{M+m_{b}}{m_{b}}\sqrt{2gh}\;,$$

the familiar ballistic-pendulum formula.  With

* $m_{b}=24\;{\rm g}=2.4\times10^{-2}\ {\rm kg}$,
* $M=4.46\ {\rm kg}$,
* $h=14.3\ {\rm cm}=0.143\ {\rm m}$,

$$v_{i}=\sqrt{2gh}=\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.143}\approx
\sqrt{2.81}\approx1.67\!-\!1.68\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$$

is the velocity of the $(M+m_{b})$ system just after the impact.  The
mass ratio is

$$\frac{M+m_{b}}{m_{b}}=\frac{4.46+0.024}{0.024}\approx1.87\times10^{2},$$

so that

$$v_{0}\approx1.87\times10^{2}\times1.68\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      \approx 3.1\!-\!3.2\times10^{2}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$$

in the usual ballistic-pendulum approximation.  With the numbers
quoted

$$v_{0}\approx\frac{4.484}{0.024}\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.143}
      \approx 3.13\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}\approx 310\!-\!315\;{\rm m/s}$$

before impact, about $3.1\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$ in the $M\gg m_{b}$
limit $v_{0}\simeq(M/m_{b})\sqrt{2gh}\approx3.11\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$,
i.e. of the order of $300\;{\rm m/s}$, the familiar rifle-muzzle
velocity.  This is the velocity which, after the inelastic loss, leaves
the combined mass with $v_{i}=\sqrt{2gh}\approx1.68\;{\rm m/s}$ and a
rise $h=0.143\;{\rm m}$.

For a projectile launched and landing at the same height the time of flight
is set by the vertical motion and the range by the horizontal motion.

* $v_{0x}=v_{0}\cos\theta$ , $v_{0y}=v_{0}\sin\theta$

$$
\begin{aligned}
v_{0x}&=22.9\cos47^{\circ}\\
     &\approx 22.9\times0.6820\approx 1.56\times10^{1}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}\\
v_{0y}&=22.9\sin47^{\circ}\\
     &\approx 22.9\times0.7314\approx 1.67\times10^{1}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Vertical motion, $y(t)=v_{0y}t-\tfrac12gt^{2}$, $y=0$ at take off and at
landing

$$
0=v_{0y}t_{f}-\tfrac12gt_{f}^{2}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
t_{f}= \frac{2v_{0y}}{g}
$$

$$
t_{f}= \frac{2\times22.9\sin47^{\circ}}{9.81}
     \approx\frac{33.49}{9.81}\approx 3.42\ {\rm s}
$$

Horizontal motion is uniform

$$
R=v_{0x}t_{f}=v_{0}\cos\theta\;\frac{2v_{0}\sin\theta}{g}
   =\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{g}\sin2\theta
$$

$$
R=\frac{(22.9)^{2}}{9.81}\sin\!\left[2\times47^{\circ}\right]
  =\frac{524.4}{9.81}\sin94^{\circ}
$$

$\sin94^{\circ}=\sin86^{\circ}\approx0.998$,

$$
R\approx 53.46\times0.9976\approx 5.3\!-\!5.4\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}
$$

about $53\;{\rm m}$ down range, $\approx 53.3\;{\rm m}$ with $g=9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$.
The familiar closed form $R=v_{0}^{2}\sin2\theta/g$ gives $R\approx 53.5\;{\rm m}$ on the usual $g\approx9.8\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$ approximation.

For a flat coil the flux through one turn is

$$\Phi_{1}=BA\cos\theta\qquad \cos\theta =1$$
for a field normal to the coil, so that for $N$ turns

$${\cal E}=-N\frac{d\Phi_{1}}{dt}=-NA\frac{dB}{dt}$$

in the average sense for a steady change

$${\cal E}_{av}\simeq -N A\frac{\Delta B}{\Delta t}$$

is the emf induced in the $N$-turn winding.  The current that can be
driven in the resistance $R$ of the winding is

$$I=\frac{|{\cal E}_{av}|}{R}= \frac{N A}{R}\,
\frac{|\Delta B|}{\Delta t}\;.$$

* Area per turn

$$A=60\;{\rm cm^{2}}=60\times10^{-4}\ {\rm m^{2}}=6.0\times10^{-3}\ {\rm m^{2}}$$

* Change of flux density

$$|\Delta B|=B_{i}-B_{f}=1.48-0.24=1.24\ {\rm T}$$

$$\Bigl|\frac{dB}{dt}\Bigr|\simeq\frac{|\Delta B|}{\Delta t}
      =\frac{1.24\ {\rm T}}{0.91\ {\rm s}}\approx1.36\ {\rm T\,s^{-1}}$$

Hence the magnitude of the average induced emf is

$$\begin{aligned}
|{\cal E}_{av}| &= N A\Bigl|\frac{dB}{dt}\Bigr|
 =395\,(6.0\times10^{-3}\,{\rm m^{2}})\,
   \frac{1.24}{0.91}\ {\rm V}\\
&\approx 2.37\times1.36\ {\rm V}\approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\ {\rm V}
\end{aligned}$$

and the average current that can flow in the $R=11.0\;\Omega$ winding is

$$I_{av}= \frac{|{\cal E}_{av}|}{R}
       \approx\frac{3.23\ {\rm V}}{11.0\;\Omega}
       \approx 2.9\!-\!3.0\times10^{-1}\ {\rm A}$$

about $0.29\!-\!0.30\;{\rm A}$, $\approx 0.29\;{\rm A}$ in magnitude.
The sign is such that the induced magnetic field tries to keep the
original $1.48\;{\rm T}$ field up, i.e. the emf is positive in the
sense that opposes the decrease of $B$.  With the usual Lenz sign
${\cal E}=-N A\Delta B/\Delta t\approx-3.2\;{\rm V}$ giving
$I\approx-0.29\;{\rm A}$ for the chosen positive orientation, magnitude
$\,|I|\approx0.29\;{\rm A}\,$, essentially $0.3\;{\rm A}$ for the
average over the $0.91\;{\rm s}$ interval.

For a launch from and to the same height the flight is symmetric in $y$.

Write the components of the launch velocity

* $v_{0x}=v_{0}\cos\theta$
* $v_{0y}=v_{0}\sin\theta$

in the horizontal $x$ and vertical $y$ directions.  With no drag

* $x(t)=v_{0x}t=v_{0}\cos\theta\,t$
* $y(t)=v_{0y}t-\tfrac12gt^{2}=v_{0}\sin\theta\,t-\tfrac12gt^{2}$

The projectile is back on the ground when $y=0$, $t>0$,

$$0=v_{0}\sin\theta\,t-\tfrac12gt^{2}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
t_{f}=\frac{2v_{0}\sin\theta}{g}  $$

is the time of flight.  The horizontal range is then

$$R=x(t_{f})=v_{0}\cos\theta\,t_{f}
   =v_{0}\cos\theta\frac{2v_{0}\sin\theta}{g}
   =\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{g}\sin2\theta  $$

on the same level.

For $v_{0}=22.8\;{\rm m/s}$ and $\theta=52^{\circ}$

* $v_{0x}=22.8\cos52^{\circ}\approx22.8\times0.6157\approx14.0\;{\rm m/s}$
* $v_{0y}=22.8\sin52^{\circ}\approx22.8\times0.7880\approx18.0\;{\rm m/s}$

Time of flight

$$t_{f}= \frac{2v_{0y}}{g}= \frac{2\times17.97}{9.81}\approx3.66\;{\rm s}$$

Range

$$R=v_{0x}t_{f}\approx14.04\times3.66\approx5.1\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}$$

in closed form

$$R=\frac{(22.8)^{2}}{9.81}\sin104^{\circ}\approx
\frac{519.8\times0.9703}{9.81}\approx5.15\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}$$

about $51\!-\!52\;{\rm m}$ down range, $\approx 51.5\;{\rm m}$ with $g=9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$, $ \approx 51.6\;{\rm m}$ on the often used $g=9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$.  This is the ideal vacuum range; any real drag will reduce it.

For a charge moving perpendicular to a uniform $B$ the magnetic Lorentz force
provides the centripetal force

$$ \frac{mv^{2}}{r}=qvB\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
r=\frac{mv}{qB} $$

For an $\alpha$ particle

* $m =6.645\times10^{-27}\ {\rm kg}$
* $q =2e =2\times1.602\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}=3.204\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}$
* $v =4.7\times10^{5}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$
* $B =1.97\ {\rm T}$

Hence

$$
r=\frac{mv}{qB}
  =\frac{\,6.645\times10^{-27}\ {\rm kg}\times4.7\times10^{5}\ {\rm m/s}\,}
         {\,3.204\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}\times1.97\ {\rm T}\,}
  =\frac{3.12\times10^{-21}}{6.31\times10^{-19}}\ {\rm m}
  \approx 4.9\times10^{-3}\ {\rm m}
$$

$$
r\approx 4.9\!-\!5.0\times10^{-3}\ {\rm m}\approx 4.9\ {\rm mm}
$$

i.e. about $4.9\;{\rm mm}\approx 0.005\;{\rm m}$ of curvature, $r\approx4.94\;{\rm mm}$ with the numbers quoted.  The sense of rotation is that of a positive charge, $r=mv/qB$ in magnitude.

For two equal sign charges the field can vanish only between them, where
the two fields are opposite.  Put $q_{1}$ at the origin and $q_{2}$ at
$L=52\;{\rm cm}$ and let the zero be a distance $x$ from $q_{1}$ on the
segment $0<x<L$.  Then

$$E_{1}(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{q_{1}}{x^{2}},\qquad 
E_{2}(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{q_{2}}{(L-x)^{2}} $$

and $E_{1}=E_{2}$ on the line between the charges, so that

$$\frac{q_{1}}{x^{2}}=\frac{q_{2}}{(L-x)^{2}}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
\frac{\sqrt{q_{1}}}{x}=\frac{\sqrt{q_{2}}}{L-x}\;.$$

Hence

$$x=\frac{L}{1+\sqrt{q_{2}/q_{1}}}
   =L\,\frac{\sqrt{q_{1}}}{\sqrt{q_{1}}+\sqrt{q_{2}}}\;.$$

With $q_{1}=6.9\;\mu{\rm C}$, $q_{2}=5.5\;\mu{\rm C}$ and $L=52\;{\rm cm}$

$$
\sqrt{\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}}=\sqrt{\frac{5.5}{6.9}}=0.893
$$

and

$$
x=\frac{52\;{\rm cm}}{1+0.893}\approx
\frac{52}{1.893}\;{\rm cm}\approx 2.7\!-\!2.8\times10^{1}\ {\rm cm}
$$

from $q_{1}$ toward $q_{2}$, i.e. about $27\!-\!28\;{\rm cm}$ from the
$6.9\;\mu{\rm C}$ charge, $L-x\approx 24.5\;{\rm cm}$ from the $5.5\;\mu{\rm C}$
charge.  In round numbers

$$x\approx 2.75\times10^{1}\ {\rm cm}\approx 27.5\;{\rm cm}$$

from $q_{1}$ on the $q_{1}q_{2}$ segment, the zero being nearer the
smaller charge, as expected.  This is $52-x\approx24.5\;{\rm cm}$ from
$q_{2}$.  Using $x=L\sqrt{q_{1}}/(\sqrt{q_{1}}+\sqrt{q_{2}})$ gives
$x\approx27.47\;{\rm cm}$, essentially $27.5\;{\rm cm}$ from $q_{1}$ toward
$q_{2}$.

For a particle of mass $m$ at the surface $R$ the mechanical energy is

$$
E=\frac12 m v^{2}-\frac{GMm}{R}\;,
$$

the second term being the Newtonian gravitational potential energy.
Escape is $E\ge 0$, i.e. in the limit $v\to v_{e}$

$$
\frac12 m v_{e}^{2}-\frac{GMm}{R}=0\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
v_{e}(R)=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}\;,
$$

so that $v_{e}\propto\sqrt{M/R}$.

For the Earth

$$
v_{e,E}=\sqrt{\frac{2GM_{E}}{R_{E}}}
      =\sqrt{\frac{2\times6.674\times10^{-11}\times5.972\times10^{24}}
                   {6.371\times10^{6}}}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      \approx 1.12\times10^{4}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}\approx 11.2\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}},
$$

the familiar $11.19\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$.

For the planet

$$
M_{p}=7.06\,M_{E},\qquad R_{p}=2.82\,R_{E},
$$

hence

$$
v_{e,p}= \sqrt{\frac{2G M_{p}}{R_{p}}}
       =\sqrt{\frac{2G\,7.06M_{E}}{2.82R_{E}}}
       =\sqrt{\frac{7.06}{2.82}}\;
         \sqrt{\frac{2GM_{E}}{R_{E}}}
       =\sqrt{\frac{7.06}{2.82}}\;v_{e,E}\; .
$$

Now

$$
\sqrt{\frac{7.06}{2.82}}=\sqrt{2.506}\approx1.58,
$$

so that in terms of the terrestrial escape speed

$$
v_{e,p}\approx1.58\,v_{e,E}\approx1.58\times11.2\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}
      \approx1.77\times10^{4}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}} .
$$

With the numbers quoted

* $M_{p}=7.06\times5.972\times10^{24}=4.22\times10^{25}\ {\rm kg}$,
* $R_{p}=2.82\times6371\ {\rm km}=1.80\times10^{4}\ {\rm km}=1.80\times10^{7}\ {\rm m}$,

$$
v_{e,p}= \sqrt{\frac{2\times6.674\times10^{-11}\times4.22\times10^{25}}
                    {1.80\times10^{7}}}
       \approx1.7\!-\!1.8\times10^{4}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

i.e. about $17\!-\!18\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$, $ \approx 17.7\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ on the
usual $v_{e,E}=11.19\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ normalisation, essentially the
$1.58$ times terrestrial escape speed.  This is the usual $\sqrt{M/R}$
scaling, $v_{e,p}/v_{e,E}=\sqrt{M_{p}/M_{E}}\;\sqrt{R_{E}/R_{p}}$.

The speed at the instant the obstacle is seen is

$$v_{0}=85\;{\rm km\,h^{-1}}=\frac{85\times10^{3}}{3600}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      =\frac{425}{18}\approx 23.6\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$$

Reaction

During the reaction time $t_{r}$ the car continues at $v_{0}$,

$$s_{r}=v_{0}t_{r}$$

$$s_{r}= \frac{425}{18}\times0.72
      =\frac{306}{18}=17.0\;{\rm m}$$

about $17\;{\rm m}$ of travel before the brakes are applied.

Braking

With a constant deceleration $a=-7.3\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$

$$0=v_{0}^{2}+2a s_{b}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
s_{b}= -\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{2a}= \frac{v_{0}^{2}}{2|a|}$$

$$s_{b}= \frac{(23.61\;{\rm m/s})^{2}}{2\times7.3\;{\rm m/s^{2}}}
      =\frac{5.57\times10^{2}}{14.6}\approx 3.8\!-\!3.9\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}$$

$$s_{b}\approx 38.2\;{\rm m}$$

in the $v_{0}^{2}/2a$ braking phase, the time to stop being
$t_{b}=v_{0}/|a|\approx 3.23\;{\rm s}$.

Stopping distance from the instant the obstacle is seen

$$s_{\rm tot}=s_{r}+s_{b}\approx 17.0\;{\rm m}+38.2\;{\rm m}
          \approx 5.5\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}$$

i.e. about $55\!-\!56\;{\rm m}$ of travel from sighting to rest, $\approx 17\;{\rm m}$ of which is covered during the $0.72\;{\rm s}$ reaction time and $\approx 38\;{\rm m}$ under braking.  With the numbers quoted this is $s_{\rm tot}\simeq 55.2\;{\rm m}$ from the moment the obstacle is first seen.

For an ideal Atwood machine the two masses have the same magnitude of
acceleration $a$ and the same string tension $T$.

Put the heavy mass $m_{1}$ down and the light mass $m_{2}$ up

* $m_{1}$ : $m_{1}g-T=m_{1}a$
* $m_{2}$ : $T-m_{2}g=m_{2}a$

Hence

$$
(m_{1}-m_{2})g=(m_{1}+m_{2})a\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
a=\frac{m_{1}-m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\,g
$$

is the common acceleration of the two bodies.  With

* $m_{1}=4.52\;{\rm kg}$,
* $m_{2}=3.65\;{\rm kg}$,

$$
a=g\,\frac{4.52-3.65}{4.52+3.65}
  =9.81\,\frac{0.87}{8.17}\approx 1.04\!-\!1.05\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}
$$

downwards for $m_{1}$ and upwards for $m_{2}$.

The tension follows from either mass, e.g. from the light mass

$$
T=m_{2}g+m_{2}a=m_{2}\bigl[g+a\bigr]
   =m_{2}g\!\left[1+\frac{m_{1}-m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\right]
   =\frac{2m_{1}m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\,g .
$$

In closed form

$$
T=g\,\frac{2m_{1}m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}
  =9.81\,\frac{2\times4.52\times3.65}{4.52+3.65}\;{\rm N}
$$

$$
T\approx 9.81\times4.04\;{\rm N}\approx 3.9\!-\!4.0\times10^{1}\ {\rm N}
$$

i.e. about $3.96\times10^{1}\ {\rm N}$, $T\approx 39\!-\!40\;{\rm N}$,
$ \approx 39.6\;{\rm N}$ on the $g=9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ convention, 
$T=m_{1}(g-a)=m_{1}g-m_{1}a$ giving the same number.  This is the
string tension while the system is accelerating; in the limit $a\to0$
it tends to the familiar $m_{1}m_{2}/(m_{1}+m_{2})g$ static value.

For an RC charge

$$V_{C}(t)=V_{\infty}\Bigl[\,1-e^{-t/RC}\Bigr] ,\qquad 
\tau =RC $$

is the $RC$ time constant.  With $V_{C}/V_{\infty}=0.60$

$$0.60=1-e^{-t/\tau}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
e^{-t/\tau}=0.40 $$

so that

$$t=-\tau\ln 0.40=\tau\ln\frac{1}{0.40}=\tau\ln 2.5 .$$

The time constant of the circuit is

$$\tau =R\,C=(60\times10^{3}\,\Omega)(69\times10^{-6}\,{\rm F})
      =4.14\;{\rm s},$$

hence

$$t=\tau\ln 2.5\approx4.14\times0.9163\approx3.7\!-\!3.8\;{\rm s}$$

about $3.8\;{\rm s}$ after the switch is closed, i.e. $t\approx
RC\ln\!\left[1/(1-0.60)\right]$.  In closed form $t=RC\ln2.5\approx
3.79\;{\rm s}\approx4.14\ln2.5\;{\rm s}$, essentially $ \sim 3.8\;{\rm s}$ 
$\approx 0.92\,\tau$ after the start.

* $d=1.87\;{\rm mm}=1.87\times10^{-3}\;{\rm m}$
* $\kappa =7.1$

$$

$$

$$

i.e. about

on the usual $C\approx4.31\times10^{-10}\,{\rm F}$ value,

For a series $R\!-\!C$ charge

$$V_{C}(t)=V_{\infty}\Bigl[\,1-e^{-t/RC}\Bigr]\qquad V_{C}(0)=0$$

so that

$$\frac{V_{C}(t)}{V_{\infty}}=1-e^{-t/RC}\;.$$

Put $V_{C}/V_{\infty}=0.75$,

$$0.75=1-e^{-t/RC}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
e^{-t/RC}=0.25$$

$$-\frac{t}{RC}=\ln 0.25=-\ln 4$$

$$t=RC\,\ln 4\;.$$

The $RC$ time constant is

$$RC=(52\times10^{3}\,\Omega)(23\times10^{-6}\,{\rm F})
      =1.196\;{\rm s}$$

Hence

$$t_{0.75}=RC\ln4=1.196\;\ln4\approx1.196\times1.3863\approx1.6\!-\!1.7\;{\rm s}$$

about $1.66\;{\rm s}$ after the switch is closed, i.e. $\approx 1.4$ time constants to $75\%$ of the asymptotic voltage $V_{\infty}$.  In the usual $t_{5\tau}\approx5RC$ notation this is $t\approx1.39\,\tau$.

*Remark:* $t_{p}=RC\ln\!\left[\,1/(1-p)\right]$ for a fraction $p$ of the final voltage.

For the motion down the plane put the $x$ axis down the plane and the $y$
axis normal to it.  With $s$ measured down the plane

* $N-mg\cos\theta=0$  so that on the plane

$$
N=mg\cos\theta
$$

* the kinetic friction is

$$
f_{k}=\mu_{k}N=\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta
$$

down the plane the component of weight is $mg\sin\theta$ so that the
net force down the plane is

$$
F_{x}=mg\sin\theta-f_{k}=mg\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]
$$

and with $m$ cancelling

$$
a=g\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]
$$

is the (constant) acceleration down the plane.  For $u=0$

$$
v^{2}=u^{2}+2as=2gs\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big] ,
$$

i.e. in work–energy form

$$
\Delta K=W_{g}+W_{f},\qquad 
W_{g}=mg s\sin\theta,\;\;W_{f}=-\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta\,s,
$$

so that

$$
\frac12mv^{2}=mgs\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big] .
$$

For $\theta=30^{\circ}$,

$$
\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta
=0.5000-0.28\frac{\sqrt3}{2}
=0.5000-0.2425\approx0.2575>0,
$$

so the block does in fact accelerate.  Hence

$$
a=g\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]
\approx9.81\times0.2575\approx2.53\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}
$$

down the plane and

$$
v(s)=\sqrt{2as}
     =\sqrt{2gs\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]}
$$

For $s=9.5\;{\rm m}$

$$
v=\sqrt{2\times9.81\times9.5\,
\Big[0.5-0.28\cos30^{\circ}\Big]}
   =\sqrt{47.99}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
   \approx 6.9\!-\!7.0\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

down the incline, about $6.9\;{\rm m/s}$ with the numbers quoted,
$ v\approx6.93\;{\rm m/s}$ for $g=9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$.  In the
usual $g\approx9.8\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ estimate $v\approx6.9\;{\rm m/s}$,
essentially $7\;{\rm m/s}$ down the $30^{\circ}$ plane.  The
corresponding constant acceleration is $a\approx2.5\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$

For a circular orbit the centripetal force is the Newtonian gravity

$$ \frac{mv^{2}}{r}=\frac{GM_{\oplus}m}{r^{2}}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
v^{2}=\frac{GM_{\oplus}}{r} $$

and $v=2\pi r/T$ so that

$$ T^{2}=\frac{4\pi^{2}}{GM_{\oplus}}\,r^{3}\;, \qquad 
T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{\mu}},\qquad \mu\equiv GM_{\oplus} $$

is Kepler's third law.  For a low earth orbit

* $R_{\oplus}=6371\;{\rm km}$
* $h=867\;{\rm km}$

$$r=R_{\oplus}+h=6371+867=7238\;{\rm km}=7.238\times10^{6}\ {\rm m}$$

Hence

$$
\frac{r^{3}}{\mu}=
\frac{(7.238\times10^{6}\,{\rm m})^{3}}{3.986\times10^{14}\ {\rm m^{3}s^{-2}}}
=
\frac{3.79\times10^{20}}{3.986\times10^{14}}\ {\rm s^{2}}
\approx 9.51\times10^{5}\ {\rm s^{2}}
$$

$$
\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{\mu}}\approx\sqrt{9.51\times10^{5}}\approx 9.75\times10^{2}\ {\rm s}
$$

and

$$
T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{\mu}}\approx2\pi\times 9.75\times10^{2}\ {\rm s}
\approx 6.1\!-\!6.3\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}
$$

$$
T\approx 6.13\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}\approx\frac{6.13\times10^{3}}{60}\ {\rm min}
\approx 1.02\times10^{2}\ {\rm min}
$$

i.e. about $6.1\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}\approx 102\;{\rm min}\approx1.7\;{\rm h}$ 
on a $r=7.24\times10^{3}\ {\rm km}$ circular orbit.  With the numbers
quoted this is $T\simeq 6.13\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}\simeq102.1\ {\rm min}$,
essentially the familiar $\sim$100 min LEO period.  The $\sim 1$–2 min
difference you get with the usual $R_{\oplus}=6378\ {\rm km}$ or with
$\mu=398600\ {\rm km^{3}s^{-2}}$ is within the round-off of the
constants.

The $R_{2}\parallel R_{3}$ combination is in series with $R_{1}$ so that the
current which leaves the battery is the current in $R_{1}$.

$$R_{p}=R_{2}\parallel R_{3}=\frac{R_{2}R_{3}}{R_{2}+R_{3}}
      =\frac{90\times 29}{90+29}=\frac{2610}{119}\approx 21.93\;\Omega $$

$$R_{T}=R_{1}+R_{p}=8+\frac{2610}{119}=\frac{3562}{119}\approx 29.93\;\Omega $$

Hence the total current taken from the 14 V ideal source is

$$I_{T}=\frac{V}{R_{T}}=\frac{14}{R_{1}+R_{p}}
      =\frac{14\times119}{3562}=\frac{833}{1781}\approx 0.47\;{\rm A}$$

in $R_{1}$.  The voltage which appears across the $R_{2}\parallel R_{3}$
pair is

$$V_{p}=V-I_{T}R_{1}=V_{p}=I_{T}R_{p}
      =\frac{14R_{p}}{R_{1}+R_{p}}
      =\frac{18270}{1781}\approx 10.3\;{\rm V},$$

so that the branch currents are

$$I_{2}=\frac{V_{p}}{R_{2}},\qquad I_{3}=\frac{V_{p}}{R_{3}},\qquad
I_{2}+I_{3}=I_{T} .$$

In closed form

$$I_{2}=V\,\frac{R_{3}}{(R_{2}+R_{3})R_{1}+R_{2}R_{3}}
     =\frac{V R_{3}}{R_{1}R_{2}+R_{1}R_{3}+R_{2}R_{3}} $$

and with the numbers

$$I_{2}= \frac{14\times 29}{8(90+29)+90\times29}
     =\frac{406}{3562}=\frac{203}{1781}\ {\rm A}\approx1.1\!-\!1.2\times10^{-1}\ {\rm A},$$

i.e. about $0.11\!-\!0.12\;{\rm A}$, $\approx 114\;{\rm mA}$, flowing from
the positive side of the parallel combination toward the negative side.
The companion branch is $I_{3}=V_{p}/R_{3}\approx 0.354\;{\rm A}$ and
$I_{2}+I_{3}\approx0.468\;{\rm A}=I_{T}$ as required.  The $0.114\;{\rm A}$
is the magnitude usually quoted as $\,I_{R2}\approx0.11\;{\rm A}$.

*Remark:* $V_{p}\approx10.26\;{\rm V}$ across the parallel pair, $V_{R1}\approx3.74\;{\rm V}$, so $V_{R1}+V_{p}=14\;{\rm V}$.

In the (very short) impact the impulse of the floor can be neglected so
that the linear momentum of the two blocks is conserved

$$p_{i}=p_{f}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
m_{1}v_{1i}+m_{2}v_{2i}=(m_{1}+m_{2})v^{\prime}$$

with $v_{2i}=0$

$$
v^{\prime}= \frac{m_{1}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\,v_{1i}
       =\frac{1.99}{1.99+2.14}\times 2.30\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
       =\frac{4.58}{4.13}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}\approx 1.1\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

is the common speed just after the perfectly inelastic impact.  
The kinetic energy just after impact is

$$
K^{\prime}=\frac12\,(m_{1}+m_{2})v^{\prime 2}
        =\frac12\,(m_{1}+m_{2})
          \left[\frac{m_{1}v_{1i}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\right]^{2}
        =\frac{m_{1}^{2}v_{1i}^{2}}{2(m_{1}+m_{2})}\; .
$$

After the impact the pair is slowed by kinetic friction

$$
F_{f}= \mu_{k}N=\mu_{k}(m_{1}+m_{2})g ,
\qquad 
a_{f}= \frac{F_{f}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}=\mu_{k}g
$$

in the direction opposite to the motion.  The work done by friction
in stopping the pair is $W_{f}= -F_{f}d$, so that on an energy basis

$$
K^{\prime}+W_{f}=0\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
\frac12\,(m_{1}+m_{2})v^{\prime 2}= \mu_{k}(m_{1}+m_{2})g\,d
$$

the total mass cancels and

$$
d=\frac{v^{\prime 2}}{2\mu_{k}g}
  =\frac{1}{2\mu_{k}g}
    \left[\frac{m_{1}v_{1i}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\right]^{2}
$$

is the sliding distance measured from the instant the two blocks move
as one.  With the numbers

$$
a_{f}= \mu_{k}g =0.34\times9.81\approx 3.34\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}
$$

$$
d=\frac{(1.108\,{\rm m/s})^{2}}{2\times0.34\times9.81}
  \approx\frac{1.23}{6.67}\approx1.8\!-\!1.9\times10^{-1}\ {\rm m}
$$

i.e. about $0.18\!-\!0.19\;{\rm m}\approx18\;{\rm cm}$ of sliding after
they have stuck together.  In the usual $g\approx9.8\!-\!10\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$
estimate this is $d\approx v^{\prime 2}/2\mu g\approx0.18\;{\rm m}$,
about $0.20\;{\rm m}$ with the rough $g=10\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ estimate.
The $m_{1}+m_{2}$ cancels so the stopping distance after the inelastic
impact depends only on the post-impact speed $v^{\prime}$ and on $\mu g$.

*Remark:*  $v^{\prime}\approx1.11\;{\rm m/s}$ is the speed immediately
after the perfectly inelastic collision; the $ \approx 0.18\;{\rm m}$
is the distance travelled by the combined mass from that instant until
rest.  The distance travelled by $m_{1}$ before the impact is not
fixed by the data given.

For the motion down the plane the component of the weight down the plane
is $mg\sin\theta$ and the kinetic friction is

$$F_{f}=\mu_{k}N=\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta $$

so that, with the $s$–axis down the plane,

$$m a = mg\sin\theta-\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta $$

$$a=g\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big] $$

is the (constant) acceleration down the plane.  With

$\sin22^{\circ}=0.3746$, $\;\cos22^{\circ}=0.9272$,

$$
a=g\Big[\sin22^{\circ}-\mu_{k}\cos22^{\circ}\Big]
  =9.81\Big[\,0.3746-0.06\times0.9272\,\Big]
  =9.81\big[\,0.31898\,\big]
  \approx 3.1\!-\!3.2\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}
$$

down the plane.  Starting from rest

$$v^{2}=v_{0}^{2}+2as\;, \qquad v_{0}=0,$$

so that on a distance $s$ down the plane

$$v(s)=\sqrt{2as}
     =\sqrt{2gs\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]}\;,$$

the familiar work–energy form

$$ \tfrac12mv^{2}=mg s\sin\theta-\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta\,s .$$

For $s=4.4\;{\rm m}$

$$
v=\sqrt{2\times9.81\times4.4\,
\Big[\sin22^{\circ}-0.06\cos22^{\circ}\Big]}
   =\sqrt{86.328\times0.31898}
   =\sqrt{27.5}\;{\rm m^{2}s^{-2}}
   \approx 5.2\!-\!5.3\;{\rm m/s}
$$

down the incline, about $5.25\;{\rm m/s}$ in the idealised
constant-$\mu_{k}$ limit.  With the usual $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this
is $v\approx5.24\;{\rm m/s}$, essentially $ \sim 5\;{\rm m/s}$ down the
$22^{\circ}$ plane after $4.4\;{\rm m}$ of travel.  The $3.13\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$
acceleration is $g\sin\theta$ reduced by the $ \mu_{k}g\cos\theta$

For the hanging mass let the downward direction be positive and let $T$ be the
tension in the (massless) string.  With $a$ the linear acceleration of the
mass and $\alpha$ the angular acceleration of the disk

* Translation of the mass
$$
\sum F_{y}=m a\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad mg-T=m a\tag{1}
$$

* Rotation of the disk about its fixed centre
$$
\sum \tau =I\alpha\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad TR=I\alpha\tag{2}
$$
For a uniform solid disc about its central axis
$$
I_{c}=\frac12 MR^{2}
$$
and for inextensible unwinding
$$
a=R\alpha\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;\alpha=\frac{a}{R}\; .
$$

Hence from (2)
$$
TR=I\alpha=\frac12MR^{2}\frac{a}{R}=\frac12MR\,a
$$
so that the tension which the string exerts on the disc, and the disc
exerts on the mass, is
$$
T=\frac{M}{2}\,a .
$$

Insert this in (1)
$$
mg-\frac{M}{2}a=m a
$$
$$
mg=a\!\left(m+\frac{M}{2}\right)
$$
i.e. in closed form
$$
a=\frac{mg}{\,m+M/2\,}=\frac{2mg}{2m+M}
      =\frac{g}{1+I/(mR^{2})}\;,
$$
the familiar $a=g/[1+I/mR^{2}]$ result.  For a solid disc $I/mR^{2}=M/2m$.

With $M=4.17\;{\rm kg}$, $R=0.25\;{\rm m}$ and $m=0.53\;{\rm kg}$

$$
m+\frac{M}{2}=0.53+\frac{4.17}{2}=0.53+2.085=2.615\;{\rm kg}
$$

$$
a=\frac{0.53\times 9.81}{2.615}\approx1.9\!-\!2.0\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}
$$

downward, about $1.99\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ with $g=9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$.
In particular

$$
\alpha=\frac{a}{R}\approx\frac{1.99}{0.25}\approx7.9\;{\rm rad/s^{2}}
$$

about the axle, the disc centre remaining at rest.  With $g\approx9.80$
m s$^{-2}$ $a\approx1.99\;{\rm m/s^{2}}\approx2.0\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ downward,
essentially $a\approx g/(1+M/2m)$.  This is the $2mg/(M+2m)$ form often
quoted.

unchanged

$$v_{x}(t)=v_{0x}=8.6\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}} $$

and the vertical motion is that of a free fall from rest in the vertical

$$v_{y}^{2}=v_{0y}^{2}+2g\Delta y\;, \qquad v_{0y}=0 $$

so that on arrival at the ground $\Delta y=h=43.4\;{\rm m}$ below the
point of projection

is the speed acquired in the vertical direction.  In magnitude

$$v_{y}= \sqrt{2\times 9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}\times 43.4\;{\rm m}}

      \approx 2.92\times10^{1}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}} $$

about $29.2\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ downwards.  The instantaneous speed is the
vector sum of the two orthogonal components

$$v=\sqrt{v_{x}^{2}+v_{y}^{2}}

i.e.

$$v=\sqrt{(8.6)^{2}+2(9.81)(43.4)}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}

conserved, the kinetic energy which is left after the impact being turned
into gravitational potential in the swing.

$$

For a reversible Carnot cycle

$$\eta_{Carnot}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}=
\frac{W}{Q_{H}}=
\frac{Q_{H}-Q_{C}}{Q_{H}} $$

with the absolute temperatures

* $T_{H}=521^{\circ}{\rm C}+273\approx 794\;{\rm K}$
* $T_{C}=73^{\circ}{\rm C}+273\approx 346\;{\rm K}$

Hence

$$\eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}
      =1-\frac{346}{794}
      \approx 1-0.436\approx 0.56\!-\!0.57 $$

i.e. about $56\!-\!57\%$ of the heat taken in from the hot
reservoir can be turned into work in the reversible limit.

For a heat input per cycle

$$Q_{H}=4.0\;{\rm kJ}$$

the reversible work per cycle is

$$W_{C}= \eta_{C}\,Q_{H}
      =\left[\,1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}\right]Q_{H}
      \approx 0.564\times 4.0\;{\rm kJ}
      \approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\;{\rm kJ}$$

per cycle.  With $T_{H}=794.15\;{\rm K}$ and $T_{C}=346.15\;{\rm K}$

$$\eta_{C}=1-\frac{346.15}{794.15}=0.564$$
$$W\approx0.564\times4.0\approx2.26\;{\rm kJ}$$

is the Carnot work, $Q_{C}=Q_{H}-W\approx1.74\;{\rm kJ}$ being
rejected to the cold sink.  In round numbers $W\approx2.3\;{\rm kJ}$
per cycle, $\approx 56\%$ of the $4.0\;{\rm kJ}$ taken in from the
hot reservoir.  Using $273\;{\rm K}$ for the Celsius offset this is
often quoted as $W\approx2.25\;{\rm kJ}$ per cycle.

* $v_{s}=36.1\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ toward the observer
* $c=343\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$

so that the effective wave speed in the denominator is

$$c-v_{s}=343-36.1=306.9\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}} .$$

Hence

$$
f_{o}=796\;\frac{343}{306.9}
     =796\;\frac{1}{1-v_{s}/c}
     \approx 796\times1.1176
     \approx 8.9\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}
$$

i.e. about $8.9\!-\!9.0\times10^{2}\,$Hz, an up-shift of $\Delta f\approx
f_{o}-f_{s}\approx 94\;{\rm Hz}$ from the emitted $796\;{\rm Hz}$.

In round numbers

$$f_{o}\approx 8.9\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}\approx 890\;{\rm Hz}$$

about $889\!-\!890\;{\rm Hz}$ on the $343\;{\rm m/s}$ value of $c$, the
usual textbook value $f_{o}\simeq 8.90\times10^{2}\,$Hz.  The shift is
$f_{o}/f_{s}-1=v_{s}/(c-v_{s})\approx 11.8\%$ toward higher frequency.

For a charge moving perpendicular to a uniform $B$ the magnetic Lorentz
force provides the centripetal force

$$F_{c}=F_{B}$$

$$\frac{mv^{2}}{r}=q v B$$

so that the cyclotron radius is

$$r=\frac{mv}{qB}$$

For an $\alpha$ particle

* $m = 6.645\times10^{-27}\ {\rm kg}$
* $q = 2e = 2\times1.602\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}=3.204\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}$
* $v = 2.3\times10^{6}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$
* $B = 1.59\ {\rm T}$

$$ 
mv = 6.645\times10^{-27}\times2.3\times10^{6}
     =1.528\times10^{-20}\ {\rm kg\,m\,s^{-1}}
$$

$$
qB = 3.204\times10^{-19}\times1.59
    =5.09\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C\,T}
$$

Hence

$$
r=\frac{mv}{qB}
  =\frac{1.528\times10^{-20}}{5.094\times10^{-19}}\ {\rm m}
  \approx 3.0\times10^{-2}\ {\rm m}
$$

$$
r\approx 0.030\ {\rm m}\approx 3.0\ {\rm cm}\approx 30\ {\rm mm}
$$

about $3\times10^{-2}\,{\rm m}$ of curvature, i.e. $\approx 29\!-\!30\,{\rm mm}$,
the sense being given by the right hand rule for a positive charge.  With
$e\approx1.60\times10^{-19}\,$C this is $r\approx 3.00\times10^{-2}\,{\rm m}\approx 30.0\,{\rm mm}$, essentially $ \sim 3\,{\rm cm}$ radius.

For a frictionless bank the normal reaction $N$ supplies the centripetal
force and the weight.  With the bank angle $\theta$ measured from the
horizontal

* normal to the surface : $N\cos\theta = mg$
* horizontal component : $N\sin\theta = m v^{2}/r$

Hence

$$
\tan\theta=\frac{N\sin\theta}{N\cos\theta}=\frac{v^{2}/r}{g}
      =\frac{v^{2}}{rg}\;,
$$

the familiar ``no-friction'' banking condition.

$$
v=70\;{\rm km\,h^{-1}}=\frac{70\times10^{3}}{3600}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
   =\frac{175}{9}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}\approx 19.44\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

$$
v^{2}\approx(19.44)^{2}\approx 3.78\times10^{2}\ {\rm m^{2}s^{-2}}
$$

$$
rg = 397\times 9.81\approx 3.89\times10^{3}\ {\rm m^{2}s^{-2}}
$$

$$
\tan\theta =\frac{v^{2}}{rg}\approx
\frac{3.78\times10^{2}}{3.894\times10^{3}}\approx 9.7\times10^{-2}
$$

$$
\theta =\arctan\!\left[\frac{v^{2}}{rg}\right]
       \approx\arctan 0.097\approx 9.7\times10^{-2}\ {\rm rad}
$$

$$
\theta\approx0.097\,{\rm rad}\approx0.097\times\frac{180}{\pi}
      \approx 5.5\!-\!5.6^{\circ}
$$

about $5\!-\!6^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, $ \theta\approx5.5^{\circ}$,
$\tan\theta\approx0.10$, i.e. roughly $5.5^{\circ}$ of bank, $ \approx
5.54^{\circ}$ with the numbers quoted.  This is the angle for which the
required centripetal force is provided by the horizontal component of
the normal reaction alone, so that in the ideal frictionless limit no
side friction is needed.  With $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$ the
conventional value is $\theta\approx5.6^{\circ}$.

For a reversible Carnot cycle

$$ \eta_{Carnot}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}} $$

the temperatures have to be absolute.

* $T_{H}=515^{\circ}{\rm C}=515+273.15\simeq 788\;{\rm K}$
* $T_{C}=39^{\circ}{\rm C}=39+273.15\simeq 312\;{\rm K}$

Hence

$$
\eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}
      =1-\frac{312.15}{788.15}
      =1-0.396\approx 0.604
$$

i.e. about $60$–$61\%$ of the heat taken from the hot source can be
converted into work in the reversible limit.

For a cycle

$$
W = \eta_{C}\,Q_{H}
$$

With $Q_{H}=10.5\;{\rm kJ}$ per cycle

$$
W =0.6039\times 10.5\;{\rm kJ}\approx 6.3\!-\!6.4\;{\rm kJ}
$$

per cycle, about $6.34\;{\rm kJ}$ with $T_{H}=788\;{\rm K}$,
$T_{C}=312\;{\rm K}$.  The heat rejected to the cold sink is

$$
Q_{C}=Q_{H}-W\approx10.5-6.34\approx4.16\;{\rm kJ}
$$

per cycle, in agreement with $Q_{C}/Q_{H}=T_{C}/T_{H}$.
Using the often quoted $T_{H}=788\;{\rm K}$, $T_{C}=312\;{\rm K}$,
$\eta_{C}=476/788=0.604$ and $W\approx0.604\times10.5\approx6.34\;{\rm kJ}$
per cycle, $\approx 6.3\;{\rm kJ}$ in round numbers.

For a source moving with respect to a stationary observer the (non-relativistic)
Doppler shift is

$$f' = f_{0}\,\frac{v}{v\mp v_{s}} $$

the minus sign being used for a source moving towards the observer and the
plus sign for a source moving away.  With $v_{o}=0$

$$f' = f_{0}\,\frac{v}{v-v_{s}} $$

is the observed frequency.  Here

* $f_{0}=605\;{\rm Hz}$ is the proper frequency of the source,
* $v=343\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ is the speed of sound in air,
* $v_{s}=32.1\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ is the speed of the source towards the
observer.

Hence

$$
f' = 605\;{\rm Hz}\;\frac{343}{343-32.1}
     = 605\;{\rm Hz}\;\frac{343}{310.9}
     \approx 6.67\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}
$$

i.e. about $6.6\!-\!6.8\times10^{2}\,$Hz, $\approx 667\;{\rm Hz}$, an
up-shift of $\Delta f\approx 62\;{\rm Hz}$ from the emitted $605\;{\rm Hz}$.
In round numbers $f'\simeq 6.7\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}\approx 668\;{\rm Hz}$,
the familiar blue-shift for an approaching source.  The $667.5\;{\rm Hz}$
value is $605\times343/310.9$.

For a reversible Carnot cycle

$$ \eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}=\frac{W}{Q_{H}} $$

so that

$$W=\,Q_{H}\left[\,1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}\right] $$

on the absolute scale

* $T_{H}=568^{\circ}{\rm C}=568+273\simeq 841\;{\rm K}$
* $T_{C}=22^{\circ}{\rm C}=22+273\simeq 295\;{\rm K}$

Hence

$$
\eta_{C}=1-\frac{295}{841}=1-0.351\approx 0.65
$$

i.e. about $64\!-\!65\%$ of the heat taken from the hot source can be
converted into work in the reversible limit.

With $Q_{H}=2.5\;{\rm kJ}$ per cycle

$$
W_{cyc}= \eta_{C}Q_{H}\approx0.649\,\times 2.5\;{\rm kJ}\approx1.6\!-\!1.7\;{\rm kJ}
$$

per cycle, about $1.62\;{\rm kJ}$ with $T_{H}=841.15\;{\rm K}$,
$T_{C}=295.15\;{\rm K}$,

$$
W\approx2.5\left[1-\frac{295.15}{841.15}\right]\approx1.62\;{\rm kJ}
$$

of which $Q_{C}=Q_{H}-W\approx0.88\;{\rm kJ}$ is rejected to the cold
reservoir.  Using $T_{H}=841\;{\rm K},\;T_{C}=295\;{\rm K}$ this is
$W\approx546/841\times2.5\approx1.62\!-\!1.63\;{\rm kJ}\approx1.6\;{\rm kJ}$
per cycle, the Carnot limit.

For an RC charge from rest

$$V_{C}(t)=V_{0}\Big[\,1-e^{-t/RC}\,\Big]$$

so that the fractional approach to the final value $V_{0}$ is

$$\frac{V_{C}(t)}{V_{0}}=1-e^{-t/RC}$$

The time constant of the circuit is

$$ \tau =RC $$

$$ \tau = 49\times10^{3}\ {\rm \Omega}\times 85\times10^{-6}\ {\rm F}
      =49\times85\times10^{-3}\ {\rm s}=4.165\ {\rm s}$$

Put $V_{C}/V_{0}=0.95$

$$0.95 = 1-e^{-t/\tau}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
e^{-t/\tau}=0.05$$

$$-\frac{t}{\tau}= \ln 0.05 = -\ln 20$$

$$t = \tau\ln 20 = RC\ln\!\left[\frac{1}{1-0.95}\right] $$

i.e. $t = RC\ln 20\approx 3.00\,\tau$.  Numerically

$$t =4.165\;{\rm s}\times\ln 20
   =4.165\times2.9957\;{\rm s}
   \approx 1.25\times10^{1}\ {\rm s}$$

about three time constants.  In the usual $3\tau$ approximation

$$t_{95}\approx 3RC\approx3\times4.17\;{\rm s}\approx12.5\;{\rm s}$$

is the time needed to get to $95.0\%$ of the supply voltage, $V_{0}\big[1-e^{-3}\big]=0.9502\,V_{0}$.  The exact $0.95$ value is $t=RC\ln20\approx12.48\;{\rm s}$ after the switch is closed.

In a ballistic pendulum the (horizontal) linear momentum is essentially
conserved during the very short inelastic impact, the impulse in the
strings being negligible on the time scale of the impact, and the
mechanical energy of the $M+m$ system after the impact is turned into
gravitational potential in the swing.

Let

* $m=26\;{\rm g}=0.026\;{\rm kg}$  bullet
* $M=2.94\;{\rm kg}$  block
* $M_{t}=M+m$  mass after impact
* $h=0.125\;{\rm m}$  rise of the centre of mass

Just after the impact the combined mass $M_{t}$ has the speed $V$ and

$$
\frac12M_{t}V^{2}=M_{t}g\,h
$$

so that the speed with which the pendulum is set in motion is the
usual free-fall speed for a rise $h$,

$$
V=\sqrt{2gh}
$$

independently of the mass.  With $g=9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$

$$
V=\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.125}
  =\sqrt{2.4525}\approx1.57\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

is the speed of the block+bullet immediately after the perfectly
inelastic capture.

Horizontal momentum in the impact

$$
m\,v_{0}=M_{t}V
$$

so that the speed of the bullet just before impact is

$$
v_{0}= \frac{M_{t}}{m}V
     =\left(1+\frac{M}{m}\right)\sqrt{2gh}
$$

$$
v_{0}= \frac{2.94+0.026}{0.026}\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.125}
     \approx 1.14\times10^{2}\times1.57\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
     \approx 1.7\!-\!1.8\times10^{2}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

i.e. about $1.8\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$, $\approx 179\;{\rm m/s}$ on the
$9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ value, $\approx 178\;{\rm m/s}$ with $g\approx9.8$.
The $M/m\approx113$ momentum amplification is the usual ballistic-
pendulum factor.  The $V\approx1.57\;{\rm m/s}$ is the post-impact
pendulum speed that gives the observed $12.5\;{\rm cm}$ rise.

For a body that rolls without slipping the loss of gravitational potential
is shared between translation of the centre of mass and rotation about the
centre of mass

$$ \Delta U = \Delta K_{tr}+\Delta K_{rot}$$

With the zero of potential at the bottom

$$ m g h = \frac12 m v^{2}+\frac12 I\omega^{2} $$

For rolling without slipping

$$ v = \omega r\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \omega = v/r $$

For a solid cylinder about its symmetry axis

$$ I_{cm}= \frac12 m r^{2}$$

so that

$$K_{rot}= \frac12 I\omega^{2}
      =\frac12\left(\frac12 m r^{2}\right)\left(\frac{v}{r}\right)^{2}
      =\frac14 m v^{2} .$$

Hence

$$ m g h = \frac12 m v^{2}+\frac14 m v^{2}
        =\frac34 m v^{2}$$

the mass cancels and

$$v^{2}= \frac{4}{3}\,g h $$

i.e. in general

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1+I/mr^{2}}}
   =\sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1+k^{2}}}$$

with $k^{2}=I/mr^{2}=1/2$ for a solid cylinder.

For $h=4.28\;{\rm m}$

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}g h}
  =\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}\times9.81\times4.28}
  =\sqrt{55.98}\;{\rm m^{2}s^{-2}}$$

$$v\approx 7.4\!-\!7.5\;{\rm m/s}$$

about $7.48\;{\rm m/s}$ down the incline, the corresponding angular
speed being $\omega=v/r$.  This is $\sqrt{4/3}$ times smaller than the
free-fall speed $\sqrt{2gh}\approx 9.18\;{\rm m/s}$ because part of the
loss in $U$ goes into rotational kinetic energy.

In the inelastic impact the linear momentum in the horizontal direction is
conserved, the kinetic energy which is left after the impact being turned
into gravitational potential in the swing.

Let

* $m$ = $28\;{\rm g}=2.8\times10^{-2}\ {\rm kg}$ the bullet,
* $M$ = $2.79\ {\rm kg}$ the block,
* $h=0.180\ {\rm m}$ the rise of the centre of mass of the $(M+m)$ system.

Immediately after the impact

$$m v_{0}=(M+m)v_{1}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
v_{1}= \frac{m}{M+m}v_{0}  $$

is the common horizontal speed of block + bullet.  In the subsequent
free swing

$$\frac12 (M+m)v_{1}^{2}=(M+m)g h $$

so that the speed just after the impact is independent of the masses

$$v_{1}=\sqrt{2gh}$$

and

$$v_{0}= \frac{M+m}{m}\,v_{1}
      =\left(1+\frac{M}{m}\right)\sqrt{2gh}\;.$$

With $g=9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$

$$v_{1}= \sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.180}
      =\sqrt{3.53}\approx1.88\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$$

is the speed of the $(M+m)$ system at the bottom of the swing.  Hence

$$v_{0}= \frac{2.79+0.028}{0.028}\sqrt{2gh}
      \approx 1.0064\times10^{2}\times1.88\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      \approx 1.9\times10^{2}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$$

about $1.9\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$ in the direction of fire.  With the
usual $M\gg m$ approximation $v_{0}\approx(M/m)\sqrt{2gh}\approx
99.6\sqrt{2gh}\approx1.87\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$, i.e. $\approx 190\;{\rm m/s}$,
essentially the $189\;{\rm m/s}$ obtained above.  This is the speed the
bullet must have had just before it struck the pendulum.

For a parallel plate

$$C=\kappa \,\varepsilon_{0}\frac{A}{d}\qquad 
U=\frac12CV^{2}=\frac12\,\kappa\varepsilon_{0}\frac{A}{d}V^{2}$$

is the electrostatic energy on the battery voltage $V$.

* $A=99\;{\rm cm^{2}}=99\times10^{-4}\;{\rm m^{2}}=9.9\times10^{-3}\;{\rm m^{2}}$
* $d=1.35\;{\rm mm}=1.35\times10^{-3}\;{\rm m}$
* $\kappa =6.8$, $V=95\;{\rm V}$

$$
C=\kappa\varepsilon_{0}\frac{A}{d}
   =6.8\,(8.854\times10^{-12})\frac{9.9\times10^{-3}}{1.35\times10^{-3}}
   \approx 4.4\times10^{-10}\ {\rm F}
$$

i.e. $C\approx 4.42\times10^{-10}\ {\rm F}\approx 442\;{\rm pF}$.

Hence

$$
U=\frac12CV^{2}
  =\frac12\,(4.42\times10^{-10}\,{\rm F})(95\,{\rm V})^{2}
  \approx\frac12\,(4.42\times10^{-10})(9.025\times10^{3})\ {\rm J}
$$

$$
U\approx1.99\times10^{-6}\ {\rm J}\approx2.0\;\mu{\rm J}
$$

about $2\;\mu{\rm J}$ of electrostatic energy is stored on the plates, 
$U\approx1.9\!-\!2.0\;\mu{\rm J}$ with the numbers quoted, $\approx1.99\;\mu{\rm J}$ on the $8.854\times10^{-12}\ {\rm F/m}$ value.

For an RC charge from rest

$$V(t)=V_{\infty}\Big[\,1-e^{-t/RC}\,\Big]$$

so that

$$ \frac{V(t)}{V_{\infty}}=1-e^{-t/RC}$$

is the fraction of the final voltage reached at time $t$.
Put $V/V_{\infty}=0.60$

$$0.60 = 1-e^{-t/RC}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
e^{-t/RC}=1-0.60=0.40 $$

$$-\frac{t}{RC}= \ln 0.40\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
t=-RC\,\ln 0.40 = RC\,\ln\frac{1}{0.40}=RC\,\ln 2.5 $$

The $RC$ time constant is

$$ \tau =RC = 60\times10^{3}\ {\rm \Omega}\times 69\times10^{-6}\ {\rm F}
      =4.14\ {\rm s} $$

Hence

$$t = \tau\ln 2.5 =4.14\;{\rm s}\times0.91629\approx 3.7\!-\!3.8\ {\rm s}$$

about $3.8\;{\rm s}$ after the switch is closed, i.e. $\,t\approx
4.14\ln(2.5)\approx3.79\;{\rm s}$ of $RC$ charging.  This is
$t=-\,RC\ln(1-0.60)$ in general.

For a coil the flux linkage is

$$\Lambda(t)=N\Phi(t)=N\,B(t)A\cos\theta$$

with $\theta=0$ for $B\perp$ the plane of the coil.  For a steady change

$$|{\cal E}|=\Bigl|\frac{d\Lambda}{dt}\Bigr|\approx
\frac{\Delta\Lambda}{\Delta t}
      =\frac{N\,A\,\Delta B}{\Delta t}$$

is the magnitude of the emf induced in the $N$ turns.  The current that
can be driven in a resistance $R$ is

$$I=\frac{|{\cal E}|}{R}=\frac{N A\,|\Delta B|}{R\,\Delta t}\;,$$

the sign being given by Lenz's law.

* Area per turn

$$A=111\;{\rm cm^{2}}=111\times10^{-4}\;{\rm m^{2}}=1.11\times10^{-2}\;{\rm m^{2}}$$

* Change of flux density

$$|\Delta B|=|B_{f}-B_{i}|=|0.88-1.16|\;{\rm T}=0.28\;{\rm T}$$

* Flux-linkage change

$$\Delta\Lambda = N A\Delta B
      =59\times0.0111\;{\rm m^{2}}\times0.28\;{\rm T}
      \approx 1.83\times10^{-1}\ {\rm Wb}$$

Hence

$$|{\cal E}|\approx\frac{\Delta\Lambda}{\Delta t}
      =\frac{0.183\;{\rm Wb}}{0.29\;{\rm s}}
      \approx 6.3\times10^{-1}\ {\rm V}$$

about $0.63\;{\rm V}$ emf, tending to keep the original flux.  With
$R=11.1\;\Omega$

$$I=\frac{|{\cal E}|}{R}\approx\frac{0.63\;{\rm V}}{11.1\;\Omega}
   \approx 5\!-\!6\times10^{-2}\ {\rm A}$$

i.e. $\approx 0.057\;{\rm A}\approx 57\;{\rm mA}$ in magnitude.  The
current flows so as to try to maintain the decreasing $B$ field, the
sign being opposite to the sense of the applied field decrease.  In
magnitude

$$I\approx \dfrac{N A| \Delta B|}{R\Delta t}\approx 5.7\times10^{-2}\ {\rm A}$$

about $0.06\;{\rm A}$; $0.056\!-\!0.057\;{\rm A}$ with the numbers quoted
above.  The negative sign in the Faraday expression is the usual Lenz
sign.

For a circular Kepler orbit the centripetal acceleration is provided by
the Newtonian attraction

$$
\frac{v^{2}}{r}=\frac{GM}{r^{2}}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
v=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}\;,
$$

so that with $r$ the geocentric radius

$$
T=\frac{2\pi r}{v}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{GM}}\;,
\qquad \mu\equiv GM ,
$$

is the Kepler period.  For a low earth orbit

$$
r=R_{E}+h
$$

is the distance of the centre of mass of the satellite from the centre
of the Earth.

Here

$$
R_{E}=6371\;{\rm km},\qquad h=1515\;{\rm km}
$$

$$
r=R_{E}+h=6371+1515=7886\;{\rm km}=7.886\times10^{6}\ {\rm m}
$$

and $\mu =GM =3.986\times10^{14}\ {\rm m^{3}s^{-2}}$.  Hence

$$
\frac{r^{3}}{\mu}=
\frac{(7.886\times10^{6}\,{\rm m})^{3}}{3.986\times10^{14}\ {\rm m^{3}s^{-2}}}
      =\frac{4.90\times10^{20}}{3.986\times10^{14}}\ {\rm s^{2}}
      \approx 1.23\times10^{6}\ {\rm s^{2}} ,
$$

$$
\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{\mu}}\approx\sqrt{1.230\times10^{6}}\ {\rm s}
      \approx 1.11\times10^{3}\ {\rm s} .
$$

The Kepler period is therefore

$$
T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{GM}}
  \approx 2\pi\times1.109\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}
  \approx 6.9\!-\!7.0\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}
$$

i.e.

$$
T\approx 6.97\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}\approx
\frac{6.97\times10^{3}}{60}\ {\rm min}\approx 1.16\times10^{2}\ {\rm min}
$$

about $1\;{\rm h}\;56\;{\rm min}$ on the usual $R_{E}=6371\;{\rm km}$
value.  With the numbers quoted this is

$$
T\approx 1.1\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}\times2\pi\approx 7.0\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}
\approx 116\;{\rm min}
$$

the familiar $\sim 115\!-\!120\;{\rm min}$ low-Earth period.  In the
commonly quoted $R_{E}=6378\;{\rm km}$ convention $r=7.893\times10^{6}\,$m
and $T\approx 6.98\times10^{3}\,{\rm s}\approx116.4\,{\rm min}$, essentially
the same result.

For an ideal Atwood the two masses have the same magnitude of acceleration
$a$ and the string is inextensible so that

* $m_{2}>m_{1}$ goes down, $m_{1}$ goes up

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
m_{1}: & T-m_{1}g=m_{1}a\\[2mm]
m_{2}: & m_{2}g-T=m_{2}a
\end{array}
$$

Adding,

$$
(m_{2}-m_{1})g=(m_{1}+m_{2})a
$$

so that on the ideal massless frictionless pulley

$$
a=\frac{m_{2}-m_{1}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\,g
$$

is the common magnitude of the acceleration.  With $m_{1}=1.91\;{\rm kg}$,
$m_{2}=4.11\;{\rm kg}$

$$
a=\frac{4.11-1.91}{4.11+1.91}\,g
  =\frac{2.20}{6.02}\,g\approx0.365\,g\approx3.6\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}
$$

down for the $4.11\;{\rm kg}$ mass and up for the $1.91\;{\rm kg}$ mass.
The string tension follows from either mass, e.g.

$$
T=m_{1}g+m_{1}a=m_{1}\Big[\,g+a\,\Big]
   =m_{2}g-m_{2}a=m_{2}\Big[\,g-a\,\Big]
$$

and in closed form

$$
T=\frac{2m_{1}m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\,g
$$

i.e. the familiar Atwood tension.  Numerically

$$
T=\frac{2(1.91)(4.11)}{1.91+4.11}\;9.81
  =\frac{15.70}{6.02}\;9.81\approx2.56\times10^{1}\ {\rm N}
$$

about $25\!-\!26\;{\rm N}$, $T\approx m_{1}(g+a)\approx m_{2}(g-a)$.
With $g=9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is $T\approx 25.6\;{\rm N}$, essentially
constant while the system is in motion.  The $4.11\;{\rm kg}$ mass
accelerates downwards at $a\approx3.58\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ and the $1.91\;{\rm kg}$
mass accelerates upwards at the same rate.  Using $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$
gives $T\approx25.5\;{\rm N}$ and $a\approx3.58\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$, the usual
text-book numbers.

For the ball + spring the mechanical energy is, to a very good
approximation, conserved while the ball is in contact with the spring.
Put the zero of gravitational potential at the initial, compressed,
position of the ball and let $x_{0}$ be the initial compression.

* Elastic energy initially stored in the spring

$$
U_{e,i}=\frac12k x_{0}^{2}
$$

* Gravitational energy at a height $y$ above the initial position

$$
U_{g}=mgy .
$$

While the ball is still on the spring

$$
\frac12k x_{0}^{2}= \frac12k x^{2}+m g\,(x_{0}-x)+\frac12m v^{2},
\qquad x_{0}>x\ge 0,
$$

where $x$ is the instantaneous compression.  The ball loses contact
with the spring when the normal reaction vanishes, $k x_{s}=mg$, i.e.

$$
x_{s}=\frac{mg}{k}
      =\frac{0.13\times9.81}{403}\approx3.2\times10^{-3}\ {\rm m},
$$

For two like charges the fields can cancel only on the line between them
where the fields are in opposite directions.  Put the origin at $q_{1}$ and
let the point be a distance $x$ towards $q_{2}$ so that

* $r_{1}=x$ , $r_{2}=L-x$ , $L=29\;{\rm cm}$,
* $E_{1}=kq_{1}/r_{1}^{2}$ to the right, $E_{2}=kq_{2}/r_{2}^{2}$ to the left.

On the segment $0<x<L$

$$
E_{net}=0\iff E_{1}=E_{2}
$$

$$
\frac{kq_{1}}{x^{2}}=\frac{kq_{2}}{(L-x)^{2}}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\frac{\sqrt{q_{1}}}{x}=\frac{\sqrt{q_{2}}}{L-x}\; .
$$

Hence

$$
\frac{L-x}{x}=\sqrt{\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}}\;,
\qquad 
\frac{L}{x}=1+\sqrt{\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}}
$$

$$
x=\frac{L}{\,1+\sqrt{q_{2}/q_{1}}\,}
   =L\,\frac{\sqrt{q_{1}}}{\sqrt{q_{1}}+\sqrt{q_{2}}}\;,
$$

the familiar $ \sqrt{q}$  rule.  With

$$
\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}=\frac{8.3}{2.2}=3.77,\qquad
\sqrt{\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}}= \sqrt{3.7727}\approx1.94,
$$

$$
x=\frac{29\;{\rm cm}}{1+1.942}\approx\frac{29}{2.942}\;{\rm cm}
   \approx 9.8\!-\!9.9\;{\rm cm}
$$

from the $2.2\;\mu{\rm C}$ charge toward the $8.3\;\mu{\rm C}$ charge,
i.e. $L-x\approx 29-9.86\approx19.1\;{\rm cm}$ from the $8.3\;\mu{\rm C}$
charge.  The zero is on the segment between the charges, much closer to
the smaller charge, as expected for like charges.  In round numbers
$x\approx 10\;{\rm cm}$ from $q_{1}$, $ \approx 19\;{\rm cm}$ from $q_{2}$.

*Remark:* No zero exists on the exterior of the two-charge system, the
fields being in the same sense to the left of $q_{1}$ and to the right of
$q_{2}$.

For a body that rolls without slipping the loss of gravitational potential
is shared between the translational kinetic energy of the centre of mass
and the rotational kinetic energy about the centre of mass.

$$ \Delta U_{g}=K_{tr}+K_{rot}$$

On the top $K_{tr}=K_{rot}=0$ and on the bottom

$$mgh=\frac12 m v_{cm}^{2}+\frac12 I_{cm}\omega^{2} $$

For rolling without slipping

$$v_{cm}= \omega r\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \omega=\frac{v_{cm}}{r}$$

For a solid cylinder about its central symmetry axis

$$I_{cm}=\frac12 m r^{2}$$

so that

$$K_{rot}= \frac12 I_{cm}\omega^{2}
       =\frac12\left(\frac12mr^{2}\right)\frac{v_{cm}^{2}}{r^{2}}
       =\frac14 m v_{cm}^{2} .$$

Hence

$$mgh=\frac12 m v_{cm}^{2}+\frac14 m v_{cm}^{2}
     =\frac34 m v_{cm}^{2}$$

and the mass cancels,

$$v_{cm}^{2}= \frac{4}{3}gh ,$$

i.e. the familiar rolling result $v_{cm}=\sqrt{4gh/3}$ for a solid
cylinder.  With $h=4.28\;{\rm m}$,

$$v_{cm}= \sqrt{\frac{4}{3}g h}
       =\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}\times 9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}\times4.28\;{\rm m}}
       =\sqrt{55.98\;{\rm m^{2}/s^{2}}}
       \approx 7.4\!-\!7.5\;{\rm m/s}$$

down the incline, about $7.5\;{\rm m/s}$ in magnitude.  The corresponding
angular speed at the bottom is $\omega=v_{cm}/r$.

*Remark:*  With $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ $v_{cm}\approx7.47\;{\rm m/s}$,
essentially the same result.  The $3/4$ factor is the $1/2$ translational
plus $1/4$ rotational partition for a solid cylinder, $I=\tfrac12mr^{2}$.

For an RC charge from zero

$$V_{C}(t)=V_{f}\Big[\,1-e^{-t/RC}\,\Big] \qquad 
V_{f}\equiv V_{s}$$

so that the fractional charge is

$$\frac{V_{C}(t)}{V_{f}}=1-e^{-t/RC}$$

Put $V_{C}/V_{f}=0.95$

$$0.95=1-e^{-t/RC}$$
$$e^{-t/RC}=1-0.95=0.05$$

$$-\frac{t}{RC}=\ln 0.05=-\ln 20$$

$$t=RC\,\ln 20=-RC\ln(0.05)$$

The $RC$ time constant is

$$RC = R\,C = 68\times10^{3}\ {\rm \Omega}\times 11\times10^{-6}\ {\rm F}$$
$$RC = 0.748\ {\rm s}$$

Hence

$$t_{0.95}=0.748\;{\rm s}\;\ln 20$$
$$t_{0.95}=0.748\;{\rm s}\times 2.9957\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\;{\rm s}$$

about three time constants.  With $\ln20\approx3$ this is often quoted as
$t_{0.95}\approx3RC\approx2.24\;{\rm s}$, i.e. $\approx2.24\;{\rm s}$ after the
switch is closed.  The source voltage cancels out, so the result is
independent of $V_{s}$.

*Remark:* $t_{0.99}=RC\ln100\approx4.61\,RC\approx3.45\;{\rm s}$ and the
conventional “$5\tau$” $ \approx 3.74\;{\rm s}$ is essentially full charge.

The elastic energy which is stored in the spring when it is compressed is
converted into kinetic energy of the ball and into gravitational potential
energy of the ball.  With the zero of gravitational potential taken at the
initial, compressed, position of the ball

* Elastic energy initially stored

$$
U_{e,i}=\frac12k\,x_{0}^{2}
$$

is

$$
U_{e,i}= \frac12(588\;{\rm N/m})(0.100\;{\rm m})^{2}
      =\frac12\,588\times10^{-2}\;{\rm J}
      =2.94\;{\rm J}
$$

$U_{e,f}=0$ when the ball is no longer in contact with the spring and
$K_{i}=0$.  With the zero of $U_{g}$ at the initial compressed position

$$
U_{e,i}+U_{g,i}+K_{i}=U_{e,f}+U_{g,f}+K_{f}
$$

and $K_{f}=0$ at the top of the trajectory, $U_{g,i}=0$ and $U_{g,f}=mgh$,
$h$ being the height measured from the initial compressed position, so
that in the idealised loss-free case

$$
\frac12k x_{0}^{2}=mgh
$$

i.e.

$$
h=\frac{kx_{0}^{2}}{2mg}
$$

is the height measured from the initial compressed position.  In
numbers

$$
h=\frac{2.94\;{\rm J}}{0.10\;{\rm kg}\times9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}}
  =\frac{2.94}{0.981}\;{\rm m}\approx 3.0\;{\rm m}
$$

above the initial compressed position.  This is $x_{0}=0.10\;{\rm m}$
above the uncompressed length of the spring.

If $h_{0}$ is measured from the instant the ball loses contact with the
spring, i.e. from the uncompressed length, the $mgx_{0}$ which is used
up in getting the ball up to the natural length has to be taken out
first.  The speed with which the ball leaves the spring is obtained from

$$
\frac12k x_{0}^{2}-mgx_{0}=\frac12mv_{0}^{2},
$$

$$
v_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{kx_{0}^{2}}{m}-2gx_{0}}
     \approx\sqrt{\frac{2\times2.94}{0.10}-2\times9.81\times0.10}
     \approx7.5\;{\rm m/s},

and the free-flight rise above the natural length is

$$
h_{0}=\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{2g}

     \approx\frac{56.84}{19.62}\;{\rm m}\approx2.9\;{\rm m},
$$

so that the total rise from the initial compressed position is
$h=h_{0}+x_{0}\approx2.90+0.10\approx3.0\;{\rm m}$, essentially the

is $h\approx3.00\;{\rm m}$ from the compressed position, $ \approx2.90\;{\rm m}$ of free flight above the uncompressed length of the spring.

For a reversible Carnot cycle

$$\eta_{C}= \frac{W}{Q_{h}}=\frac{Q_{h}-Q_{c}}{Q_{h}}=1-\frac{Q_{c}}{Q_{h}}
      =1-\frac{T_{c}}{T_{h}} $$

on the absolute scale.  The temperatures have to be taken on the
Kelvin scale

* $T_{h}=320^{\circ}{\rm C}=320+273.15\simeq 593\;{\rm K}$
* $T_{c}= 63^{\circ}{\rm C}= 63+273.15\simeq 336\;{\rm K}$

Hence the Carnot thermal efficiency between the two reservoirs is

$$
\eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{c}}{T_{h}}
       =1-\frac{336.15}{593.15}
       =1-\frac{257}{593.15}\approx 0.43\!-\!0.44
$$

i.e. about $43\%$ of the heat taken from the hot source can be turned
into work in the reversible limit.  With the usual $273\;{\rm K}$
conversion

$$
\eta_{C}=1-\frac{336}{593}=\frac{257}{593}\approx0.433
$$

so that for a heat intake per cycle

$$
Q_{h}=6.4\;{\rm kJ}
$$

the reversible work per cycle is

$$
W_{C}= \eta_{C}Q_{h}=Q_{h}\!\left[\,1-\frac{T_{c}}{T_{h}}\right]
$$

$$
W_{C}=6.4\;{\rm kJ}\times\frac{257}{593}\approx2.7\!-\!2.8\;{\rm kJ}
$$

per cycle.  With $T_{h}=593.15\;{\rm K},\;T_{c}=336.15\;{\rm K}$

$$
W_{C}=6.4\left[1-\frac{336.15}{593.15}\right]\approx2.77\;{\rm kJ}
\approx 2.8\;{\rm kJ}
$$

per cycle, the remainder

$$
Q_{c}=Q_{h}-W_{C}\approx6.4-2.77\approx3.6\;{\rm kJ}
$$

being rejected to the $63^{\circ}{\rm C}$ sink.  In the $273\;{\rm K}$
approximation $W_{C}\approx0.433\times6.4\approx2.77\;{\rm kJ}\approx
2.8\;{\rm kJ}$ per cycle, essentially the $43\%$ Carnot limit.

The rise $h$ is

$$

$$

$$

about $1.89\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$ $\approx 190\;{\rm m/s}$ in the

\theta=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{v_{yf}}{v_{xf}}\right)
      =\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{37.1}{7.2}\right)\approx 79^{\circ}
$$

below the horizontal, essentially the free-fall speed $\sqrt{2gh}\approx
37.1\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ with the small $7.2\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ horizontal
component added in quadrature.  This is $\approx 38\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$
in magnitude, $ \sim 37.1\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ vertical and $7.2\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$
horizontal on impact.

For a reversible change

$$w_{rev}=-\int_{V_{1}}^{V_{2}}P_{ext}\,dV=-\int_{V_{1}}^{V_{2}}P\,dV
\qquad{\rm  ideal\;gas}$$

and for an isothermal ideal gas $P V=nRT$ so that

$$w_{rev}= -nRT\int_{V_{1}}^{V_{2}}\frac{dV}{V}
      =-nRT\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}} $$

is the work done on the system in the chemistry sign convention.
The work done by the system is the opposite sign

$$w_{by}=nRT\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}  $$

in magnitude

* $nRT$  

$$
nRT = 2.97\;{\rm mol}\times 8.314\;{\rm J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\times 549\;{\rm K}
     \approx 1.36\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}
$$

* $\displaystyle\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}=\ln\frac{8.4}{3.5}
      =\ln 2.40\approx0.8755$

Hence in magnitude

$$
|w| = nRT\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}
     \approx 1.3556\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}\times0.8755
     \approx 1.2\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}
$$

i.e. about $1.19\!-\!1.20\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}\approx 11.9\;{\rm kJ}$ of
expansion work is obtained from the gas.  In the usual chemistry
sign convention work done by the system is taken as negative,

$$
w_{rev}\approx -\,nRT\ln\!\left(V_{2}/V_{1}\right)\approx
-1.19\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}\approx-11.9\ {\rm kJ}
$$

the minus sign denoting work done by the gas on the surroundings.
The magnitude of the reversible isothermal work is $ \approx 1.19\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}$ of work done by the gas, $ \approx 11.9\;{\rm kJ}$ expansion work.  If the sign is kept with the physics convention $w_{by}=+11.9\;{\rm kJ}$ is the work delivered by the gas.

The component of weight down the plane is $mg\sin\theta$ and the normal
reaction on the plane is $N=mg\cos\theta$ so that the kinetic friction
which opposes the motion is

$$F_{f}=\mu_{k}N=\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta $$

down the plane the resultant force is

$$F_{\parallel}=mg\sin\theta-\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta
      =mg\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]$$

so that with $m$ cancelling

$$a=g\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]$$

is the (constant) acceleration down the chute.  For

* $\theta =42^{\circ}$ , $\sin\theta =0.6691$, $\cos\theta =0.7431$
* $\mu_{k}=0.30$

$$
\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta
 =0.6691-0.30\times0.7431
 =0.4462
$$

$$
a=g\,(0.4462)\approx 9.81\times0.4462\approx 4.4\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}
$$

down the plane.  With $v_{0}=0$ and a constant $a$ over the
distance $s$ down the plane

$$v^{2}=v_{0}^{2}+2as\;,$$

i.e. in energy form

$$ \tfrac12mv^{2}=mg s\sin\theta-W_{f}
      =mg s\sin\theta-\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta\,s
      =mgs\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big] ,$$

so that

$$
v=\sqrt{\,2gs\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]\,}
  =\sqrt{2\,a\,s}\; .
$$

For $s=5.3\;{\rm m}$

$$
v=\sqrt{2\times9.81\times5.3\,
       \big[\sin42^{\circ}-0.30\cos42^{\circ}\big]}
  \approx\sqrt{46.4}\approx 6.8\!-\!6.9\;{\rm m/s}
$$

down the $42^{\circ}$ incline, about $6.8\;{\rm m/s}$ in the direction
of the plane.  In magnitude

$$v\approx\sqrt{2gs\big(\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\big)}\approx
6.8\;{\rm m/s}\approx7\;{\rm m/s}$$

down the ramp, attained in $t=\sqrt{2s/a}\approx1.6\;{\rm s}$.
The $ \approx 4.38\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ acceleration is the net $g\sin\theta-
\mu_{k}g\cos\theta$ down the slope.  With $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$
this is $v\approx6.81\;{\rm m/s}$, essentially the same.

For a source moving with respect to a stationary observer the Doppler
shift for sound in air is

$$f' = f_{0}\,\frac{v}{v\mp v_{s}}$$

the minus sign being used for a source moving toward the observer and
the plus sign for a source moving away.  $v$ is the speed of sound in the
medium and $v_{s}$ the speed of the source relative to the medium.

* $f_{0}=459\;{\rm Hz}$
* $v=343\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$
* $v_{s}=12.3\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ toward the observer

Hence

$$
f' = f_{0}\frac{v}{\,v-v_{s}\,}
     = 459\;\frac{343}{343-12.3}\;{\rm Hz}
$$

$$
v-v_{s}=343-12.3=330.7\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

$$
f' = 459\times\frac{343}{330.7}
    =\frac{157\,437}{330.7}\approx 4.76\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}
$$

$$
f'\approx 4.76\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}\approx 476\;{\rm Hz}
$$

about $17\;{\rm Hz}$ higher than the emitted $459\;{\rm Hz}$.  The
increase is the usual blue-shift for a source approaching the observer.
With the numbers quoted this is $f'\simeq 476\!-\!477\;{\rm Hz}$, 
$\approx 476.1\;{\rm Hz}$ on the $343\;{\rm m/s}$ value.

For a source moving with respect to a stationary observer the wave-fronts are
compressed in front of the source so that

$$f_{o}=f_{s}\;\frac{v}{v\mp v_{s}}$$

the minus sign being used for a source moving towards the observer and
the plus sign for a source moving away from the observer.  $v$ is the
speed of sound in the medium and $v_{s}$ the component of the source
velocity along the line of sight.

For a source approaching

$$f_{o}=f_{s}\frac{v}{v-v_{s}}$$

with

* $f_{s}=723\;{\rm Hz}$
* $v=343\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$
* $v_{s}=23.7\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$

$$
f_{o}=723\;\frac{343}{343-23.7}
     =723\;\frac{343}{319.3}
     \approx 7.23\times10^{2}\times1.074
$$

$$
f_{o}\approx 7.77\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}\approx 7.8\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}
$$

i.e. about $7.7\!-\!7.8\times10^{2}\,$Hz, $\approx 777\;{\rm Hz}$,
an upward shift of $\Delta f\approx 54\;{\rm Hz}$ from the emitted
$723\;{\rm Hz}$.  With the numbers quoted this is $f_{o}\simeq 7.77\times10^{2}\,$Hz, $\approx 776\!-\!777\;{\rm Hz}$ in the usual three-significant-figure rounding.

In the (practically) instantaneous impact the horizontal linear momentum
of the system is conserved, the mechanical energy after the impact being
converted into gravitational potential energy in the swing.

Let

* $m$ = mass of the bullet, $m=29\,{\rm g}=2.9\times10^{-2}\ {\rm kg}$,
* $M$ = mass of the block, $M=3.75\ {\rm kg}$,
* $v_{0}$ = speed of the bullet just before impact,
* $V$ = speed of the $(M+m)$ system just after the impact,
* $h$ = rise of the centre of mass of the $(M+m)$ system.

Impact

$$
p_{i}=p_{f}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
m v_{0}=(M+m)V ,
\tag{1}
$$

the block being at rest before impact.  Hence

$$
V=\frac{m}{M+m}\,v_{0}\; .
$$

Swing

After the perfectly inelastic impact the kinetic energy
$\tfrac12(M+m)V^{2}$ of the combined mass is turned into
gravitational potential energy $(M+m)gh$ at the highest point of the
swing, the tension doing no work.  With the zero of potential at the
lowest point

$$
\frac12(M+m)V^{2}=(M+m)gh ,
$$

so that the speed immediately after impact is the speed which will
raise the mass through $h$,

$$
V=\sqrt{2gh}\;,
$$

independently of the mass.  From (1)

$$
v_{0}=\frac{M+m}{m}\,V
     =\frac{M+m}{m}\sqrt{2gh}
$$

is the speed of the bullet just before it strikes the block.  In the
usual $M\gg m$ approximation $M+m\simeq M$.

For the numbers

$$
V=\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.242}\approx\sqrt{4.748}\approx2.18\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

and

$$
v_{0}= \frac{3.75+0.029}{0.029}\,
\sqrt{2gh}
      \approx 1.30\times10^{2}\times2.179\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      \approx 2.8\!-\!2.9\times10^{2}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}},
$$

i.e. about $2.8\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$ in the centre-of-mass rise.
With $M+m\simeq M$,

$$
v_{0}\simeq\frac{M}{m}\sqrt{2gh}
      =\frac{3.75}{0.029}\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.242}
      \approx 2.82\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}\approx 284\;{\rm m/s},
$$

about $280\!-\!285\;{\rm m/s}$ before impact, the $M+m$ correction being
$\approx 0.8\%$.  This is the familiar ballistic-pendulum result
$v_{0}=(M/m)\sqrt{2gh}$ to the accuracy usually quoted.

For a reversible Carnot cycle

$$\eta_{Carnot}= \frac{W}{Q_{h}}=\frac{Q_{h}-Q_{c}}{Q_{h}}
      =1-\frac{T_{c}}{T_{h}} $$

with the absolute temperatures.

* $T_{h}=568^{\circ}{\rm C}+273\approx 841\;{\rm K}$
* $T_{c}=22^{\circ}{\rm C}+273\approx 295\;{\rm K}$

Hence

$$\eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{c}}{T_{h}}
      =1-\frac{295}{841}
      =\frac{841-295}{841}
      =\frac{546}{841}\approx 0.65$$

i.e. about $65\%$ of the heat taken in from the hot reservoir can in principle be turned into work.

For a heat input per cycle

$$Q_{h}=2.5\;{\rm kJ}$$

the reversible work per cycle is

$$W=\eta_{C}\,Q_{h}
   =\left[1-\frac{T_{c}}{T_{h}}\right]Q_{h}
   \approx0.649\times2.5\;{\rm kJ}\approx1.6\!-\!1.7\;{\rm kJ}$$

about $1.62\;{\rm kJ}$ per cycle.  With $T_{h}=841.15\;{\rm K}$,
$T_{c}=295.15\;{\rm K}$,

$$\eta_{C}=1-295.15/841.15=0.6491$$

$$W\approx0.6491\times2.5\;{\rm kJ}\approx1.62\;{\rm kJ}$$

per cycle, the remainder

$$Q_{c}=Q_{h}-W=Q_{h}\frac{T_{c}}{T_{h}}\approx0.88\;{\rm kJ}$$

being rejected to the $22^{\circ}{\rm C}$ sink.  Using $273\;{\rm K}$ for the Celsius offset gives $W\approx1.62\!-\!1.63\;{\rm kJ}$ per cycle, essentially $\sim1.6\;{\rm kJ}$ of mechanical work per $2.5\;{\rm kJ}$ heat intake.

For a projectile launched and landing at the same height the time of flight
is set by the vertical motion

* $v_{0x}=v_{0}\cos\theta$ , $v_{0y}=v_{0}\sin\theta$

* $v_{y}(t)=v_{0y}-gt$

The projectile is back at $y=0$ when $v_{y}=0$ on the way down

$$0=v_{0y}-g\,t_{up}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;t_{up}=\frac{v_{0y}}{g}$$

so that the total time in the air is

$$T=2t_{up}=2\frac{v_{0y}}{g}=2\frac{v_{0}\sin\theta}{g}$$

The horizontal motion is uniform

$$x(t)=v_{0x}t=v_{0}\cos\theta\,t$$

Hence the range on level ground is

$$R=v_{0}\cos\theta\,T
   =v_{0}\cos\theta\,\frac{2v_{0}\sin\theta}{g}
   =\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{g}\sin2\theta  $$

For $v_{0}=23.3\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ and $\theta=55^{\circ}$

* $v_{0x}=23.3\cos55^{\circ}=23.3\times0.5736\approx13.4\;{\rm m/s}$
* $v_{0y}=23.3\sin55^{\circ}=23.3\times0.8192\approx19.1\;{\rm m/s}$

$$t_{up}=\frac{19.08}{9.81}\approx1.94\;{\rm s},\qquad 
T\approx3.89\;{\rm s}$$

$$R\approx v_{0x}T\approx13.37\times3.886\approx5.2\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}$$

i.e. about $52\;{\rm m}$ down range from the launch point, 
$R=v_{0}^{2}\sin110^{\circ}/g\approx 52.0\;{\rm m}$ on the $g=9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ 
level-ground idealisation.  With $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is $\approx52.1\;{\rm m}$.

In a ballistic pendulum the (practically) instantaneous impact is
inelastic in the horizontal direction and the motion after the impact is
conservative.

Let

* $m=15\;{\rm g}=1.5\times10^{-2}\ {\rm kg}$ the bullet,
* $M=1.93\;{\rm kg}$ the block,
* $M_{t}=M+m$ the mass which moves after the impact,
* $v_{0}$ the speed of the bullet just before impact,
* $V$ the common speed of block+bullet immediately after the impact,
* $h=10.8\;{\rm cm}=0.108\;{\rm m}$ the rise of the centre of mass.

Horizontal linear momentum is conserved in the impact, the block being
at rest before the shot,

$$m v_{0}=M_{t}V\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
v_{0}=\frac{M_{t}}{m}V\tag{1}$$

After the impact the kinetic energy of the $M_{t}$ system is converted
into gravitational potential energy in the swing.  With the zero of
potential at the lowest point

$$\frac12M_{t}V^{2}=M_{t}g\,h $$

so that the speed immediately after the impact is independent of the
mass

$$V=\sqrt{2gh}$$

in the idealised point-mass swing.  Numerically

$$V=\sqrt{2\times9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}\times0.108\;{\rm m}}
   =\sqrt{2.119}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}\approx1.46\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$$

is the speed of the combined block+bullet at the bottom of the swing.
From (1)

$$v_{0}= \frac{M+m}{m}\sqrt{2gh}$$

is the speed of the bullet just before it strikes the block.  With
$M_{t}=1.93+0.015=1.945\;{\rm kg}$

$$v_{0}= \frac{1.945}{0.015}\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.108}
      \approx 1.2967\times10^{2}\times1.456\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      \approx 1.9\times10^{2}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}} ,$$

i.e. about $1.9\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$ in the horizontal direction.
With the usual $M\approx1.93\;{\rm kg}$ for the post-impact kinetic
energy this is

$$v_{0}\approx\frac{M}{m}\sqrt{2gh}\approx
\frac{1.93}{0.015}\times1.46\approx1.87\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}\approx
188\!-\!190\;{\rm m/s},$$

about $189\;{\rm m/s}$ for $g=9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$, essentially the
$ \sim 190\;{\rm m/s}$ normally quoted for the ballistic-pendulum
experiment.  The $m\ll M$ approximation $v_{0}\simeq(M/m)\sqrt{2gh}$
is the one normally used.

In the ideal frictionless SHM the mechanical energy is conserved

$$E =U_{el}+K=\frac12k x^{2}+\frac12 m v^{2}= {\rm const}$$

so that with the turning point $x=A$, $v=0$,

$$E=\frac12kA^{2}$$

and at a general displacement $x$

$$\frac12kA^{2}= \frac12k x^{2}+\frac12 m v^{2}$$

i.e.

$$v(x)=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}\Big(A^{2}-x^{2}\Big)}
      =\omega\sqrt{A^{2}-x^{2}},\qquad 
\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$$

is the speed at the displacement $x$.  In magnitude

* $A=10.4\;{\rm cm}=0.104\;{\rm m}$
* $x=6.4\;{\rm cm}=0.064\;{\rm m}$
* $\displaystyle\omega=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}=\sqrt{\frac{44}{1.80}}\approx4.94\;{\rm rad\,s^{-1}}$

Hence

$$
v=\sqrt{\frac{44}{1.80}\Big[\,0.104^{2}-0.064^{2}\Big]}
  =\sqrt{\frac{44}{1.80}\times0.00672}
  \approx\sqrt{0.164}\approx0.40\!-\!0.41\;{\rm m/s}
$$

toward the equilibrium position.  The maximum speed at the
equilibrium point would be $v_{\max}= \omega A\approx0.51\;{\rm m/s}$.

The kinetic energy at $x=6.4\;{\rm cm}$ is
$K=\tfrac12k(A^{2}-x^{2})\approx0.148\;{\rm J}$, the remainder
$U=\tfrac12k x^{2}\approx0.090\;{\rm J}$ being stored as elastic
potential.  The sign is reversed on the way out, the magnitude being
the same.

For a reversible change the external pressure is at every instant the
equilibrium pressure of the gas

$$P_{ext}=P=\frac{nRT}{V}$$

so that for an infinitesimal change

$$ \delta w_{rev}= -P_{ext}\,dV=-P\,dV=-\frac{nRT}{V}\,dV $$

is the work done on the system in the IUPAC sign convention.  For an
isothermal change $T={\rm const}$,

$$w_{rev}= -\int_{V_{1}}^{V_{2}}P\,dV
      =-nRT\int_{V_{1}}^{V_{2}}\frac{dV}{V}
      =-nRT\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}  $$

is the work done on the gas, the work done by the gas on the
surroundings being $w_{by}=-w_{rev}$.

In the present case

* $n=0.64\;{\rm mol}$,
* $T=538\;{\rm K}$,
* $V_{1}=4.1\;{\rm L}$, $V_{2}=19.1\;{\rm L}$,

$$nRT =0.64\times 8.314\;{\rm J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\times 538\;{\rm K}
      \approx 2.86\times10^{3}\ {\rm J}$$

and

$$\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}=\ln\frac{19.1}{4.1}
      =\ln 4.66\approx 1.54\;.$$

Hence on the chemist's sign convention

$$w_{rev}= -nRT\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}
       \approx -\,2.86\times10^{3}\times1.539\;{\rm J}
       \approx -4.4\times10^{3}\ {\rm J}$$

i.e. about $4.4\;{\rm kJ}$ of work is done by the system on the
surroundings.  In the physics sign convention, work done by the gas,

$$w_{by}=-w_{rev}=nRT\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}\approx
+4.4\times10^{3}\ {\rm J}\approx 4.40\;{\rm kJ}$$

of expansion work is obtained, the negative sign in the
$w_{rev}=-nRT\ln(V_{2}/V_{1})$ expression being the usual chemical
thermodynamics sign in which work done by the system is negative.
The magnitude of the reversible isothermal work is $|\,w\,|\approx
4.3\!-\!4.5\times10^{3}\ {\rm J}$, about $4.4\;{\rm kJ}$ of work done
by the gas on the surroundings, $w_{rev}\approx-4.4\;{\rm kJ}$ in the
IUPAC convention.

The speed at the instant the obstacle is seen is

$$v_{0}=50\;{\rm km\,h^{-1}}=\frac{50\times10^{3}}{3600}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      =\frac{125}{9}\approx 13.9\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}} $$

During the (unbraked) reaction time $t_{r}$ the car continues at $v_{0}$

$$s_{r}=v_{0}t_{r}\approx 13.89\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}\times0.72\;{\rm s}

in fact $s_{r}= \dfrac{125}{9}\times0.72=10.0\;{\rm m}$.

$v^{2}=v_{0}^{2}+2as$, $v=0$,

$$s_{b}=\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{2a}
     =\frac{\left(125/9\right)^{2}}{2\times5.2}
     =\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{10.4}\approx

about $18.5\!-\!18.6\;{\rm m}$ of braking.

Hence from the instant the obstacle is seen

$$s_{\rm tot}=s_{r}+s_{b}\approx 10.0\;{\rm m}+18.5\;{\rm m}
