For a roll without slipping the loss of gravitational potential is
taken up in translational and rotational kinetic energy

$$ \Delta U = \Delta K_{t}+\Delta K_{r}$$

$$m g h = \frac12 m v^{2}+\frac12 I\omega^{2}$$

For a solid sphere

$$I=\frac25 m r^{2}\qquad {\rm and}\qquad \omega=\frac{v}{r}$$

for rolling without slipping, so that

$$K_{r}= \frac12 I\omega^{2}
      =\frac12\frac25 m r^{2}\frac{v^{2}}{r^{2}}
      =\frac15 m v^{2}$$

Hence

$$m g h = \frac12 m v^{2}+\frac15 m v^{2}
       =\frac{7}{10}m v^{2}$$

the mass cancels and

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{10}{7}g h}$$

is the speed that depends only on the vertical drop $h$, not on the
shape of the ramp.  With $h=1.82\;{\rm m}$

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{10}{7}\times 9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}\times1.82\;{\rm m}}
  =\sqrt{\frac{10}{7}\times17.85\;{\rm m^{2}/s^{2}}}
  =\sqrt{25.5\;{\rm m^{2}/s^{2}}}\approx 5.0\!-\!5.1\;{\rm m/s}$$

about $5.05\;{\rm m/s}$ down the ramp, $ \approx 5.0\;{\rm m/s}$ with
$g\approx9.8\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$.  The translational part is $\tfrac12mv^{2}$
and the rotational part is $\tfrac15mv^{2}$, i.e. $2/7$ of the total
kinetic energy is rotational, $5/7$ translational.  In terms of an
effective acceleration $a=\dfrac{g}{1+I/mr^{2}}\sin\theta
=\tfrac57g\sin\theta$ the same result is $v^{2}=2a s$ with $s\sin\theta=h$.

For a source moving with respect to a stationary observer the wave-fronts are
compressed in front of the source

$$f' = f_{0}\,\frac{v}{v\mp v_{s}} $$

the minus sign being for a source moving towards the observer and the
plus sign for a source moving away.  With $v_{s}<v$

* $f_{0}=815\;{\rm Hz}$  emitted frequency
* $v=343\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$  speed of sound in air
* $v_{s}=31.5\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$  speed of the source towards the observer

$$f' = f_{0}\frac{v}{\,v-v_{s}\,}$$

is the frequency actually received.  Hence

$$
f' = 815\;\frac{343}{343-31.5}
     =815\;\frac{343}{311.5}
     \approx 8.97\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}
$$

i.e. about $9.0\times10^{2}\,$Hz, an up-shift of $\approx 82\,$Hz from the
emitted $815\,$Hz.  In round numbers

$$f'\approx 8.9\!-\!9.0\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}\approx 897\;{\rm Hz}$$

about $897\!-\!898\,$Hz, the familiar blue-shift of the Doppler effect for
a source approaching the observer.  Using $f' = 815\times343/311.5$ gives
$f'\simeq 897.4\,$Hz.

The component of the weight down the plane is $mg\sin\theta$ and the
kinetic friction opposing the motion is

$$F_{k}=\mu_{k}N=\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta $$

so that the net force down the plane is

$$F_{\parallel}=mg\sin\theta-\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta
      =mg\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big] $$

and the (constant) acceleration down the plane is

$$a=\frac{F_{\parallel}}{m}=g\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big] .$$

For $\theta =44^{\circ}$

$$\sin\theta =0.6947\qquad \cos\theta =0.7193$$

$$\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta
      =0.6947-0.26\times0.7193
      =0.6947-0.1870\approx0.508 $$

Hence

$$a\approx g\,(0.508)\approx 9.81\times0.508\approx 4.9\!-\!5.0\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$$

down the incline.  With $u=0$ and $s=4.5\;{\rm m}$

$$v^{2}=u^{2}+2as=2gs\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big] $$

i.e. from work–energy

$$\Delta K =W_{g}+W_{f}=mg s\sin\theta-\mu_{k}mg s\cos\theta
       =\tfrac12 m v^{2},$$

so that

$$v=\sqrt{\,2gs\big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\big]\,}
   =\sqrt{2(9.81)(4.5)(0.5076)}\approx\sqrt{44.8}\approx6.7\;{\rm m/s}$$

down the plane, about $6.6\!-\!6.8\;{\rm m/s}$ with the usual
rounding.  In magnitude

$$v\approx 6.7\;{\rm m/s}$$

down the $44^{\circ}$ incline, the direction being $44^{\circ}$ below
the horizontal.  With $a\approx4.98\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is $v=\sqrt{2as}$,
$ \approx 6.69\;{\rm m/s}$ for the quoted $g$.

The motion is the sum of a uniform motion during the reaction time and a
uniformly decelerated motion after the brakes are applied.

* Speed at the instant the obstacle is seen

$$
v_{0}=90\;{\rm km\,h^{-1}}=\frac{90\times10^{3}}{3600}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      =25.0\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

Reaction

During $t_{r}$ the speed is still $v_{0}$ so that, with the usual
$s=v_{0}t$,

$$
s_{r}=v_{0}t_{r}
$$

is the distance covered before the brakes become effective.  With
$t_{r}=0.97\;{\rm s}$

$$
s_{r}=25.0\times0.97\approx 2.43\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}
$$

is the reaction distance.

Braking

After the brakes are on $a=-a_{b}$ with $a_{b}=5.3\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$ is
constant.  For $v_{f}=0$

$$
v_{f}^{2}=v_{0}^{2}+2a s_{b}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
0=v_{0}^{2}-2a_{b}s_{b}
$$

so that

$$
s_{b}=\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{2a_{b}}
$$

is the distance covered while braking.  In time

$$
t_{b}=\frac{v_{0}}{a_{b}}=\frac{25.0}{5.3}\approx4.72\;{\rm s}
$$

the mean speed during braking is $(v_{0}+0)/2$, i.e. $s_{b}=v_{0}t_{b}/2$,
as above.

$$
s_{b}= \frac{(25.0)^{2}}{2\times5.3}
     =\frac{625}{10.6}\approx 5.90\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}\approx 59\;{\rm m}
$$

Hence from the instant the obstacle is first seen

$$
s_{\rm tot}=s_{r}+s_{b}=v_{0}t_{r}+\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{2a_{b}}
$$

$$
s_{\rm tot}=25.0(0.97)+\frac{25.0^{2}}{2\times5.3}
          \approx 24.3\;{\rm m}+59.0\;{\rm m}
          \approx 8.3\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}
$$

about $83\!-\!84\;{\rm m}$ of travel, $ \approx 24\;{\rm m}$ of which is
covered in the $0.97\;{\rm s}$ reaction time and $\approx 59\;{\rm m}$
under braking.  The total time to rest is $t_{r}+t_{b}\approx0.97+4.72\approx5.7\;{\rm s}$.

*Remark:*  With the quoted two-significant-figure data the result is
commonly quoted as $s_{\rm tot}\simeq 8.3\times10^{1}\,{\rm m}\approx83\,{\rm m}$,
$83.2\;{\rm m}$ with the numbers as given.

For a series $R-C$ charging circuit

$$V_{s}=iR+V_{C}\qquad i=C\frac{dV_{C}}{dt}$$

so that on the capacitor

$$RC\frac{dV_{C}}{dt}+V_{C}=V_{s}\;,$$

with $V_{C}(0)=V_{0}$.  The linear equation is

$$\frac{dV_{C}}{dt}+\frac{1}{RC}V_{C}=\frac{V_{s}}{RC}$$

and with the integrating factor $e^{t/RC}$

$$V_{C}(t)=V_{s}+\Big[V_{0}-V_{s}\Big]e^{-t/RC}\;.$$

For an initially uncharged capacitor $V_{0}=0$

$$V_{C}(t)=V_{s}\Big[\,1-e^{-t/RC}\,\Big] ,$$

so that the normalised charge is

$$\frac{V_{C}(t)}{V_{s}}=1-e^{-t/RC} .$$

The $R C$ time constant is

$$\tau =RC=(83\times10^{3}\,\Omega)(51\times10^{-6}\,{\rm F})
      =4.233\;{\rm s}$$

and

$$\frac{V_{C}}{V_{s}}=0.90=1-e^{-t/\tau}$$

gives

$$e^{-t/\tau}=0.10\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
t=-\tau\ln 0.10=\tau\ln 10 .$$

Hence in terms of the time constant

$$t_{0.9}=RC\ln 10\approx2.303\,\tau $$

and numerically

$$t_{0.9}=4.233\,\ln10\;{\rm s}\approx 9.7\!-\!9.8\;{\rm s}\approx 10\;{\rm s}$$

about $2.30$ time constants.  With $\tau=4.23\;{\rm s}$ this is
$t_{0.9}\simeq 9.75\;{\rm s}$ for the $90\%$ point, the familiar
$1-e^{-t/RC}$ charging law.  The $63.2\%$ point is $t=\tau=4.23\;{\rm s}$,
etc.

The induced emf in a coil is Faraday's law

$$\mathcal E = -N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}=-N A\frac{dB}{dt}$$

for a field normal to the plane of the coil.  For a steady change

$$\left|\mathcal E\right| = N A\frac{|\Delta B|}{\Delta t}$$

is the magnitude of the emf and

$$I=\frac{|\mathcal E|}{R}$$

is the magnitude of the current in the resistance $R$.

* $N = 351$
* $A = 44\;{\rm cm^{2}} = 44\times10^{-4}\;{\rm m^{2}} = 4.4\times10^{-3}\;{\rm m^{2}}$
* $\Delta B = B_{2}-B_{1}=1.44-0.59 = 0.85\;{\rm T}$
* $\Delta t =0.09\;{\rm s}$
* $R = 16.4\;\Omega$

$$ 
N A = 351\times4.4\times10^{-3}\;{\rm m^{2}} = 1.5444\;{\rm m^{2}}
$$

$$
|\mathcal E| = \frac{N A |\Delta B|}{\Delta t}
          =\frac{1.5444\times0.85}{0.09}\;{\rm V}
          \approx 1.46\times10^{1}\ {\rm V}\approx 14.6\;{\rm V}
$$

Hence

$$
I=\frac{|\mathcal E|}{R}= \frac{N A |\Delta B|}{R\,\Delta t}
  =\frac{351\,(4.4\times10^{-3})\,(0.85)}{16.4\times0.09}
  \approx 8.9\times10^{-1}\ {\rm A}
$$

i.e. about $0.9\;{\rm A}$ of induced current, $\approx 0.89\;{\rm A}$ in magnitude, the sign being given by Lenz's law.  The emf is $\approx 14.6\;{\rm V}$.

*Remark:* $|\mathcal E| = N A \Delta B/\Delta t$ is the usual form; with the numbers quoted the current is $\sim 0.89\;{\rm A}$, essentially $0.9\;{\rm A}$.

In the (essentially) horizontal impact the external impulse of the floor
is negligible on the time scale of the impact so that the horizontal
linear momentum of the two blocks is conserved.

* Before impact

$$
p_{i}=m_{1}v_{1}+m_{2}0=m_{1}v_{1}
$$

$$
p_{i}=2.68\times 3.70=9.92\;{\rm kg\,m/s}
$$

* After the perfectly inelastic impact

$$
M=m_{1}+m_{2}=2.68+4.96=7.64\;{\rm kg}
$$

$$
p_{f}=Mv_{f}=p_{i}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
v_{f}=\frac{m_{1}v_{1}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}
$$

$$
v_{f}= \frac{2.68\times3.70}{7.64}\approx 1.30\;{\rm m/s}
$$

in the direction of the incident block.  The kinetic energy just after
impact is

$$
K_{f}=\tfrac12 Mv_{f}^{2}
      =\tfrac12\frac{(m_{1}v_{1})^{2}}{M}\approx
      6.4\;{\rm J}
$$

which is the mechanical energy that has to be dissipated by sliding
friction.

For sliding on a horizontal floor

$$
F_{\rm fr}= \mu_{k}N=\mu_{k}Mg
$$

so that the (constant) deceleration of the stuck-together mass is

$$
a=\frac{F_{\rm fr}}{M}= \mu_{k}g
$$

and with $v_{0}=v_{f}$ and $v=0$

$$
0=v_{f}^{2}-2a s\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
s=\frac{v_{f}^{2}}{2a}=\frac{v_{f}^{2}}{2\mu_{k}g}
   =\frac{1}{2\mu_{k}g}\left[\frac{m_{1}v_{1}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\right]^{2}.
$$

With $\mu_{k}=0.25$ and $g=9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$

$$
s=\frac{(1.30)^{2}}{2\times0.25\times9.81}
  \approx\frac{1.68}{4.91}\approx 0.34\;{\rm m}
$$

about $3\!-\!4\times10^{1}\,{\rm cm}$ of sliding after the impact.
In energy form $W_{\rm fr}= \mu_{k}Mg\,s=K_{f}$, i.e.

$$
s=\frac{K_{f}}{\mu_{k}Mg}
  =\frac{\tfrac12Mv_{f}^{2}}{\mu_{k}Mg}\approx0.34\!-\!0.35\;{\rm m},
$$

$\approx 0.34\;{\rm m}$ with the numbers quoted, $\approx 0.34\;{\rm m}$
$\approx 34\;{\rm cm}$ of post-collision travel.  Using $g\approx9.8\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is $s\approx0.34\!-\!0.35\;{\rm m}$, essentially $0.34\;{\rm m}$ of slide after they stick together.

In the inelastic impact the linear momentum of the bullet–block system is
conserved, the kinetic energy which remains after the impact being
converted into gravitational potential energy in the subsequent swing.

Let

* $m$ = mass of the bullet $=26\;{\rm g}=2.6\times10^{-2}\ {\rm kg}$
* $M$ = mass of the block $=2.94\ {\rm kg}$
* $M_{t}=M+m$ the mass after impact
* $v_{0}$ the speed of the bullet just before impact
* $v_{1}$ the common speed of the block+bullet immediately after impact
* $h=0.125\;{\rm m}$ the rise of the centre of mass

Momentum, block initially at rest,

$$m v_{0}=M_{t}v_{1}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
v_{1}= \frac{m}{M_{t}}\,v_{0}  $$

After the impact the kinetic energy $ \tfrac12M_{t}v_{1}^{2}$ is turned
into $M_{t}gh$ at the top of the swing,

$$\frac12M_{t}v_{1}^{2}=M_{t}gh $$

so that the speed immediately after impact is independent of the masses

$$v_{1}=\sqrt{2gh}\;,$$

the familiar pendulum rise.  With $g=9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$

$$v_{1}= \sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.125}
      =\sqrt{2.4525}\approx1.57\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}} $$

is the speed of the $M_{t}$ system just after the bullet is embedded.
Eliminating $v_{1}$,

$$v_{0}= \frac{M_{t}}{m}\,v_{1}
      =\frac{M+m}{m}\sqrt{2gh}\;,$$

i.e. the bullet speed is amplified by the mass ratio $M_{t}/m$.

$$ \frac{M_{t}}{m}= \frac{2.94+0.026}{0.026}
      =\frac{2.966}{0.026}\approx1.14\times10^{2} $$

Hence

$$v_{0}\approx 1.14\times10^{2}\times\sqrt{2gh}
      \approx 1.14\times10^{2}\times1.566\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      \approx 1.8\!-\!1.9\times10^{2}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}},$$

about $1.79\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$ in the usual $M_{t}/m$ form.  With
the numbers quoted

$$v_{0}\simeq\frac{2.966}{0.026}\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.125}
      \approx 1.79\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}\approx 179\;{\rm m/s}$$

just before impact, $\approx 178\!-\!180\;{\rm m/s}$ depending on the
rounding of $g$ and $h$.  In the often used $M/m$ approximation
$v_{0}\approx(M/m)\sqrt{2gh}\approx1.77\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$, essentially
the same result.  This is the speed which, after the perfectly inelastic
collision, leaves the combined $M+m$ mass with $v_{1}=\sqrt{2gh}\approx1.57\;{\rm m/s}$ and a rise $h=12.5\;{\rm cm}$.

For a string that is tied at both ends the standing wave condition is

* $\lambda_{n}=2L/n$  $n=1,2,\dots$
* $v=\sqrt{T/\mu}$ is the transverse wave speed on the string

so that

$$
f_{n}=\frac{v}{\lambda_{n}}=\frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}\;,
\qquad 
f_{1}=\frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}
$$

is the normal mode frequency.  With

* $T=69\;{\rm N}$
* $\mu =2.9\;{\rm g\,m^{-1}}=2.9\times10^{-3}\;{\rm kg\,m^{-1}}$
* $L=0.57\;{\rm m}$

the wave speed is

$$
v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}
   =\sqrt{\frac{69}{2.9\times10^{-3}}}
   =\sqrt{2.38\times10^{4}}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
   \approx 1.54\times10^{2}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}} ,
$$

and for the $n=1$ mode $\lambda_{1}=2L$

$$
f_{1}= \frac{v}{2L}
     =\frac{1}{2\times0.57}\sqrt{\frac{69}{2.9\times10^{-3}}}
     \approx\frac{1.54\times10^{2}}{1.14}\ {\rm Hz}
     \approx 1.3\!-\!1.4\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}
$$

about $1.35\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}$, i.e. $\approx 135\;{\rm Hz}$ for the
fundamental.  The $n^{\rm th}$ harmonic is $f_{n}=n f_{1}$.

*Remark:* $v\approx154\;{\rm m/s}$ is the speed of transverse waves on the
string under the quoted tension and linear mass density.  This is the
usual $f_{1}=v/2L$ result for a string fixed at both ends.

For an ideal Atwood the two masses have the same magnitude of
acceleration $a$ and the same string tension $T$.

Put the heavy mass $m_{1}=3.01\;{\rm kg}$ down positive and the light
mass $m_{2}=1.60\;{\rm kg}$ up positive.

* $m_{1}$ : $m_{1}g-T=m_{1}a$
* $m_{2}$ : $T-m_{2}g=m_{2}a$

Hence

$$
a=\frac{m_{1}-m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\,g
$$

and eliminating $a$

$$
T=m_{1}g-m_{1}a=m_{2}g+m_{2}a
     =\frac{2m_{1}m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\,g .
$$

On the numbers

$$
a=\frac{3.01-1.60}{3.01+1.60}\;9.81
  =\frac{1.41}{4.61}\;9.81\approx 3.0\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}
$$

downwards for the $3.01\;{\rm kg}$ mass and upwards for the $1.60\;{\rm kg}$
mass.  The common string tension is then

$$
T=m_{2}(g+a)=m_{1}(g-a)
  =\frac{2(3.01)(1.60)}{3.01+1.60}\;9.81
  =\frac{9.632\times9.81}{4.61}\;{\rm N}
  \approx 2.0\!-\!2.1\times10^{1}\ {\rm N}
$$

i.e. about $20\!-\!21\;{\rm N}$, $T\approx 20.5\;{\rm N}$ on the
$9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$ value, $T=m_{1}(g-a)\approx3.01(9.81-3.00)\approx
20.5\;{\rm N}$.  In the often quoted $g\approx9.8\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$ form
$T\approx20.4\;{\rm N}$, essentially $ \sim 20\;{\rm N}$ of string pull,
with the $3.01\;{\rm kg}$ mass accelerating down at $\approx3.0\;{\rm
m\,s^{-2}}$.  This is the familiar $T=2m_{1}m_{2}g/(m_{1}+m_{2})$ Atwood
result.

For a charge moving perpendicular to a uniform $B$ the magnetic Lorentz
force

$$F_{B}=q v B$$

provides the centripetal force

$$F_{c}= \frac{mv^{2}}{r}$$

so that on the circular orbit

$$q v B = \frac{mv^{2}}{r}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
r=\frac{mv}{qB}$$

is the Larmor / cyclotron radius.  In SI

* $m_{p}=1.673\times10^{-27}\ {\rm kg}$
* $q_{p}=1.602\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}$
* $v=9.0\times10^{6}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$
* $B=1.53\ {\rm T}$

Hence

$$
r=\frac{m_{p}v}{q_{p}B}
  =\frac{\,1.673\times10^{-27}\ {\rm kg}\times9.0\times10^{6}\ {\rm m/s}\,}
         {\,1.602\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}\times1.53\ {\rm T}\,}
  =\frac{1.51\times10^{-20}}{2.45\times10^{-19}}\ {\rm m}
  \approx 6.1\times10^{-2}\ {\rm m}
$$

i.e. about $6$ cm of curvature.  In millimetres

$$
r\approx 0.061\;{\rm m}\approx 6.1\times10^{1}\ {\rm mm}\approx 61\!-\!62\;{\rm mm}
$$

about $6.1\,{\rm cm}$ radius, the sense being such that the proton
circulates with the $q>0$ right-hand rule about the field lines.  With
the usual $m_{p}=1.67\times10^{-27}\,$kg this is $r\approx 6.13\times10^{-2}\,$m $\approx 61.3\,$mm, essentially the $ \sim 61\,$mm quoted in the text.

For the motion up to the instant at which the mass loses contact with the
spring you can put the zero of gravitational potential at the release
point $y=0$ and put the zero of elastic potential at the natural length
of the spring.  With the usual textbook idealisation that the mass stays
on the spring up to the natural length

* $E_{i}$ :  $U_{e,i}+U_{g,i}+T_{i}$

$$
E_{i}= \frac12k x_{0}^{2}+0+0
$$

* $E_{f}$ :  $U_{e,f}=0$, $T_{f}=0$ at the top of the flight and
$U_{g,f}=mgH$ measured from the release point $y=0$,

$$
E_{f}=mgH .
$$

Hence, on the idealised $U_{e}\to U_{g}$ conversion

$$
\frac12k x_{0}^{2}=mgH\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
H=\frac{kx_{0}^{2}}{2mg}
$$

is the height measured from the release, i.e. from the $x_{0}=6.4\,{\rm
cm}$ compressed position, to the top of the free flight.  With

* $k=1.072\times10^{3}\ {\rm N\,m^{-1}}$,
* $x_{0}=6.4\times10^{-2}\ {\rm m}$,
* $m=0.32\ {\rm kg}$,

$$
U_{e,i}= \tfrac12k x_{0}^{2}
      =\tfrac12(1072)(0.064)^{2}\approx2.20\ {\rm J}
$$

and

$$
H_{\rm rel}\approx\frac{2.20}{mg}
      =\frac{1072(0.064)^{2}}{2(0.32)(9.81)}
      \approx 6.9\!-\!7.0\times10^{-1}\ {\rm m}
$$

above the point of release, about $0.70\;{\rm m}$ of free rise.  In
particular

$$
H_{\rm rel}\simeq0.70\;{\rm m}\approx 70\;{\rm cm}
$$

above the compressed release position.  The natural length of the
spring is $x_{0}=6.4\,{\rm cm}$ above the release point, so the height
above the uncompressed spring is

$$
H_{0}=H_{\rm rel}-x_{0}\approx0.70-0.064\approx0.64\;{\rm m}
$$

above the spring’s natural length, $\approx 0.63\!-\!0.64\,{\rm m}$ in
the more exact treatment in which the mass actually loses contact when
the normal reaction vanishes, $x_{s}=mg/k\approx2.9\,{\rm mm}$, 
$H_{\rm rel}=x_{0}-x_{s}+v_{s}^{2}/2g\approx0.698\,{\rm m}$, essentially
the same number to the accuracy normally required.  This is the
text-book $k x^{2}/2mg$ estimate; the $x_{s}$ correction is $\sim1\,{\rm mm}$
and is normally neglected.

For a body that rolls without slipping the translational kinetic energy and the rotational kinetic energy about the centre of mass are both present.

Loss of gravitational potential energy

$$
\Delta U = mgh
$$

is converted into

$$
K_{tr}+K_{rot}= \frac12 m v_{cm}^{2}+\frac12 I_{cm}\omega^{2}
$$

For rolling without slipping

$$
v_{cm}= \omega r\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \omega =v_{cm}/r
$$

For a uniform solid sphere

$$
I_{cm}= \frac25 mr^{2}
$$

so that

$$
K_{rot}= \frac12\left(\frac25 mr^{2}\right)\left(\frac{v_{cm}}{r}\right)^{2}
      =\frac15 m v_{cm}^{2}
$$

Hence

$$
K_{tot}= \frac12 m v_{cm}^{2}+\frac15 m v_{cm}^{2}
       =\frac{7}{10}m v_{cm}^{2}
$$

Energy conservation from rest, $K_{i}=0$,

$$
mgh = \frac{7}{10}m v_{cm}^{2}
$$

the mass cancels and

$$
v_{cm}= \sqrt{\frac{10}{7}gh}
$$

is independent of the radius and of the inclination angle.  With
$h=2.33\;{\rm m}$ and $g=9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$

$$
v_{cm}= \sqrt{\frac{10}{7}\times 9.81\times 2.33}
      =\sqrt{\frac{10\times 22.8573}{7}}
      =\sqrt{32.65}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

$$
v_{cm}\approx 5.7\!-\!5.8\;{\rm m/s}
$$

about $5.71\;{\rm m/s}$ down the incline.  The corresponding angular speed at the bottom is $\omega=v_{cm}/r$.

In the familiar form $v_{cm}=\sqrt{10gh/7}$ the $7/10$ factor is the
$1/2+1/5$ translational + rotational partition for a solid sphere rolling without slipping.

In the (very short) impact the external impulse of the friction can be
neglected so that the linear momentum of the two blocks is conserved

$$p_{i}=m_{1}v_{1}\approx (m_{1}+m_{2})v^{*}$$

$$v^{*}= \frac{m_{1}v_{1}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}=
\frac{1.99\times 2.30}{1.99+2.14}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      =\frac{4.58}{4.13}\approx 1.1\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}} $$

is the common speed just after the perfectly inelastic impact.  
After the impact the only horizontal work is that of kinetic friction

$$F_{k}= \mu_{k}N=\mu_{k}(m_{1}+m_{2})g $$

so that the (mass independent) deceleration of the stuck pair is

$$a=\frac{F_{k}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}=\mu_{k}g
      =0.34\times 9.81\approx 3.34\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}} $$

in the sense opposite to the motion.  With $v_{0}=v^{*}$ and $v=0$,

$$0=v_{0}^{2}-2a s_{f}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
s_{f}=\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{2\mu_{k}g}
     =\frac{1}{2\mu_{k}g}\left[\frac{m_{1}v_{1}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\right]^{2} .
$$

Hence

$$s_{f}= \frac{\left(1.108\;{\rm m/s}\right)^{2}}{2\times0.34\times9.81}
      \approx\frac{1.23}{6.67}\approx1.8\!-\!1.9\times10^{-1}\ {\rm m}$$

about $0.18\!-\!0.19\;{\rm m}$ of sliding after the impact, i.e. $\approx
18\;{\rm cm}$ of post-collision travel.  With the numbers quoted

$$s_{f}\approx\frac{(1.99\times2.3)^{2}}{(4.13)^{2}\,2(0.34)(9.81)}
      \approx0.18\;{\rm m}\approx0.184\;{\rm m}$$

from the point of impact, the stopping time being $t_{s}=v^{*}/a\approx
0.33\;{\rm s}$.  The $v^{*}$ quoted above is the speed immediately after
the stick together; the kinetic energy lost in the inelastic impact is
$ \Delta K =\tfrac12m_{1}v_{1}^{2}-\tfrac12(m_{1}+m_{2})v^{*2}$ and the
remaining $\tfrac12(m_{1}+m_{2})v^{*2}$ is dissipated by friction over
the $s_{f}$ quoted.

For a body that rolls without slipping the loss of gravitational potential
is shared between translational kinetic energy of the centre of mass and
rotational kinetic energy about the centre of mass.

Loss of potential

$$\Delta U = m g h$$

with $h=4.28\;{\rm m}$ the vertical drop.

Translational kinetic energy

$$K_{t}= \tfrac12 m v^{2}$$

Rotational kinetic energy about the CM

$$K_{r}= \tfrac12 I_{cm}\omega^{2}$$

For a solid cylinder

$$I_{cm}= \tfrac12 m r^{2}$$

and for rolling without slipping

$$v = \omega r\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \omega = v/r$$

so that

$$K_{r}= \tfrac12\left(\tfrac12 m r^{2}\right)\left(\frac{v}{r}\right)^{2}
      =\tfrac14 m v^{2} .$$

Hence with no non-conservative work

$$m g h = K_{t}+K_{r}= \tfrac12 m v^{2}+\tfrac14 m v^{2}
       =\tfrac34 m v^{2}$$

the mass cancels and

$$v^{2}= \frac{4}{3}\,g h
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
v=\sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1+I_{cm}/mr^{2}}}
   =\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}gh}$$

for a solid cylinder, $I_{cm}/mr^{2}=1/2$.

Numerically

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}\,9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}\times4.28\;{\rm m}}
  =\sqrt{55.98\;{\rm m^{2}/s^{2}}}
  \approx 7.4\!-\!7.5\;{\rm m/s}$$

down the ramp, about $7.5\;{\rm m/s}$ centre-of-mass speed, 
$\omega=v/r\approx7.48/r\;{\rm rad/s}$.  The familiar $v=\sqrt{2gh}$ for
free fall is reduced by the factor $\sqrt{4/3}$ because part of the
gravitational energy goes into spin.

For a body that rolls without slipping the loss in gravitational potential
is taken up in translational and rotational kinetic energy

$$ \Delta U = \Delta K_{tr}+\Delta K_{rot}$$

$$mgh = \tfrac12 m v^{2}+\tfrac12 I\omega^{2}$$

For rolling without slipping

$$v = \omega r\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \omega = v/r$$

For a uniform solid cylinder about its central axis

$$I_{cm}= \tfrac12 m r^{2}$$

so that

$$K_{rot}= \tfrac12 I_{cm}\omega^{2}
       =\tfrac12\left(\tfrac12 m r^{2}\right)\left(\frac{v}{r}\right)^{2}
       =\tfrac14 m v^{2}$$

Hence

$$mgh = \tfrac12 m v^{2}+\tfrac14 m v^{2}= \tfrac34 m v^{2}$$

the mass cancels and

$$v^{2}= \frac{4}{3}gh
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
v=\sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1+I/mr^{2}}}
   =\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}gh}$$

for a solid cylinder, $I/mr^{2}=1/2$.  With $h=0.89\;{\rm m}$,

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}\,g\,h}
  =\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}\times9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}\times0.89\;{\rm m}}
  =\sqrt{11.64\;{\rm m^{2}/s^{2}}}
  \approx 3.4\!-\!3.5\;{\rm m/s}$$

about $3.41\;{\rm m/s}$ down the incline, the corresponding angular
speed being $\omega=v/r$.  This is $\sqrt{3/4}$ of the $ \sqrt{2gh}$ speed
that a particle sliding without rotation would have.  For $g\approx9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is $\approx 3.4\;{\rm m/s}$ translational, $\approx 3.4/r\;{\rm rad/s}$ rotational.

For an ideal Atwood the two masses have the same magnitude of acceleration
$a$ and the same tension $T$ in the (massless, inextensible) string.

For the heavy mass $m_{1}>m_{2}$

$$m_{1}g-T=m_{1}a\qquad{\rm 1}$$

and for the light mass

$$T-m_{2}g=m_{2}a\qquad{\rm 2}$$

Adding 1 and 2

$$\big(m_{1}-m_{2}\big)g=\big(m_{1}+m_{2}\big)a$$

so that on the ideal pulley

$$a=\frac{m_{1}-m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\,g $$

is the common magnitude of the acceleration.  With $m_{1}=1.61\;{\rm kg}$,
$m_{2}=0.97\;{\rm kg}$

$$
a=\frac{1.61-0.97}{1.61+0.97}\;g
  =\frac{0.64}{2.58}\;g\approx0.2481\,g\approx2.4\!-\!2.5\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}
$$

about $2.43\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ down for the $1.61\;{\rm kg}$ mass and up for
the $0.97\;{\rm kg}$ mass.

From 2, $T=m_{2}g+m_{2}a=m_{2}\big(g+a\big)$, and from 1,
$T=m_{1}g-m_{1}a$.  In closed form

$$
T=\frac{2m_{1}m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\,g
$$

which is the familiar Atwood tension.  Numerically

$$
T=\frac{2(1.61)(0.97)}{1.61+0.97}\;9.81
  =\frac{3.1234}{2.58}\;9.81\approx1.209\times9.81\approx1.19\times10^{1}\ {\rm N}
$$

i.e. $\approx 11\!-\!12\;{\rm N}$, about $11.9\;{\rm N}$ with $g=9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$.
In the $m_{1}g-m_{1}a$ form

* $m_{1}g=1.61\times9.81=15.79\;{\rm N}$
* $m_{1}a=1.61\times2.43\approx3.92\;{\rm N}$

$T=15.79-3.92\approx11.9\;{\rm N}$, the same as $T=m_{2}g+m_{2}a$
$=0.97\times9.81+0.97\times2.43\approx11.9\;{\rm N}$.

The tension is constant during the motion, the $1.61\;{\rm kg}$ mass
accelerating downwards at $a\approx2.4\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$.  With $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is $T\approx11.8\!-\!11.9\;{\rm N}$.

For a flat launch and landing the horizontal motion is uniform and the
vertical motion is free fall.

* $v_{0x}=v_{0}\cos\theta$ , $v_{0y}=v_{0}\sin\theta$

$$
\begin{aligned}
v_{0x}&=26.2\cos71^{\circ}\\
     &=26.2\times0.3256\approx 8.5\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}\\
v_{0y}&=26.2\sin71^{\circ}\\
     &=26.2\times0.9458\approx 24.8\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Time to the apex

$$
t_{up}=\frac{v_{0y}}{g}
$$

and the total time of flight to the same height $y=0$ is

$$
T=2t_{up}= \frac{2v_{0y}}{g}
   =\frac{2\times24.78}{9.81}\approx 5.05\;{\rm s}
$$

The horizontal range is the uniform horizontal displacement in that time

$$
R=v_{0x}T
  =v_{0x}\frac{2v_{0y}}{g}
  =\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{g}\sin2\theta  ,
$$

i.e. the familiar projectile range.  In numbers

$$
R=\frac{(26.2)^{2}}{9.81}\sin\!\left[2\times71^{\circ}\right]
  =\frac{686.4}{9.81}\sin142^{\circ}
  =\frac{686.4}{9.81}\sin38^{\circ}
  \approx\frac{422.6}{9.81}\approx 4.3\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}
$$

about $43\!-\!44\;{\rm m}$ down range.  With the numbers quoted above

* $T\approx5.0\;{\rm s}$ in the air,
* $H_{\max}=v_{0y}^{2}/2g\approx31\;{\rm m}$,

and $R\approx 8.53\,{\rm m/s}\times5.05\,{\rm s}\approx 43.1\;{\rm m}$ from the
launch point on level ground.  Using $g\approx9.8\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is
$R\approx43.1\!-\!43.3\;{\rm m}$, essentially $\sim 43\;{\rm m}$ for the
$71^{\circ}$ launch, well below the $45^{\circ}$ maximum $v_{0}^{2}/g\approx
70\;{\rm m}$ for this speed.

For two equal sign charges the fields can cancel only on the line between
them.  Put the origin at $q_{1}$ and let the zero of the field be a distance
$x$ from $q_{1}$ on the way to $q_{2}$ so that

$$r_{1}=x\qquad r_{2}=L-x\qquad L=0.91\;{\rm m}$$

On the segment the two fields are opposite in sign and

$$E_{1}=k\frac{q_{1}}{r_{1}^{2}},\qquad 
E_{2}=k\frac{q_{2}}{r_{2}^{2}} $$

so that $E_{1}=E_{2}$ at the null

$$\frac{q_{1}}{x^{2}}=\frac{q_{2}}{(L-x)^{2}}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
\frac{L-x}{x}=\sqrt{\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}}\;.$$

Hence

$$x=\frac{L}{1+\sqrt{q_{2}/q_{1}}}
   =L\,\frac{\sqrt{q_{1}}}{\sqrt{q_{1}}+\sqrt{q_{2}}}\;.$$

With $q_{1}=5.0\;\mu{\rm C}$, $q_{2}=8.6\;\mu{\rm C}$ and $L=91\;{\rm cm}$

$$\sqrt{\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}}=\sqrt{\frac{8.6}{5.0}}=1.31$$

and

$$x=\frac{91\;{\rm cm}}{1+1.311}\approx 3.9\!-\!4.0\times10^{1}\ {\rm cm}$$

from $q_{1}$ toward $q_{2}$, i.e. about $39\!-\!40\;{\rm cm}$ from the
$5.0\;\mu{\rm C}$ charge, $L-x\approx 51.6\;{\rm cm}$ from the $8.6\;\mu{\rm C}$
charge.  In closed form $x=L\sqrt{q_{1}}/(\sqrt{q_{1}}+\sqrt{q_{2}})\approx
39.4\;{\rm cm}$ on the inter-charge segment, the familiar $x\approx 39\;{\rm cm}$
from $q_{1}$.  This is the unique interior null; no null exists on the
exterior of two like charges.

The series current is the same in $R_{1}$ and in the $R_{2}\!\parallel\!R_{3}$ block.

* Parallel resistance

$$
R_{p}=R_{2}\parallel R_{3}=\frac{R_{2}R_{3}}{R_{2}+R_{3}}
      =\frac{14\times 43}{14+43}\;\Omega
      =\frac{602}{57}\;\Omega\approx 10.56\;\Omega
$$

* Total resistance seen by the ideal 7 V source

$$
R_{T}=R_{1}+R_{p}=49+\frac{602}{57}
     =\frac{49\times57+602}{57}
     =\frac{3395}{57}\;\Omega\approx 59.6\;\Omega
$$

* Total / series current

$$
I_{T}=I_{1}=\frac{V}{R_{T}}=\frac{7}{3395/57}
     =\frac{399}{3395}\ {\rm A}\approx 1.18\times10^{-1}\ {\rm A}
$$

The voltage which appears across the parallel block is

$$
V_{p}=V-I_{T}R_{1}=7-I_{T}\times49\approx
7-0.1176\times49\approx1.24\;{\rm V}
$$

and it is the same voltage which appears across $R_{2}$ and across $R_{3}$.
Hence

$$
I_{2}=\frac{V_{p}}{R_{2}}
     =\frac{V}{R_{1}+R_{2}\parallel R_{3}}\;\frac{R_{3}}{R_{2}+R_{3}}
$$

i.e. in the usual current-division form

$$
I_{2}=I_{T}\frac{R_{3}}{R_{2}+R_{3}}
     =\frac{399}{3395}\frac{43}{57}
     =\frac{17157}{193515}\ {\rm A}
     =\frac{5719}{64505}\ {\rm A}
$$

$$
I_{2}\approx 8.9\times10^{-2}\ {\rm A}\approx 0.089\;{\rm A}
$$

about $88\!-\!89\;{\rm mA}$ from the node after $R_{1}$ toward the negative terminal of the battery.  In the idealised numbers

* $V_{p}\approx1.24\;{\rm V}$ across $R_{2}\parallel R_{3}$,
* $I_{1}=I_{T}\approx0.118\;{\rm A}$ in $R_{1}$,
* $I_{3}=V_{p}/R_{3}\approx0.0289\;{\rm A}$,

so that $I_{1}=I_{2}+I_{3}$ as required.  The often quoted $I_{2}\simeq0.088\!-\!0.089\;{\rm A}\approx 89\;{\rm mA}$ is the $R_{2}$ branch current.

For a circular Kepler orbit

$$ \frac{GMm}{r^{2}}=m\omega^{2}r\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\omega^{2}=\frac{GM}{r^{3}} $$

so that with $r=R_{E}+h$

$$T= \frac{2\pi}{\omega}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{GM}} $$

is the Kepler period.  In SI

* $R_{E}=6371\;{\rm km}=6.371\times10^{6}\ {\rm m}$
* $h=867\;{\rm km}=0.867\times10^{6}\ {\rm m}$

$$r=R_{E}+h=6371+867=7238\;{\rm km}=7.238\times10^{6}\ {\rm m}$$

Hence

$$
\frac{r^{3}}{GM}=
\frac{(7.238\times10^{6}\,{\rm m})^{3}}{3.986\times10^{14}\ {\rm m^{3}s^{-2}}}
\approx 9.51\times10^{5}\ {\rm s^{2}}
$$

$$
\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{GM}}\approx\sqrt{9.51\times10^{5}}\approx 9.75\times10^{2}\ {\rm s}
$$

and

$$
T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{GM}}\approx2\pi\times9.75\times10^{2}\ {\rm s}
\approx6.1\!-\!6.3\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}
$$

$$
T\approx 6.13\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}\approx\frac{6.13\times10^{3}}{60}\ {\rm min}
\approx 1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{2}\ {\rm min}
$$

i.e. about $1.02\times10^{2}\ {\rm min}\approx 102\!-\!103\ {\rm min}$,
$\approx 1.7\ {\rm h}$, for the nominal $r=7.238\times10^{6}\ {\rm m}$.
With the numbers quoted this is $T\approx6.13\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}\approx102\,{\rm min}$,
about $102.1\;{\rm min}$ on the $R_{E}=6371\;{\rm km}$, $GM=3.986\times10^{14}\ {\rm m^{3}s^{-2}}$ convention, essentially the familiar $\sim$ 100 min low-Earth orbit period.  Using $GM=398600\;{\rm km^{3}s^{-2}}$ the often quoted value is $T\approx 6.13\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}\approx102.1\ {\rm min}\approx1.70\ {\rm h}$.

For a block on an incline the component of weight down the plane is
$mg\sin\theta$ and the normal reaction is $N=mg\cos\theta$ so that the
kinetic friction down the plane is

$$F_{f}=\mu_{k}N=\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta $$

The net force down the plane is therefore

$$F_{\parallel}=mg\sin\theta-\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta
      =mg\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]$$

and with $m$ cancelling

$$a=g\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]$$

is the (constant) acceleration down the slope.  With
$\theta =43^{\circ}$

* $\sin\theta\simeq0.6820$
* $\cos\theta\simeq0.7314$

$$
a=g\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]
  =9.81\Big[\,0.6820-0.17\times0.7314\,\Big]
  =9.81\big[\,0.6820-0.1243\,\big]
  =9.81\times0.5577\approx5.5\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}
$$

down the plane.  For constant $a$ from rest

$$v^{2}=v_{0}^{2}+2a\Delta s\;, \qquad v_{0}=0$$

so that on a distance $s$ down the ramp

$$v=\sqrt{\,2gs\big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\big]\,}$$

is the speed acquired from the loss of gravitational potential
$mg s\sin\theta$ minus the work of friction $\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta\,s$.

For $s=2.1\;{\rm m}$

$$
v=\sqrt{2\times9.81\times2.1\,
       \big[\sin43^{\circ}-0.17\cos43^{\circ}\big]}
  =\sqrt{2\times9.81\times2.1\times0.5577}
  \approx\sqrt{22.98}\approx4.8\;{\rm m/s}
$$

down the $43^{\circ}$ incline, about $4.7\!-\!4.9\;{\rm m/s}$ with the
usual roundings, i.e. $\approx 5.5\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ acceleration and
$\,v\approx4.8\;{\rm m/s}$ after $2.1\;{\rm m}$ of slip.  In energy form

$$ \tfrac12mv^{2}=mgs\big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\big] ,$$

which is the same result.  With $g\approx9.8\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is
$v\approx4.79\;{\rm m/s}\approx4.8\;{\rm m/s}$ down the plane.

For a projectile launched from and landing on the same horizontal level

* $v_{0x}=v_{0}\cos\theta$ , $v_{0y}=v_{0}\sin\theta$
* $a_{x}=0$ , $a_{y}=-g$

The time of flight to return to $y=0$ is

$$y(t)=v_{0y}t-\tfrac12gt^{2}=0\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
t_{f}=\frac{2v_{0y}}{g}=\frac{2v_{0}\sin\theta}{g}$$

and the horizontal displacement in that time is

$$R=v_{0x}t_{f}=v_{0}\cos\theta\;\frac{2v_{0}\sin\theta}{g}
      =\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{g}\;2\sin\theta\cos\theta
      =\frac{v_{0}^{2}\sin2\theta}{g} .$$

With $v_{0}=14.3\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ and $\theta=24^{\circ}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
v_{0x}&=v_{0}\cos24^{\circ}=14.3\times0.9135\approx 13.1\;{\rm m/s}\\
v_{0y}&=v_{0}\sin24^{\circ}=14.3\times0.4067\approx 5.82\;{\rm m/s}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
t_{f}= \frac{2v_{0y}}{g}= \frac{2\times5.82}{9.81}\approx1.19\;{\rm s}
$$

$$
R=v_{0x}t_{f}\approx13.06\times1.19\approx1.5\!-\!1.6\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}
$$

In closed form

$$
R=\frac{(14.3)^{2}\sin48^{\circ}}{9.81}\approx
\frac{204.5\times0.7431}{9.81}\approx1.55\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}\approx15\!-\!16\;{\rm m},
$$

about $15.5\;{\rm m}$ on the level ground, $ \approx 15.5\;{\rm m}$ for $g=9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$.  This is the familiar $R=v_{0}^{2}\sin2\theta/g$ result.

For a stationary observer the Doppler shift for a moving source is

$$f' = f_{0}\,\frac{c}{c\mp v_{s}}$$

the minus sign being for a source moving towards the observer and the
plus sign for a source moving away.  $c$ is the speed of sound in the
medium and $v_{s}$ the component of the source velocity along the line
of sight.

Here

* $f_{0}=459\;{\rm Hz}$ is the proper frequency of the source,
* $c=343\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$,
* $v_{s}=+12.3\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ towards the observer,

so that

$$
f' = f_{0}\,\frac{c}{c-v_{s}}
    = 459\;\frac{343}{343-12.3}\;{\rm Hz}
    = 459\;\frac{343}{330.7}\;{\rm Hz}
$$

$$
f' \approx 4.76\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}
$$

i.e. about $476\;{\rm Hz}$, $\approx 17\;{\rm Hz}$ higher than the
emitted 459 Hz.  In the more usual $476.1\;{\rm Hz}$ rounding

$$f'\approx 459\frac{c}{c-v_{s}}\approx 476\;{\rm Hz}$$

towards the observer.  The sign reverses for recession,
$f' = f_{0}c/(c+v_{s})\approx 443.5\;{\rm Hz}$ for the same speed away
from the observer.

For a reversible Carnot cycle the thermal efficiency is set by the two
reservoir temperatures only

$$\eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}} $$

with the temperatures on an absolute scale.

* $T_{H}=311^{\circ}{\rm C}=311+273.15=584.15\;{\rm K}\approx 584\;{\rm K}$
* $T_{C}= 21^{\circ}{\rm C}=21+273.15=294.15\;{\rm K}\approx 294\;{\rm K}$

Hence

$$\eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}
      =1-\frac{294.15}{584.15}
      =1-0.5035\approx 0.50 $$

about $49\!-\!50\%$ of the heat taken from the hot reservoir can in
principle be turned into work.  In the ideal Carnot limit

$$W_{\rm out}= \eta_{C}\,Q_{H}$$

is the work obtained per cycle from the heat $Q_{H}$ taken from the hot
reservoir.

With $Q_{H}=19.8\;{\rm kJ}$ per cycle

$$W_{\rm out}\approx\Bigl[\,1-\frac{294}{584}\Bigr]\,19.8\;{\rm kJ}
      =\frac{290}{584}\times19.8\;{\rm kJ}
      \approx 9.8\!-\!9.9\;{\rm kJ}$$

per cycle, i.e. about $0.50\,Q_{H}$.  In the usual $T/273$ approximation
$T_{H}=584\;{\rm K},\;T_{C}=294\;{\rm K}$,

$$\eta_{C}\approx1-294/584\approx0.497\approx49.7\%$$

$$W\approx0.497\times19.8\;{\rm kJ}\approx9.8\;{\rm kJ}\approx9.83\;{\rm kJ}$$

per cycle.  The remainder

$$Q_{C}=Q_{H}-W=Q_{H}\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}\approx9.97\;{\rm kJ}$$

is rejected to the cold reservoir per cycle.  Using $T_{H}=584.15\;{\rm K}$,
$T_{C}=294.15\;{\rm K}$ gives $\eta_{C}=0.496$ and $W\approx9.83\;{\rm kJ}$
per cycle, essentially the $ \sim 10\;{\rm kJ}$ quoted above.

For an RC charge from rest

$$V_{C}(t)=V_{\infty}\Big[\,1-e^{-t/RC}\,\Big]$$

so that

$$\frac{V_{C}(t)}{V_{\infty}}=1-e^{-t/RC}$$

is the fraction of the final voltage that is reached.  Put
$V_{C}/V_{\infty}=0.95$

$$0.95 = 1-e^{-t/RC}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
e^{-t/RC}=0.05$$

$$t = -RC\;\ln 0.05 = RC\;\ln\frac{1}{0.05}=RC\;\ln 20 .$$

The time constant is

$$ \tau = RC = 68\times10^{3}\ {\rm \Omega}\times 11\times10^{-6}\ {\rm F}
      =0.748\ {\rm s} $$

Hence

$$t_{0.95}= \tau\ln 20 \approx 0.748\;{\rm s}\times 2.9957\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\;{\rm s}$$

i.e. about three time constants.  In the usual $3\tau$ rule

$$t_{95}\approx 3RC\approx 3\times0.748\;{\rm s}\approx 2.24\;{\rm s},$$

$1-e^{-3}=0.9502$, essentially $95\%$ of $V_{\infty}$ reached after $\approx 2.2$ s of charging.

The motion is the sum of the motion with constant speed during the
reaction time and the uniformly decelerated motion after the brakes are
applied.

* Speed

$$
v_{0}=65\;{\rm km\,h^{-1}}=\frac{65\times10^{3}}{3600}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      =\frac{65}{3.6}\approx 1.81\times10^{1}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

$ v_{0}\approx 18.1\;{\rm m/s}$.

* Reaction distance

During the reaction time $t_{r}$ the speed is essentially unchanged

$$
s_{r}=v_{0}t_{r}
$$

$$
s_{r}\approx 18.06\;{\rm m/s}\times0.77\;{\rm s}\approx 1.39\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}
$$

about $13.9\;{\rm m}$ of travel before the brakes actually begin to act.

* Braking distance

After the brakes are on $a=5.2\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$ is constant and
$v_{f}=0$,

$$
v_{f}^{2}=v_{0}^{2}-2a s_{b}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
s_{b}=\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{2a}
$$

$$
s_{b}= \frac{(18.06\;{\rm m/s})^{2}}{2\times5.2\;{\rm m/s^{2}}}
     =\frac{3.26\times10^{2}}{10.4}\approx 3.13\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}
$$

$\approx 31.3\!-\!31.5\;{\rm m}$ of braking.

* Total stopping distance from the instant the obstacle is seen

$$
s_{\rm tot}=s_{r}+s_{b}=v_{0}t_{r}+\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{2a}
$$

$$
s_{\rm tot}\approx 13.9\;{\rm m}+31.3\;{\rm m}\approx 4.5\!-\!4.6\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}
$$

i.e. about $45\;{\rm m}$ of travel, $ \approx 45.2\!-\!45.3\;{\rm m}$ with the
numbers quoted, $13.9\;{\rm m}$ of which is covered during the $0.77\;{\rm s}$
reaction time and $\approx 31.3\;{\rm m}$ under braking.  This is the
usual “thinking + braking’’ stopping distance.

For a moving source and a stationary observer the (non-relativistic) Doppler shift is

$$f' = f_{0}\,\frac{v}{v\mp v_{s}}$$

toward $-$ in the denominator for a source moving toward the observer.

* $f_{0}=967\;{\rm Hz}$  source proper frequency
* $v=343\;{\rm m/s}$  speed of sound in air
* $v_{s}=18.5\;{\rm m/s}$  source speed toward the observer

$$f' = f_{0}\frac{v}{v-v_{s}}$$

$$f' = 967\;\frac{343}{343-18.5}\;{\rm Hz}$$

$$f' = 967\;\frac{343}{324.5}\;{\rm Hz}$$

$$f' = \frac{967\times 343}{324.5}\;{\rm Hz}
     =\frac{331\,681}{324.5}\;{\rm Hz}$$

$$f' \approx 1.022\times10^{3}\ {\rm Hz}$$

about $55\;{\rm Hz}$ higher than the emitted $967\;{\rm Hz}$, i.e. $\approx 1.02\;{\rm kHz}$ heard on approach.  With the numbers quoted this is $\approx 1022\!-\!1023\;{\rm Hz}$, $\approx 1022.1\;{\rm Hz}$ on the $343\;{\rm m/s}$ value.

For a reversible Carnot cycle

$$ \eta_{Carnot}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}} = \frac{W}{Q_{H}} $$

the temperatures have to be absolute.

* $T_{H}=291^{\circ}{\rm C}=291+273.15=564.15\;{\rm K}$
* $T_{C}= 80^{\circ}{\rm C}= 80+273.15=353.15\;{\rm K}$

Hence the Carnot thermal efficiency is

$$
\eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}
      =1-\frac{353.15}{564.15}
      =1-0.626\approx 0.374
$$

i.e. about $37\!-\!38\%$ of the heat taken from the hot source can be
converted into work in the reversible limit.

For a heat input per cycle

$$
Q_{H}=10.6\;{\rm kJ}
$$

the reversible work per cycle is

$$
W=\eta_{C}\,Q_{H}
  =\left[\,1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}\right]Q_{H}
$$

$$
W =\left[1-\frac{353.15}{564.15}\right]\times10.6\;{\rm kJ}
   \approx 0.374\times10.6\;{\rm kJ}
   \approx 3.9\!-\!4.0\;{\rm kJ}
$$

per cycle.  In terms of the rejected heat

$$
Q_{C}=Q_{H}\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}
     =10.6\frac{353.15}{564.15}\approx 6.64\;{\rm kJ}
$$

so that on the energy balance

$$
W=Q_{H}-Q_{C}\approx10.6-6.64\approx3.96\;{\rm kJ}
$$

per Carnot cycle.  With the usual $T/{\rm K}=t/^{\circ}{\rm C}+273$ this is
$\eta_{C}\approx 37.3\%$ and $W\approx3.95\;{\rm kJ}\approx4.0\;{\rm kJ}$
per cycle, essentially the reversible limit for the $291^{\circ}{\rm C}/80^{\circ}{\rm C}$ pair.

For a stretched string the transverse wave speed is

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$$

where $T$ is the tension and $\mu$ the mass per unit length.  For a
string fixed at both ends the normal modes are

$$\lambda_{n}=\frac{2L}{n}\qquad n=1,2,\dots$$

so that

$$f_{n}=\frac{v}{\lambda_{n}}=\frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} $$

is the $n^{\rm th}$ harmonic.  The $n=1$ mode is the fundamental.

* $\mu =1.3\;{\rm g\,m^{-1}}=1.3\times10^{-3}\ {\rm kg\,m^{-1}}$
* $T =192\ {\rm N}$
* $L =0.64\ {\rm m}$

Wave speed

$$
v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}
   =\sqrt{\frac{192}{1.3\times10^{-3}}}
   =\sqrt{1.48\times10^{5}}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
   \approx 3.8\!-\!3.9\times10^{2}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

about $3.84\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$.

The fundamental wavelength for a string fixed at both ends is
$\lambda_{1}=2L$,

$$
\lambda_{1}=2\times0.64=1.28\ {\rm m}
$$

Hence

$$
f_{1}=\frac{v}{\lambda_{1}}=\frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}
     =\frac{1}{1.28}\sqrt{\frac{192}{1.3\times10^{-3}}}
     \approx\frac{384\ {\rm m/s}}{1.28\ {\rm m}}
     \approx 3.0\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}
$$

i.e. $\approx 300\;{\rm Hz}$, about $299\!-\!300\;{\rm Hz}$ on the
numbers quoted, the usual $n\,f_{1}$ harmonics being $n\times\approx300\;{\rm Hz}$.
This is the $n=1$ normal mode; $f_{n}=n f_{1}$ for the higher modes.

In the inelastic impact the linear momentum of the bullet–block system is
conserved, the kinetic energy which is left after the impact being
converted into gravitational potential energy in the swing.

Let

* $m=0.015\;{\rm kg}$ be the mass of the bullet,
* $M=1.93\;{\rm kg}$ be the mass of the block,
* $h=0.108\;{\rm m}$ the rise of the centre of mass of the $(M+m)$ system,
* $v_{0}$ the speed of the bullet before impact,
* $v_{1}$ the common speed of the $(M+m)$ system just after impact.

Momentum

$$
m v_{0}=(M+m)v_{1}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
v_{1}= \frac{m}{M+m}v_{0}
$$

is conserved in the (essentially horizontal) impact.  After the impact
the $(M+m)$ system rises a height $h$ under gravity, so that, with the
zero of potential at the point of impact,

$$
\frac12 (M+m)v_{1}^{2}=(M+m)g h ,
$$

i.e. the speed just after impact is the speed acquired in a free fall
through $h$,

$$
v_{1}=\sqrt{2gh}\; .
$$

Hence

$$
v_{0}= \frac{M+m}{m}\,v_{1}
     =\frac{M+m}{m}\sqrt{2gh}\; .
$$

With $M+m=1.93+0.015=1.945\;{\rm kg}$,

$$
v_{1}= \sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.108}
     =\sqrt{2.11896}\approx1.46\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

is the speed of the block–bullet system immediately after the
embedding.  The speed of the bullet before impact is therefore

$$
v_{0}= \frac{1.945}{0.015}\sqrt{2gh}
     \approx 1.2967\times10^{2}\times1.456\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
     \approx 1.9\times10^{2}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}},
$$

about $1.88\!-\!1.90\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$, i.e. $\approx 189\;{\rm m/s}$
in the usual $g=9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$ convention.  With the numbers
quoted this is

$$
v_{0}\approx\frac{M+m}{m}\sqrt{2gh}\approx 1.9\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}
$$

$\approx 188\!-\!190\;{\rm m/s}$ before impact, about $130$ times the
post-impact swing speed $v_{1}\approx1.46\;{\rm m/s}$.  This is the
usual ballistic-pendulum result $v_{0}=(M+m)/m\,\sqrt{2gh}$.

For a body that rolls without slipping the mechanical energy is conserved
in the absence of non-conservative work

$$E_{i}=E_{f}$$

$$U_{i}+K_{t,i}+K_{r,i}=U_{f}+K_{t,f}+K_{r,f}$$

From rest $K_{t,i}=K_{r,i}=0$ and with the zero of potential at the bottom
$U_{f}=0$, $U_{i}=mgh$

$$mgh=\frac12mv_{f}^{2}+\frac12I\omega_{f}^{2}$$

For rolling without slipping

$$\omega_{f}=\frac{v_{f}}{r}$$

For a uniform solid sphere

$$I=\frac25mr^{2}$$

so that

$$K_{r,f}=\frac12I\omega_{f}^{2}
      =\frac12\frac25mr^{2}\frac{v_{f}^{2}}{r^{2}}
      =\frac15mv_{f}^{2}$$

Hence

$$mgh=\frac12mv_{f}^{2}+\frac15mv_{f}^{2}
     =\frac{7}{10}mv_{f}^{2}$$

The mass cancels and

$$v_{f}=\sqrt{\frac{10}{7}gh}
     =\sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1+I/mr^{2}}}
     =\sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1+2/5}} $$

is the translational speed at the bottom.  With $h=1.95\;{\rm m}$ and
$g=9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$

$$v_{f}= \sqrt{\frac{10}{7}\times9.81\times1.95}
      =\sqrt{27.33}\;{\rm m/s}\approx 5.2\!-\!5.3\;{\rm m/s}$$

about $5.23\;{\rm m/s}$ down the incline.  The corresponding angular
speed is $\omega_{f}=v_{f}/r$.  In the familiar form $v=\sqrt{2gh/(1+k^{2})}$
with $k^{2}=2/5$ for a solid sphere.

For a reversible Carnot cycle

$$\eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{L}}{T_{H}}=\frac{W}{Q_{H}} $$

with the absolute temperatures

* $T_{H}=577^{\circ}{\rm C}=577+273.15=850.15\;{\rm K}\approx 850\;{\rm K}$
* $T_{L}=61^{\circ}{\rm C}=61+273.15=334.15\;{\rm K}\approx 334\;{\rm K}$

Hence

$$
\eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{L}}{T_{H}}
      =1-\frac{334.15}{850.15}
      \approx 1-0.393\approx 0.607
$$

i.e. about $60.7\%$ of the heat taken in from the hot side can in principle be converted into work on a reversible cycle.

For a heat input per cycle

$$
Q_{H}=9.1\;{\rm kJ}
$$

$$
W_{C}= \eta_{C}\,Q_{H}
     =\left[\,1-\frac{T_{L}}{T_{H}}\right]Q_{H}
$$

$$
W_{C}\approx0.606\!-\!0.607\times 9.1\;{\rm kJ}\approx5.5\!-\!5.6\;{\rm kJ}
$$

per cycle.  With the usual $T[K]=T[^{\circ}{\rm C}]+273$,

$$
\eta_{C}=1-\frac{334}{850}=0.6065
$$

$$
W_{C}=0.6065\times9.1\;{\rm kJ}\approx5.52\;{\rm kJ}
$$

is the reversible Carnot work.  The heat rejected to the cold sink is

$$
Q_{L}=Q_{H}-W_{C}=Q_{H}\frac{T_{L}}{T_{H}}\approx
9.1\frac{334}{850}\approx3.58\;{\rm kJ}
$$

so that $Q_{H}=W_{C}+Q_{L}$ as required.  Using $273.15\;{\rm K}$ the
formal value is $W_{C}=9.1\bigl[1-334.15/850.15\bigr]\approx5.52\!-\!5.53\;{\rm kJ}$ per cycle, $\approx 60.7\%$ of the $9.1\;{\rm kJ}$ taken in.

The work done on the block by the component of its weight down the plane
and by kinetic friction is the change in its kinetic energy

$$W_{g}+W_{f}=\Delta K $$

on the incline

* $N=mg\cos\theta$
* $f_{k}=\mu_{k}N=\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta$

For a displacement $s$ down the plane

$$W_{g}=mg\sin\theta\,s\qquad 
W_{f}=-f_{k}s=-\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta\,s $$

Hence with $K_{i}=0$

$$\frac12mv^{2}=mg s\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]$$

the mass cancels and

$$v=\sqrt{\,2gs\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]}$$

is the speed after a distance $s$ down the plane.  The (constant)
acceleration down the plane is

$$a=g\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big] .$$

For $\theta=35^{\circ}$,

$$\sin\theta=0.5736,\qquad \cos\theta=0.8192$$

$$\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta
=0.5736-0.24\times0.8192
=0.5736-0.1966\approx0.377$$

so that

$$a=g\big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\big]
\approx9.81\times0.377\approx3.70\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$$

down the plane.  With $s=2.3\;{\rm m}$

$$v=\sqrt{2as}=\sqrt{2gs\big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\big]}
      =\sqrt{2(9.81)(2.3)(0.37698)}\approx\sqrt{17.0}\approx4.1\!-\!4.2\;{\rm m/s}$$

down the incline, about $4.1\;{\rm m/s}$ in the direction of motion.
In terms of the energy balance

$$h=s\sin\theta,\qquad 
\Delta K=mgh-\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta\,s,$$

$$v=\sqrt{2g\big(h-\mu_{k}s\cos\theta\big)}\approx4.1\;{\rm m/s},$$

i.e. $\approx 4.12\;{\rm m/s}$ with the numbers quoted, essentially
$4\;{\rm m/s}$ down the plane.  The familiar kinematic form
$v^{2}=v_{0}^{2}+2as$ with $v_{0}=0$ and $a=g(\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta)$
gives the same result.

For a flat launch the horizontal and vertical motions are independent

* $v_{0x}=v_{0}\cos\theta$
* $v_{0y}=v_{0}\sin\theta$

$$v_{0x}=38.1\cos53^{\circ}\approx38.1\times0.6018\approx 22.9\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$$
$$v_{0y}=38.1\sin53^{\circ}\approx38.1\times0.7986\approx 30.4\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$$

In the vertical direction, with zero initial height,

$$y(t)=v_{0y}t-\tfrac12gt^{2}=0\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
t_{f}= \frac{2v_{0y}}{g}$$

is the time back to ground.  Hence

$$t_{f}= \frac{2\times30.4}{9.81}\approx\frac{60.8}{9.81}\approx 6.2\;{\rm s}$$

The horizontal motion is uniform

$$R=v_{0x}t_{f}=v_{0}\cos\theta\;\frac{2v_{0}\sin\theta}{g}
      =\frac{v_{0}^{2}\sin2\theta}{g}$$

i.e.

$$R=\frac{(38.1)^{2}\sin106^{\circ}}{9.81}
   =\frac{1.452\times10^{3}\times0.9613}{9.81}
   \approx 1.40\times10^{3}/9.81\approx 1.42\times10^{2}\ {\rm m}$$

about $1.4\!-\!1.5\times10^{2}\,$m down range, $\approx 142\;{\rm m}$ on the
flat ground, $t_{f}\approx6.2\;{\rm s}$ in the air.  With the usual
$g\approx9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$ this is $R\approx 142\!-\!143\;{\rm m}$,
$\,R\approx v_{0}^{2}\sin2\theta/g$, the familiar projectile range.

In the idealised no-drag case the horizontal motion is decoupled from the
vertical motion

* $v_{x}(t)=v_{x0}$  is constant
* $v_{y}(t)=v_{y0}-g t$  with $v_{y0}=0$ for a horizontal launch

so that the horizontal component is unchanged on the way down

$$
v_{x}=v_{x0}=15.0\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

and the time of flight to a geometrical drop $h$ is obtained from

$$
\Delta y = v_{y0}t-\tfrac12gt^{2}\approx -h
$$

$$
0 = h-\tfrac12 g t_{f}^{2}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
t_{f}= \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}
$$

For $h=20.1\;{\rm m}$

$$
t_{f}= \sqrt{\frac{2\times20.1}{9.81}}\approx
\sqrt{4.10}\approx 2.02\;{\rm s}
$$

The vertical speed acquired in that time is

$$
|v_{y,f}| = g t_{f}= \sqrt{2gh}
$$

$$
|v_{y,f}|=\sqrt{2\times9.81\times20.1}
        =\sqrt{394.4}\approx 1.99\times10^{1}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

downwards.  The resultant speed on impact is the vector sum of the
unchanged horizontal part and the acquired vertical part

$$
v_{f}= \sqrt{v_{x}^{2}+v_{y,f}^{2}}
     =\sqrt{v_{x0}^{2}+2gh}\;,
$$

i.e.

$$
v_{f}= \sqrt{(15.0)^{2}+2(9.81)(20.1)}
     =\sqrt{225+394.36}
     =\sqrt{619.4}\approx 2.5\times10^{1}\ {\rm m/s}
$$

about $24.9\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ at impact.  In components

* $v_{x,f}=15.0\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$  horizontal, unchanged,
* $v_{y,f}\approx -19.9\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$  downwards,

so that the velocity vector makes

$$
\theta =\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{|v_{y,f}|}{v_{x}}\right)
       =\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{2gh}}{v_{x0}}\right)
       \approx \tan^{-1}(1.32)\approx 52\!-\!53^{\circ}
$$

below the horizontal.  The $15.0\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ horizontal component is
the “rightwards’’ speed, which in the absence of drag is the same all the
way down.  This is the $ \sqrt{v_{x0}^{2}+2gh}$ $\approx 25\;{\rm m/s}$
impact speed often quoted.

The series current is the current in $R_{1}$.

$$R_{p}=R_{2}\parallel R_{3}=\frac{R_{2}R_{3}}{R_{2}+R_{3}}
      =\frac{70\times 61}{70+61}\;{\rm \Omega}
      =\frac{4270}{131}\approx 32.6\;{\rm \Omega}$$

$$R_{T}=R_{1}+R_{p}=21+\frac{4270}{131}=\frac{7021}{131}\approx 53.6\;{\rm \Omega}$$

$$I_{T}=I_{1}=\frac{V}{R_{T}}=\frac{13}{7021/131}
      =\frac{13\times131}{7021}\approx 2.43\times10^{-1}\ {\rm A}$$

is the current which leaves the battery, goes through $R_{1}$ and then
splits between $R_{2}$ and $R_{3}$.  The voltage which appears across the
parallel pair is

$$V_{p}=I_{T}R_{p}=V-I_{T}R_{1}\approx 13-0.2426\times21\approx7.91\;{\rm V},$$

so that on $R_{2}$

$$I_{2}=\frac{V_{p}}{R_{2}}=\frac{I_{T}R_{p}}{R_{2}}
     =I_{T}\frac{R_{3}}{R_{2}+R_{3}}
     =\frac{13\times131}{7021}\frac{61}{131}
     =\frac{103\,883}{919\,751}\ {\rm A}\approx1.1\!-\!1.2\times10^{-1}\ {\rm A}$$

i.e. about $0.11\!-\!0.13\;{\rm A}$, $\approx 0.113\;{\rm A}$ from the
positive side of the parallel combination to the negative side, the
corresponding current in $R_{3}$ being $I_{3}=I_{T}-I_{2}\approx0.130\;{\rm A}$.
In particular

$$I_{2}\approx\frac{7.9\;{\rm V}}{70\;\Omega}\approx 1.13\times10^{-1}\ {\rm A}\approx113\;{\rm mA}$$

in the direction of the battery voltage, the total series current being
$I_{T}\approx0.243\;{\rm A}$.

For a string fixed at both ends the normal modes are

$$\lambda_{n}= \frac{2L}{n}\qquad n=1,2,\dots$$

so that with the wave speed on the string

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$$

the $n^{\rm th}$ normal frequency is

$$f_{n}= \frac{v}{\lambda_{n}}=\frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} $$

The fundamental is $n=1$.

* $L=0.74\;{\rm m}$
* $T=62\;{\rm N}$
* $\mu =7.7\;{\rm g\,m^{-1}}=7.7\times10^{-3}\;{\rm kg\,m^{-1}}
      =0.0077\;{\rm kg\,m^{-1}}$

Wave speed

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}
   =\sqrt{\frac{62\;{\rm N}}{0.0077\;{\rm kg\,m^{-1}}}}
   =\sqrt{8.05\times10^{3}\;{\rm m^{2}s^{-2}}}
   \approx 8.97\times10^{1}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$$

The fundamental wavelength for a string fixed at both ends is

$$\lambda_{1}=2L=2\times0.74\;{\rm m}=1.48\;{\rm m}$$

Hence

$$f_{1}= \frac{v}{\lambda_{1}}=\frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}
      =\frac{89.7\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}}{1.48\;{\rm m}}
      \approx 6.0\!-\!6.1\times10^{1}\ {\rm Hz}$$

i.e. about $60\!-\!61\;{\rm Hz}$, $f_{1}\approx 60.6\;{\rm Hz}$ on the
numbers quoted, essentially the $60\;{\rm Hz}$ mains frequency.  The
$n^{\rm th}$ harmonic is $f_{n}=n\,f_{1}$.

For a level launch $y_{0}=y_{f}$ the horizontal motion is uniform and the
vertical motion is uniformly accelerated

* $v_{0x}=v_{0}\cos\theta$ , $v_{0y}=v_{0}\sin\theta$

$$
v_{0x}=14.3\cos24^{\circ}=14.3\times0.9135\approx 1.31\times10^{1}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

$$
v_{0y}=14.3\sin24^{\circ}=14.3\times0.4067\approx 5.82\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

The horizontal speed is constant so that

$$
x(t)=v_{0x}t .
$$

In the vertical direction

$$
y(t)=v_{0y}t-\tfrac12gt^{2}
$$

and $y=0$ again at take-off for the time of flight $t_{f}>0$

$$
0=v_{0y}t_{f}-\tfrac12gt_{f}^{2}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
t_{f}= \frac{2v_{0y}}{g}
$$

i.e. the time up is $t_{up}=v_{0y}/g$ and the total time in the air is
twice that.

$$
t_{up}=\frac{5.82}{9.81}\approx0.59\;{\rm s},\qquad 
t_{f}=2t_{up}\approx1.19\;{\rm s}
$$

Hence on the level ground

$$
R = v_{0x}t_{f}=v_{0x}\frac{2v_{0y}}{g}
     =\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{g}\sin2\theta
$$

is the familiar range formula.  In numbers

$$
R =\frac{(14.3)^{2}}{9.81}\sin48^{\circ}
   =\frac{204.5}{9.81}\times0.7431
   \approx 20.85\times0.7431\approx 1.5\!-\!1.6\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}
$$

about $1.5\times10^{1}\,{\rm m}$ down range, $ \approx 15\!-\!16\,{\rm m}$
from the launch point, $ \approx 15.5\,{\rm m}$ with $g=9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$.
With the often used $g\approx9.8\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$ this is $R\approx15.5\;{\rm m}$,
essentially $15\,{\rm m}$ to the usual two significant figures.  The
$15.5\,{\rm m}$ is $v_{0x}t_{f}\approx13.06\,{\rm m/s}\times1.186\,{\rm s}$.

*Remark:*  $R=v_{0}^{2}\sin2\theta/g$ is the closed form.  For $\theta=24^{\circ}$
$\sin2\theta=\sin48^{\circ}$ and the maximum range for this speed would be
$v_{0}^{2}/g$ at $45^{\circ}$.

The 21 V is applied to the series chain

* $R_{1}$ in series with the $R_{2}\!\parallel\!R_{3}$ combination

so that the current which leaves the battery is the current which goes
through $R_{1}$ and then divides between $R_{2}$ and $R_{3}$.

The parallel combination

$$
R_{23}=R_{2}\parallel R_{3}=\frac{R_{2}R_{3}}{R_{2}+R_{3}}
      =\frac{65\times 46}{65+46}\;{\rm \Omega}
      =\frac{2990}{111}\;{\rm \Omega}\approx 26.9\;{\rm \Omega}
$$

is in series with $R_{1}$,

$$
R_{T}=R_{1}+R_{23}=32+\frac{2990}{111}
     =\frac{6542}{111}\;{\rm \Omega}\approx 58.9\;{\rm \Omega}
$$

so that the total current drawn from the ideal 21 V source is

$$
I_{T}=\frac{V}{R_{T}}=\frac{21}{R_{1}+R_{23}}
     =21\frac{111}{6542}\approx 0.36\;{\rm A}
$$

which is the current in $R_{1}$.  The voltage which appears across the
$R_{2}\!\parallel\!R_{3}$ node is

$$
V_{23}=V-I_{T}R_{1}=V\frac{R_{23}}{R_{1}+R_{23}}
      \approx 21-0.356\times32\approx 9.6\;{\rm V},
$$

the same voltage being present across $R_{2}$ and across $R_{3}$.
Hence

$$
I_{2}=\frac{V_{23}}{R_{2}}
     =\frac{V}{R_{1}+R_{2}R_{3}/(R_{2}+R_{3})}\frac{1}{R_{2}}
$$

and in closed form

$$
I_{2}=V\,\frac{R_{3}}{R_{1}(R_{2}+R_{3})+R_{2}R_{3}}
     =\frac{21\times46}{32(65+46)+65\times46}
     =\frac{966}{6542}\ {\rm A}\approx1.5\times10^{-1}\ {\rm A}
$$

i.e. about $0.14\!-\!0.15\;{\rm A}$, $\approx 148\;{\rm mA}$, flowing
from the $R_{1}$ node through $R_{2}$ back to the battery.  The
corresponding current in $R_{3}$ is

$$
I_{3}=V\frac{R_{2}}{R_{1}(R_{2}+R_{3})+R_{2}R_{3}}
     \approx0.208\;{\rm A},
$$

and $I_{2}+I_{3}=I_{T}\approx0.356\;{\rm A}$ is the total current taken
from the 21 V ideal source.  The $0.356\;{\rm A}$ is the current in the
series resistor $R_{1}$.

*Remark.*  If you meant the $R_{1}+R_{2}$ series string to be in
parallel with $R_{3}$, the $R_{1}\!-\!R_{2}$ branch current is
$V/(R_{1}+R_{2})=21/97\approx0.22\;{\rm A}$, which is the current that
flows in $R_{2}$ in that topology, with $I_{3}=21/46\approx0.46\;{\rm A}$
in the $R_{3}$ branch.

For a mass–spring system on a frictionless surface the mechanical energy
is conserved

$$E=\frac12k x^{2}+\frac12 m v^{2}= {\rm const}$$

so that with the amplitude $A$

$$E_{0}= \frac12kA^{2}= \frac12k x^{2}+\frac12 m v^{2} $$

Hence

$$v(x)=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}\Big(A^{2}-x^{2}\Big)}$$

is the speed at the displacement $x$ from equilibrium.

Here

* $k=169\;{\rm N/m}$,
* $m=0.77\;{\rm kg}$,
* $A=14.1\;{\rm cm}=0.141\;{\rm m}$,
* $x=4.8\;{\rm cm}=0.048\;{\rm m}$,

so that

$$
\frac{k}{m}=\frac{169}{0.77}=2.19\times10^{2}\ {\rm s^{-2}}
$$

and

$$
A^{2}-x^{2}=0.141^{2}-0.048^{2}=0.019881-0.002304
      =1.7577\times10^{-2}\ {\rm m^{2}} .
$$

$$
v=\sqrt{\frac{169}{0.77}\big(0.141^{2}-0.048^{2}\big)}
  =\sqrt{219.48\times1.7577\times10^{-2}}\;{\rm m/s}
  \approx\sqrt{3.86}\;{\rm m/s}
  \approx 1.9\!-\!2.0\;{\rm m/s}
$$

about $1.96\;{\rm m/s}$ in magnitude, directed toward the equilibrium
position.  The total energy is $E_{0}=\tfrac12kA^{2}\approx1.68\;{\rm J}$,
of which $\tfrac12kx^{2}\approx0.19\;{\rm J}$ is elastic at $x=4.8\;{\rm cm}$,
leaving $\tfrac12mv^{2}\approx1.49\;{\rm J}$ as kinetic.

For a body that rolls without slipping the loss of gravitational potential
is the translational kinetic energy of the centre of mass plus the
rotational kinetic energy about the centre of mass

$$ \Delta U = \Delta K_{tr}+\Delta K_{rot}$$

$$m g h = \frac12 m v_{cm}^{2}+\frac12 I_{cm}\omega^{2} $$

For rolling without slipping

$$v_{cm}= \omega r\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \omega =v_{cm}/r $$

For a uniform solid sphere

$$I_{cm}= \frac25 m r^{2}$$

so that

$$K_{rot}= \frac12 I_{cm}\omega^{2}
       =\frac12\frac25 m r^{2}\frac{v_{cm}^{2}}{r^{2}}
       =\frac15 m v_{cm}^{2} .$$

Hence

$$m g h = \frac12 m v^{2}+\frac15 m v^{2}
       =\frac{7}{10}m v^{2}$$

and the mass cancels,

$$v^{2}= \frac{10}{7}\,g h\;, \qquad 
v=\sqrt{\frac{10}{7}g h}
   =\sqrt{\frac{2g h}{1+I/mr^{2}}}$$

the familiar rolling result.  With $h=1.94\;{\rm m}$,

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{10}{7}\times 9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}\times1.94\;{\rm m}}
  =\sqrt{\frac{10}{7}\times19.03\;{\rm m^{2}/s^{2}}}
  =\sqrt{27.19\;{\rm m^{2}/s^{2}}}
  \approx 5.2\!-\!5.3\;{\rm m/s}$$

about $5.21\;{\rm m/s}$ down the incline for the centre of mass.  
The corresponding angular speed is $\omega=v/r$.

In the idealised $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ limit $v\approx

$$ \frac{mv^{2}}{r}=\frac{GM_{\oplus}m}{r^{2}}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
v^{2}=\frac{GM_{\oplus}}{r} $$

so that with $r=R_{\oplus}+h$

$$T=\frac{2\pi r}{v}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{GM_{\oplus}}}$$

is the Kepler period.  In SI

* $R_{\oplus}=6371\;{\rm km}=6.371\times10^{6}\ {\rm m}$
* $h=1680\;{\rm km}=1.680\times10^{6}\ {\rm m}$

$$r=R_{\oplus}+h=6371+1680=8051\;{\rm km}=8.051\times10^{6}\ {\rm m}$$

Hence

$$
\frac{r^{3}}{GM_{\oplus}}=
\frac{(8.051\times10^{6}\,{\rm m})^{3}}{3.986\times10^{14}\ {\rm m^{3}s^{-2}}}
\approx1.31\times10^{6}\ {\rm s^{2}}
$$

$$
\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{GM_{\oplus}}}\approx\sqrt{1.309\times10^{6}}\approx
1.144\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}
$$

and

$$
T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{GM_{\oplus}}}
   \approx2\pi\times1.144\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}

$$

i.e.

$$

\approx 119\!-\!120\ {\rm min}
$$

about $7.19\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}\simeq1\ {\rm h}\;59.8\ {\rm min}$,

In the inelastic impact the linear momentum of the bullet is taken up by
the block+bullet system

$$m_{b}v_{b}=(M+m_{b})v_{0}$$

and after the impact the kinetic energy of the $(M+m_{b})$ system is
turned into gravitational potential

$$\frac12\,(M+m_{b})v_{0}^{2}=(M+m_{b})g\,h $$

so that the speed just after the impact is independent of the masses

$$v_{0}=\sqrt{2gh}$$

on the swing.  With $h=0.143\;{\rm m}$

$$v_{0}=\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.143}\approx\sqrt{2.81}\approx1.67\;{\rm m/s}$$

is the speed of the block+bullet immediately after the bullet is
embedded.  Hence from momentum

$$v_{b}= \frac{M+m_{b}}{m_{b}}\,v_{0}
      =\frac{M+m_{b}}{m_{b}}\sqrt{2gh}\approx
      \frac{4.46+0.024}{0.024}\sqrt{2gh}$$

$$v_{b}\approx 1.87\times10^{2}\times1.68\;{\rm m/s}\approx 3.1\!-\!3.2\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$$

about $3.1\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$ in the direction of the swing, 
$\approx 313\;{\rm m/s}$ with the numbers quoted.  Ignoring the $24\;{\rm g}$
in the total mass, $v_{b}\simeq (M/m_{b})\sqrt{2gh}\approx 3.11\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$, essentially the same.

For the ball + spring system the mechanical energy is conserved in the
absence of dissipation.  Put the zero of gravitational potential in the
initially compressed position $y=0$ and let $y>0$ be upwards.  In the
initial state

* $E_{s,i}=\dfrac12k\Delta^{2}$ , $\Delta =10.4\,{\rm cm}$,
* $E_{k,i}=0$,
* $E_{g,i}=0$,

so that, with the mass of the spring neglected,

$$E_{i}= \frac12k\Delta^{2} .$$

If the ball is allowed to rise to a height $H$ above the initial
compressed position the spring is no longer in contact with the ball,
$E_{s,f}=0$, $E_{k,f}=0$ at the top of the motion and

$$E_{f}=E_{g,f}=mgH .$$

Hence, on the idealised energy balance

$$E_{i}=E_{f}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\frac12k\Delta^{2}=mgH
$$

i.e. in the ideal limit

$$
H_{0}=\frac{k\Delta^{2}}{2mg}
$$

above the position in which the ball is first put on the spring.
With

* $k=733\;{\rm N\,m^{-1}}$,
* $\Delta =0.104\;{\rm m}$,
* $m=0.070\;{\rm kg}$,
* $g=9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$,

$$
E_{s}= \frac12k\Delta^{2}
      =\frac12(733)(0.104)^{2}\approx 3.96\;{\rm J},
$$

and

$$
H_{0}= \frac{E_{s}}{mg}
     =\frac{3.96}{0.07\times9.81}\approx 5.7\!-\!5.8\;{\rm m}
$$

above the initial compressed position.  In round numbers

$$
H_{0}\approx 5.8\;{\rm m}
$$

above the point at which the ball is placed on the compressed spring.
The $ \Delta =10.4\,{\rm cm}$ of rise which is obtained while the spring
is still in contact with the ball is contained in this number.  If the
height is measured from the unstressed length of the spring, i.e. from
the point of loss of contact, the gravitational work $mg\Delta$ done
during the $ \Delta$ of spring expansion has to be removed,

$$
\frac12m v_{0}^{2}= \frac12k\Delta^{2}-mg\Delta ,
\qquad 
h_{0}= \frac{v_{0}^{2}}{2g}
     =\frac{k\Delta^{2}}{2mg}-\Delta ,
$$

so that the free flight above the natural length of the spring is

$$
h_{0}=H_{0}-\Delta\approx5.77-0.104\approx5.67\;{\rm m}\approx5.7\;{\rm m}
$$

above the unstressed spring, the $ \approx 1.8\%$ $mg\Delta$ correction
being $mg\Delta\approx0.07\,{\rm J}$ compared with $E_{s}\approx3.96\,{\rm J}$.
Neglecting the $mg\Delta$ term altogether gives the often quoted
estimate $h_{0}\simeq k\Delta^{2}/2mg\approx5.8\,{\rm m}$ of free flight,
which is the $H_{0}$ quoted above.

For the ball + spring system the mechanical energy is conserved in the
idealised limit

$$E_{i}=E_{s}+E_{g}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
E_{f}=E_{g}\;,$$

the spring being taken to be massless and the air drag to be zero.
Put the zero of gravitational potential at the initial, compressed,
position of the ball, $x_{0}=8.5\,{\rm cm}=0.085\,{\rm m}$, and let $H$
be the height of the ball above that initial position when the
instantaneous velocity vanishes.  With the spring unstressed at the
top of the motion

$$E_{i}=U_{e}(x_{0})+0=\frac12k x_{0}^{2}, \qquad 
E_{f}=mgH+0, $$

so that in the ideal energy balance

$$ \frac12k x_{0}^{2}=mgH $$

is the height measured from the initial compressed position.  In
numbers

$$U_{e}= \frac12\,859\,(0.085)^{2}\approx 3.10\;{\rm J}, $$

$$H_{0}= \frac{U_{e}}{mg}
      =\frac{\tfrac12k x_{0}^{2}}{m g}
      =\frac{3.10}{0.15\times9.81}\approx 2.1\;{\rm m}$$

above the compressed position, i.e. about $2.1\,{\rm m}$ of rise
measured from the point at which the ball is set on the spring.

If the rise is referred to the point at which the ball actually loses
contact with the spring, the natural length of the spring, the
$mgx_{0}$ of gravitational work done in the $x_{0}$ of decompression
has to be taken out of the elastic energy.  The launch speed at the
natural length is

$$ \frac12 m v_{0}^{2}= \frac12k x_{0}^{2}-mgx_{0}, $$

$$v_{0}= \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}x_{0}^{2}-2gx_{0}}\approx 6.3\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}},$$

and the free flight above the unstressed spring is

$$h_{f}= \frac{v_{0}^{2}}{2g}
      =\frac{\,k x_{0}^{2}/m-2gx_{0}\,}{2g}
      =\frac{\tfrac12k x_{0}^{2}}{mg}-x_{0}
      \approx 2.02\;{\rm m},$$

so that the total rise from the initial compressed position is
$h_{f}+x_{0}\approx2.11\,{\rm m}$, essentially the $2.1\,{\rm m}$ quoted
above.  The $2.0\,{\rm m}$ of free flight is the quantity usually quoted
as the height gained after the ball has left the spring.

In an insulated container the heat lost by the hot iron is taken up by the cold water

$$Q_{lost}=Q_{gained}$$

$$m_{Fe}c_{Fe}\,(T_{Fe,i}-T_{f})=m_{w}c_{w}\,(T_{f}-T_{w,i})$$

with

* $m_{Fe}=0.83\;{\rm kg}$ , $c_{Fe}=450\;{\rm J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}$ , $T_{Fe,i}=77^{\circ}{\rm C}$
* $m_{w}=0.50\;{\rm kg}$ , $c_{w}=4186\;{\rm J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}$ , $T_{w,i}=26.4^{\circ}{\rm C}$

The heat capacities are

$$C_{Fe}=m_{Fe}c_{Fe}=0.83\times450=3.735\times10^{2}\ {\rm J\,K^{-1}}$$
$$C_{w}=m_{w}c_{w}=0.50\times4186=2.093\times10^{3}\ {\rm J\,K^{-1}}$$

Hence

$$C_{Fe}\,(T_{Fe,i}-T_{f})=C_{w}\,(T_{f}-T_{w,i})$$

$$373.5\,(77-T_{f})=2093\,(T_{f}-26.4)$$

$$373.5\times77-373.5T_{f}=2093T_{f}-2093\times26.4$$

$$28\,759.5+55\,255.2=(2093+373.5)T_{f}$$

$$84\,014.7=2\,466.5\,T_{f}$$

$$T_{f}= \frac{84\,014.7}{2\,466.5}\approx 3.41\times10^{1}\;^{\circ}{\rm C}$$

$$T_{f}\approx 34\!-\!35^{\circ}{\rm C}$$

about $34.1^{\circ}{\rm C}$ on the numbers quoted, i.e. $\approx 34^{\circ}{\rm C}$ in the laboratory.  The iron cools from $77^{\circ}{\rm C}$ to $\sim34^{\circ}{\rm C}$ while the water warms from $26.4^{\circ}{\rm C}$ to $\sim34^{\circ}{\rm C}$, the common final equilibrium temperature in the idealised no-loss calorimeter.

In the perfectly inelastic impact the linear momentum in the horizontal
direction is conserved

$$m_{1}v_{1}+m_{2}0=(m_{1}+m_{2})v_{*}$$

so that the common speed just after the impact is

$$v_{*}=\frac{m_{1}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\,v_{1}
      =\frac{2.32}{2.32+1.71}\times 9.5\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      =\frac{22.04}{4.03}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}\approx 5.47\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}} $$

After the impact the only horizontal work is that of kinetic friction.
For the mass $M=m_{1}+m_{2}$

$$F_{k}=\mu_{k}Mg$$

and

$$W_{f}= -F_{k}s =-\mu_{k}Mg\,s$$

is the loss of mechanical energy.  With $K_{*}= \tfrac12 Mv_{*}^{2}$,

$$0-K_{*}=W_{f}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
\frac12 Mv_{*}^{2}= \mu_{k}Mg\,s ,$$

i.e. the mass cancels,

$$s=\frac{v_{*}^{2}}{2\mu_{k}g}
   =\frac{1}{2\mu_{k}g}\left[\frac{m_{1}v_{1}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\right]^{2} .
$$

With the numbers

$$v_{*}\approx5.47\;{\rm m/s},\qquad 
2\mu_{k}g=2\times0.41\times9.81=8.04\;{\rm m/s^{2}},$$

$$s\approx\frac{(5.47)^{2}}{2\times0.41\times9.81}\approx
\frac{29.9}{8.04}\approx3.7\!-\!3.8\;{\rm m},$$

about $3.7\;{\rm m}$ of sliding.  Using $v_{*}=22.04/4.03\;{\rm m/s}$,

$$s=\frac{\,v_{*}^{2}}{2\mu_{k}g}\approx3.72\;{\rm m}$$

of travel after the impact, the $M$ cancelling so that the result is
essentially $v_{1}^{2}m_{1}^{2}/[(m_{1}+m_{2})^{2}2\mu_{k}g]$.  This is
$\approx 3.7\;{\rm m}$ before the combined $4.03\;{\rm kg}$ mass comes to
rest.

For a charge moving perpendicular to a uniform $B$ the magnetic Lorentz
force provides the centripetal force

$$
F_{c}=F_{B}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\frac{mv^{2}}{r}=qvB
$$

so that, in the non-relativistic limit $v\ll c$,

$$
r=\frac{mv}{qB}
$$

is the Larmor / cyclotron radius.  With $v\perp B$

* $m_{p}=1.673\times10^{-27}\ {\rm kg}$
* $q_{p}=1.602\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}$
* $v=3.9\times10^{6}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$
* $B=1.03\ {\rm T}$

$$
r=\frac{m_{p}v}{q_{p}B}
   =\frac{\,1.673\times10^{-27}\ {\rm kg}\times3.9\times10^{6}\ {\rm m/s}\,}
          {\,1.602\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}\times1.03\ {\rm T}\,}
$$

$$
r=\frac{6.52\times10^{-21}}{1.65\times10^{-19}}\ {\rm m}
  \approx 3.96\times10^{-2}\ {\rm m}
$$

i.e. about $4.0\times10^{-2}\ {\rm m}$ of curvature.  In more convenient
units

$$
r\approx 0.040\ {\rm m}\approx 39\!-\!40\ {\rm mm}\approx 4.0\ {\rm cm}
$$

about $39.6\;{\rm mm}$ with the numbers quoted, $\,r\approx m v/qB\,$.
The sign of the charge gives the sense of rotation, the magnitude is
as above.  Using $m_{p}=1.67\times10^{-27}\,$kg this is $r\approx3.95\times10^{-2}\,$m $\approx 39.5\,$mm, essentially the $\sim 40\,$mm cyclotron orbit quoted in the literature.

For a moving source and a stationary observer the Doppler shift is

$$f' = f\,\frac{v}{v\mp v_{s}}$$

$-$ for source moving toward the observer, $+$ for source moving away.

$v$ = speed of sound, $v_{s}$ = speed of source

$$f' = 525\;{\rm Hz}\;\frac{343}{343-28.5}$$

$$f' = 525\;\frac{343}{314.5}\approx 525\times1.091$$

$$f' \approx 5.7\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}$$

about $48\;{\rm Hz}$ up-shifted from the 525 Hz emitted, $\approx 572\!-\!573\;{\rm Hz}$ heard on approach.  The shift goes to zero as $v_{s}\to0$ and diverges as $v_{s}\to v$.

For a particle of mass $m$ at the surface $R$ the mechanical energy is

$$
E=\frac12 m v^{2}-\frac{GMm}{R}\;,
$$

and the limiting escape velocity is obtained for $E\to0$ at $r\to\infty$,
i.e. for

$$
\frac12 m v_{e}^{2}-\frac{GMm}{R}=0\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
v_{e}(R)=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}\;,
$$

the familiar $v_{e}\propto\sqrt{M/R}$ law.

For the Earth

$$
v_{e\oplus}=\sqrt{\frac{2GM_{\oplus}}{R_{\oplus}}}
$$

is

$$
v_{e\oplus}= \sqrt{\frac{2\times6.674\times10^{-11}\,
{\rm N\,m^{2}kg^{-2}}\times5.972\times10^{24}{\rm kg}}
{6.371\times10^{6}{\rm m}}}
      =\sqrt{1.25\times10^{8}}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      \approx 1.12\times10^{4}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}\approx 11.2\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}},
$$

the usual $11.19\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$.

For the planet

$$
M_{p}=3.19\,M_{\oplus},\qquad R_{p}=2.47\,R_{\oplus},
$$

so that

$$
v_{e,p}= \sqrt{\frac{2G M_{p}}{R_{p}}}
       =\sqrt{\frac{2G M_{\oplus}}{R_{\oplus}}
               \frac{3.19}{2.47}}
       =\sqrt{\frac{3.19}{2.47}}\;v_{e\oplus}\; .
$$

In numbers

$$
M_{p}=3.19\times5.972\times10^{24}\approx1.90\times10^{25}\ {\rm kg},
$$
$$
R_{p}=2.47\times6.371\times10^{6}\approx1.57\times10^{7}\ {\rm m},
$$

and

$$
v_{e,p}= \sqrt{\frac{2\times6.674\times10^{-11}\times1.90\times10^{25}}
{1.57\times10^{7}}}
       \approx\sqrt{1.62\times10^{8}}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
       \approx1.27\times10^{4}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}} .
$$

Hence, with the usual Earth value $v_{e\oplus}\simeq11.19\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$,

$$
v_{e,p}\approx\sqrt{1.291}\;v_{e\oplus}\approx1.14\,v_{e\oplus}
      \approx 1.27\times10^{4}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}\approx 12\!-\!13\ {\rm km\,s^{-1}},
$$

about $12.7\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$, i.e. $\approx 12.7$–$12.8\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$,
$12.73\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ with $v_{e\oplus}=11.186\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$, 
$14\%$ larger than the terrestrial escape speed.  This is the
$\sqrt{M/R}$ scaling $v_{e,p}= \sqrt{3.19/2.47}\,v_{e\oplus}$ quoted
above.

For a string fixed at both ends the normal modes are

$$L=n\frac{\lambda_{n}}{2}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\lambda_{n}=\frac{2L}{n}$$

and the wave speed on the string is

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$$

so that

$$f_{n}=\frac{v}{\lambda_{n}}=\frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}\;, \qquad 
n=1,2,\dots$$

is the $n$-th harmonic.  For the fundamental $n=1$

$$f_{1}=\frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} $$

is the speed of transverse waves on the string.

* $L=0.74\;{\rm m}$
* $T=62\;{\rm N}$
* $\mu =7.7\;{\rm g\,m^{-1}}=7.7\times10^{-3}\;{\rm kg\,m^{-1}}$

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}=\sqrt{\frac{62}{7.7\times10^{-3}}}
      =\sqrt{8.05\times10^{3}}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}\approx 8.97\times10^{1}\;{\rm m/s}$$

Hence

$$f_{1}=\frac{v}{2L}=\frac{\, \sqrt{T/\mu}\,}{2L}
      =\frac{1}{2\times0.74}\sqrt{\frac{62}{0.0077}}
      \approx\frac{89.7\;{\rm m/s}}{1.48\;{\rm m}}
      \approx 6.0\!-\!6.1\times10^{1}\ {\rm Hz}$$

about $60\!-\!61\;{\rm Hz}$, essentially the $60\;{\rm Hz}$ mains note.  
The $n$-th mode is $f_{n}=n\,f_{1}\approx n\times60.6\;{\rm Hz}$.

*Remark:* $v\approx 90\;{\rm m/s}$ is the phase speed of the transverse wave on the string.  With the usual $f_{1}=v/2L$ this is the familiar guitar-string result.

For the motion down the plane the tangential acceleration is the
component of weight down the plane minus the kinetic friction force
per unit mass

* $N=mg\cos\theta$
* $F_{k}=\mu_{k}N=\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta$

so that on the plane

$$
a=g\sin\theta-\frac{F_{k}}{m}=g\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]
$$

is constant.  With $v_{0}=0$

$$
v^{2}=v_{0}^{2}+2as=2gs\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]
$$

is the work–energy form.  On the $30^{\circ}$ plane

$$
\sin\theta = \sin30^{\circ}=0.5000,\qquad 
\cos\theta =\cos30^{\circ}=0.8660,
$$

$$
\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta
=0.5000-0.14\times0.8660
=0.5000-0.1212\approx0.3788 .
$$

Hence

$$
a=g\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]
\approx9.81\times0.3788\approx3.71\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}
$$

down the plane and

$$
v=\sqrt{2as}
   =\sqrt{2g s\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]}
$$

For $s=9.7\;{\rm m}$

$$
v=\sqrt{2\times9.81\times9.7\times0.3788}
  =\sqrt{7.21\times10^{1}}\;{\rm m/s}
  \approx 8.4\!-\!8.5\;{\rm m/s}
$$

down the incline, about $8.5\;{\rm m/s}$ in magnitude.  With the
numbers quoted $v\approx\sqrt{72.1}\approx8.49\;{\rm m/s}$, i.e. $\approx
3.7\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ acceleration down the $30^{\circ}$ slope.  The
$1/2mv^{2}$ gain is $m g s\big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\big]$, the
gravitational work $mgs\sin\theta$ less the frictional dissipation
$\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta\,s$.

For a circular Kepler orbit the gravitational pull provides the
centripetal acceleration

$$
\frac{v^{2}}{r}=\frac{GM}{r^{2}}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
v(r)=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}
$$

so that the time for one revolution is

$$
T=\frac{2\pi r}{v}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{GM}}\;,
$$

the Kepler third law.  The geocentric radius of the orbit is

$$
r=R_{\oplus}+h
$$

$$
r=6371\;{\rm km}+1823\;{\rm km}=8194\;{\rm km}=8.194\times10^{6}\ {\rm m}
$$

Hence

$$
T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{GM}}
   =2\pi\sqrt{\frac{(8.194\times10^{6}\,{\rm m})^{3}}
                 {3.986\times10^{14}\ {\rm m^{3}s^{-2}}}}
$$

$$
r^{3}=5.50\times10^{20}\ {\rm m^{3}},\qquad 
\frac{r^{3}}{GM}= \frac{5.5016\times10^{20}}{3.986\times10^{14}}
      \approx1.38\times10^{6}\ {\rm s^{2}}
$$

$$
\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{GM}}\approx\sqrt{1.3802\times10^{6}}\approx
1.175\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}
$$

and

$$
T\approx2\pi\times1.175\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}\approx7.3\!-\!7.4\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}
$$

$$
T\approx7.38\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}\approx\frac{7.38\times10^{3}}{60}
      \approx1.23\times10^{2}\ {\rm min}
$$

i.e. about $7.4\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}\simeq 122\!-\!124\ {\rm min}$,
$\approx 2.0\ {\rm h}$, for the nominal $R_{\oplus}=6371\ {\rm km}$.
With the usual $R_{\oplus}=6378\ {\rm km}$ this is $T\approx7.40\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}\approx123.3\ {\rm min}$, essentially the familiar $\sim 2\ {\rm h}$ low-Earth orbit period.  The $2\pi\sqrt{r^{3}/GM}$ form is the usual Kepler expression.

For a frictionless bank the normal reaction $N$ has to supply the
centripetal force and the component of the weight in the plane of the
curve.  With the bank $\theta$ measured from the horizontal

* $N\cos\theta = mg$  normal to the road
* $N\sin\theta = m v^{2}/r$  horizontal towards the centre of the curve

so that on eliminating $N$

$$
\tan\theta=\frac{N\sin\theta}{N\cos\theta}
          =\frac{mv^{2}/r}{mg}
          =\frac{v^{2}}{rg}\;,
$$

the familiar “ideal’’ banking condition.  In the ideal case the
required centripetal force is provided by the component of the weight
down the plane of the bank and no lateral tyre force is needed.

For

* $r=162\;{\rm m}$
* $v=110\;{\rm km\,h^{-1}}=110/3.6=30.56\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$
* $g=9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$

$$
\frac{v^{2}}{rg}=
\frac{(30.56)^{2}}{162\times9.81}
      =\frac{9.34\times10^{2}}{1.588\times10^{3}}
      \approx 0.59 .
$$

Hence

$$
\theta_{\rm ideal}= \arctan\!\left[\frac{v^{2}}{rg}\right]
      =\arctan\!\left[\frac{(110/3.6)^{2}}{162\times9.81}\right]
      \approx\arctan 0.588\approx 3.0\!-\!3.1\times10^{1}\,^{\circ}
$$

i.e. about $30\!-\!31^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, $\approx 30.4\!-\!30.6^{\circ}$
on the usual $g=9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$ value, $\approx 30.5^{\circ}$ bank
towards the centre of the curve.  With the often used $g\approx10\;{\rm
m\,s^{-2}}$ this is $\tan\theta\approx0.576$ i.e. $\theta\approx30^{\circ}$,
the textbook ideal banking for $110\;{\rm km\,h^{-1}}$ on a $162\;{\rm m}$
radius.  The bank is measured from the horizontal, the inner edge being
lower than the outer edge.

The speed has to be in SI before you can use $v^{2}=u^{2}+2as$.

* $u=40\;{\rm km\,h^{-1}}$

$$
u=\frac{40\times10^{3}}{3600}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}=\frac{100}{9}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
\approx 11.1\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

is the speed that is kept up during the driver's reaction time.

Reaction, $t_{r}=1.17\;{\rm s}$,  $a\approx0$

$$
s_{r}=u\,t_{r}= \frac{100}{9}\times1.17\approx 13.0\;{\rm m}
$$

is the distance covered before the brakes are actually applied.  In
fact $s_{r}=117/9=13.0\;{\rm m}$ exactly for the numbers quoted.

Braking, $a=-a_{b}$ with $a_{b}=4.8\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$, $v=0$, $u_{b}=u$

$$
0=u^{2}-2a_{b}s_{b}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
s_{b}=\frac{u^{2}}{2a_{b}}
$$

$$
s_{b}= \frac{\left(100/9\right)^{2}}{2\times4.8}
     =\frac{10\,000}{81\times9.6}
