For a reversible Carnot engine the thermal efficiency is set by the two
reservoir temperatures only

$$ \eta_{Carnot}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}} $$

with the temperatures on an absolute scale.

* Hot reservoir
$$
T_{H}=344^{\circ}{\rm C}=344+273.15=617.15\;{\rm K}\approx 617\;{\rm K}
$$

* Cold reservoir
$$
T_{C}=72^{\circ}{\rm C}=72+273.15=345.15\;{\rm K}\approx 345\;{\rm K}
$$

Hence

$$
\eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}
      =1-\frac{345.15}{617.15}
      =1-0.5595
      \approx 0.44
$$

i.e. about $44\%$ of the heat taken from the hot reservoir can be turned
into work in the ideal Carnot limit.

For a cycle

$$
W = \eta_{C}\,Q_{H}
$$

with $Q_{H}=7.1\;{\rm kJ}$ absorbed from the hot side per cycle,

$$
W = \left[1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}\right]Q_{H}
   =\frac{T_{H}-T_{C}}{T_{H}}Q_{H}
   =\frac{617.15-345.15}{617.15}\times7.1\;{\rm kJ}
$$

$$
W\approx0.440\!-\!0.441\times7.1\;{\rm kJ}\approx3.1\!-\!3.13\;{\rm kJ}
$$

per cycle.  With the usual $T(K)=T(^{\circ}{\rm C})+273$ approximation

$$
\eta_{C}\approx1-\frac{345}{617}=0.4405,\qquad 
W\approx0.4405\times7.1\approx3.13\;{\rm kJ}
$$

The heat rejected to the cold reservoir in the same cycle is

$$
Q_{C}=Q_{H}-W\approx7.1-3.13\approx3.97\;{\rm kJ},
$$

and indeed $Q_{C}/Q_{H}=T_{C}/T_{H}$ for a reversible Carnot cycle.  This is the ideal upper-limit work; any real engine operating between the same two temperatures will do less.

For the hanging mass and the disk the tangential and the translational
kinematics are linked by no slip

$$a_{t}=R\alpha\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \alpha=\frac{a}{R}$$

For the hanging mass $m$

$$ \sum F_{y}=m a $$
$$ m g-T=m a\tag{1}$$

For the disk the only external torque about the axle is the torque of
the string tension

$$ \tau =TR = I\alpha $$

For a uniform solid disc

$$ I_{0}= \frac12 M_{d}R^{2}$$

so that with $\alpha=a/R$

$$TR = I_{0}\frac{a}{R}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
T=\frac{I_{0}}{R^{2}}\,a
   =\frac12M_{d}\,a  \tag{2}$$

Insert (2) in (1)

$$ m g-\frac{I_{0}}{R^{2}}a=m a $$

$$ a\Bigl[m+\frac{I_{0}}{R^{2}}\Bigr]=mg $$

$$ a=\frac{mg}{\,m+I_{0}/R^{2}\,}
   =\frac{mg}{\,m+\tfrac12M_{d}\,}$$

The $R$ cancels for a solid disc.  With

* $M_{d}=1.75\;{\rm kg}$
* $m=2.08\;{\rm kg}$
* $I_{0}/R^{2}= \tfrac12M_{d}=0.875\;{\rm kg}$

$$ a=\frac{2.08\times 9.81}{2.08+0.875}\;{\rm m/s^{2}}
   =\frac{20.40}{2.955}\;{\rm m/s^{2}}
   \approx 6.9\;{\rm m/s^{2}} $$

down the string, about $0.70\,g$.  In terms of the disc

$$ \alpha=\frac{a}{R}=\frac{6.9}{0.09}\approx 7.7\times10^{1}\ {\rm rad/s^{2}} $$

and the string tension is $T=\tfrac12M_{d}a\approx 6.0\;{\rm N}$.
The result is independent of the 9 cm radius for a solid disc; 
$I_{0}/R^{2}=M_{d}/2$ is all that matters.  With $g=9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$
$a\approx6.90\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ essentially the same.

$$v=105\;{\rm km\,h^{-1}}=\frac{105\times10^{3}}{3600}=29.17\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}

For a uniform solid disc about its central axis

For a string fixed at both ends the standing wave condition is

$$L=n\frac{\lambda_{n}}{2}\qquad n=1,2,\dots$$

so that for the $n^{\rm th}$ mode

$$\lambda_{n}=\frac{2L}{n}\;,$$

and the phase speed of transverse waves on the string is

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$$

where $T$ is the tension and $\mu$ the mass per unit length.  Hence

$$f_{n}=\frac{v}{\lambda_{n}}=\frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} .$$

* $L=1.22\;{\rm m}$
* $T=158\;{\rm N}$
* $\mu =2.2\;{\rm g\,m^{-1}}=2.2\times10^{-3}\;{\rm kg\,m^{-1}}$

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}=\sqrt{\frac{158}{2.2\times10^{-3}}}
      =\sqrt{7.18\times10^{4}}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}\approx 2.68\times10^{2}\;{\rm m/s}$$

The fundamental wavelength is

$$\lambda_{1}=2L=2\times1.22=2.44\;{\rm m}$$

so that

$$f_{1}=\frac{v}{\lambda_{1}}=\frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}
      =\frac{2.68\times10^{2}}{2.44}\approx 1.1\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}$$

For a mass-spring system on a frictionless surface the mechanical energy
is conserved

$$E =U_{s}+K=\frac12k x^{2}+\frac12 m v^{2}= {\rm const}$$

At the turning point $v=0$ and $|x|=A$ so that

$$E_{0}= \frac12kA^{2}$$

is the total energy.  At a general displacement $x$

$$ \frac12kA^{2}= \frac12k x^{2}+\frac12 m v^{2}$$

so that

$$v(x)=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}\Big(A^{2}-x^{2}\Big)}
      =\omega\sqrt{A^{2}-x^{2}},\qquad 
\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$$

is the speed at the displacement $x$.

Here

* $m=0.70\;{\rm kg}$
* $k=360\;{\rm N\,m^{-1}}$
* $A=17.6\;{\rm cm}=0.176\;{\rm m}$
* $x=13.4\;{\rm cm}=0.134\;{\rm m}$

$$\omega=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}=\sqrt{\frac{360}{0.70}}
      =\sqrt{5.14\times10^{2}}\approx 2.27\times10^{1}\ {\rm s^{-1}}$$

$$A^{2}-x^{2}=0.176^{2}-0.134^{2}=0.030976-0.017956
          =1.302\times10^{-2}\ {\rm m^{2}}$$

Hence

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{360}{0.70}\,(1.302\times10^{-2})}
   =\sqrt{6.70}\ {\rm m/s}\approx 2.6\ {\rm m/s}$$

in magnitude.  In terms of energy

$$E_{0}=\tfrac12kA^{2}= \tfrac12(360)(0.176)^{2}=5.58\ {\rm J}$$
$$U(x)=\tfrac12k x^{2}= \tfrac12(360)(0.134)^{2}=3.23\ {\rm J}$$
$$K(x)=E_{0}-U(x)=2.34\ {\rm J},\qquad 
v=\sqrt{2K/m}\approx2.59\;{\rm m/s},$$

directed toward the equilibrium position.  The sign is opposite to the
sign of $x$; the magnitude is $\approx 2.6\;{\rm m/s}$, about $2.59\;{\rm m/s}$ with the numbers quoted.

Along the incline the component of weight down the plane is balanced by
the kinetic friction up the plane so that the net acceleration down the
plane is constant

* $a = g\sin\theta - f_{k}/m$

$f_{k}= \mu_{k}N =\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta$ so that

$$
a = g\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]
$$

is the constant acceleration down the ramp.  With $\theta =30^{\circ}$

$$
\sin\theta =0.500,\qquad \cos\theta =0.8660
$$

$$
a =9.81\Big[\,0.500-0.14\times0.8660\,\Big]
   =9.81\big[\,0.500-0.1212\,\big]
   =9.81\times0.3788\approx 3.7\;{\rm m/s^{2}}
$$

down the plane.  From rest

$$
v^{2}=v_{0}^{2}+2as\approx 2as
$$

on a distance $s$ measured along the plane.  For $s=9.7\;{\rm m}$

$$
v^{2}\approx 2\times3.72\times9.7\approx 7.2\times10^{1}\;{\rm m^{2}/s^{2}}

i.e. $v=\sqrt{2gs\big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\big]}$, the familiar

For a roll without slipping the loss in gravitational potential goes into
translational + rotational kinetic energy

$$ \Delta U = \Delta K_{trans}+\Delta K_{rot}$$

$$ m g h = \tfrac12 m v^{2}+\tfrac12 I\omega^{2}$$

For a solid cylinder $I=\tfrac12 m r^{2}$ and for rolling without slipping
$\omega = v/r$, so

$$ \tfrac12 I\omega^{2}= \tfrac12\left(\tfrac12 m r^{2}\right)\left(\frac{v}{r}\right)^{2}

Hence

$$ m g h = \tfrac12 m v^{2}+\tfrac14 m v^{2}= \tfrac34 m v^{2}$$

the mass cancels and

$$ v = \sqrt{\frac{4}{3} g h}

$$E_{1}(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{q_{1}}{x^{2}}\qquad

and $E_{1}+E_{2}=0$ in magnitude on the segment $q_{1}q_{2}$ gives

$$\frac{q_{1}}{x^{2}}=\frac{q_{2}}{(L-x)^{2}}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;

$$x=L\,\frac{\sqrt{q_{1}}}{\sqrt{q_{1}}+\sqrt{q_{2}}}

For a source moving with respect to a stationary observer the (non-relativistic)

$$f' = f_{0}\,\frac{v}{v\mp v_{s}}$$

the minus sign being for a source moving towards the observer and the plus
sign for a source moving away.  $v$ is the speed of sound in the medium and
$v_{s}$ the component of the source velocity along the line of sight.

For a source approaching

$$f' = f_{0}\frac{v}{v-v_{s}}$$

with

* $f_{0}=796\;{\rm Hz}$
* $v=343\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$
* $v_{s}=36.1\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$

$$f' = 796\;\frac{343}{343-36.1}
     = 796\;\frac{343}{306.9}
     \approx 8.9\!-\!9.0\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}$$

i.e. about $8.9\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}$, $\approx 890\;{\rm Hz}$ in the
usual rounding, $f'\approx 889\!-\!890\;{\rm Hz}$ on the $343\;{\rm m/s}$
value.  The shift is

$$\Delta f = f'-f_{0}\approx 889.6-796\approx 93.6\;{\rm Hz}$$

In the (practically) instantaneous impact the external impulse of the
friction is negligible so that the linear momentum of the two–body
system is conserved in the impact

$$p_{i}=p_{f}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
m_{1}u_{1}+m_{2}\cdot0=(m_{1}+m_{2})v_{0}  $$

so that the common velocity just after the perfectly plastic impact is

$$v_{0}=\frac{m_{1}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\,u_{1} $$

the kinetic energy which remains in the system after the impact is

$$K_{0}=\frac12\,(m_{1}+m_{2})v_{0}^{2}
      =\frac12\,\frac{m_{1}^{2}u_{1}^{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}  .$$

After the impact the only horizontal work is that of kinetic friction

$$F_{k}=\mu_{k}N=\mu_{k}(m_{1}+m_{2})g $$

on the distance $d$ travelled by the stuck–together mass until $v=0$.
With the work–energy theorem

$$W_{f}= \Delta K\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
-F_{k}d =0-K_{0},$$

i.e.

$$\mu_{k}(m_{1}+m_{2})g\,d=\frac12\,(m_{1}+m_{2})v_{0}^{2},$$

the total mass cancelling.  With $a_{f}=F_{k}/(m_{1}+m_{2})=\mu_{k}g$
the familiar $v_{0}^{2}=2a_{f}d$ is recovered,

$$d=\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{2\mu_{k}g}
   =\frac{1}{2\mu_{k}g}\left[\frac{m_{1}u_{1}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\right]^{2}
   =\frac{m_{1}^{2}u_{1}^{2}}{2\mu_{k}g\,(m_{1}+m_{2})^{2}} .
$$

\qquad

$$

For an RC charge from rest

$$V_{C}(t)=V_{\infty}\Big[\,1-e^{-t/RC}\,\Big] $$

with the time constant

$$\tau =RC$$

so that

$$\frac{V_{C}(t)}{V_{\infty}}=1-e^{-t/\tau}$$

is the fraction of the final voltage reached at time $t$.

Put $V_{C}/V_{\infty}=0.95$

$$0.95=1-e^{-t/\tau}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;e^{-t/\tau}=0.05$$

$$-\frac{t}{\tau}=\ln 0.05=-\ln 20$$

$$t=\tau\ln 20=-\tau\ln(1-0.95)$$

The $RC$ time constant is

$$\tau =R\,C=(49\times10^{3}\,\Omega)(85\times10^{-6}\,{\rm F})
      =49\times85\times10^{-3}\ {\rm s}=4.165\ {\rm s}\approx4.17\ {\rm s}$$

Hence

$$t=\tau\ln 20 =4.165\,\ln 20\;{\rm s}\approx4.165\times2.996\;{\rm s}
   \approx 1.25\times10^{1}\ {\rm s}$$

i.e. about three time constants.  In the usual $1-e^{-t/\tau}\approx
1-e^{-3}$ approximation

$$t\approx3\tau\approx3\times4.165\;{\rm s}\approx12.5\;{\rm s}$$

which is $t\approx12.48\;{\rm s}$ with the exact logarithm, essentially

* $T_{H}=577^{\circ}{\rm C}=577+273\simeq 850\;{\rm K}$
* $T_{C}=61^{\circ}{\rm C}=61+273\simeq 334\;{\rm K}$

      =1-\frac{334}{850}
      =1-0.3935\approx 0.606\;,
$$

i.e. about $60.6\%$ of the heat taken from the hot side can in principle
be turned into work.

In the (practically) instantaneous impact the linear momentum in the
horizontal direction is conserved, the kinetic energy is not.  If $v_{0}$
is the common horizontal velocity of the block+bullet immediately after
the impact and $v_{b}$ the velocity of the bullet just before impact

$$m_{b}v_{b}=(M+m_{b})v_{0}\qquad{\rm i.e.}\qquad 
v_{0}=\frac{m_{b}}{M+m_{b}}\,v_{b}  $$

is the velocity with which the pendulum is set in motion.  After the
impact the mechanical energy of the $(M+m_{b})$ system is conserved up
to the top of the swing

$$\frac12\,(M+m_{b})v_{0}^{2}=(M+m_{b})g\,h ,$$

so that the velocity immediately after impact is the velocity which
will raise the centre of mass through the height $h$,

$$v_{0}=\sqrt{2gh}$$

independently of the masses.  Hence

$$v_{b}= \frac{M+m_{b}}{m_{b}}\sqrt{2gh}
      =\left(1+\frac{M}{m_{b}}\right)\sqrt{2gh}\;,$$

the familiar ballistic-pendulum formula.

For

* $m_{b}=15\;{\rm g}=1.5\times10^{-2}\ {\rm kg}$,
* $M=1.96\ {\rm kg}$,
* $h=13.8\ {\rm cm}=0.138\ {\rm m}$,

$$v_{0}=\sqrt{2g h}=\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.138}\approx
1.64\!-\!1.65\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$$

is the velocity of the block+bullet just after the impact.  The
corresponding pre-impact speed of the bullet is

$$v_{b}= \frac{1.96+0.015}{0.015}\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.138}
      \approx 1.32\times10^{2}\times1.645\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      \approx 2.1\!-\!2.2\times10^{2}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}},$$

about $2.2\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$.  With the usual $M+m_{b}\simeq M$
approximation

$$v_{b}\simeq\frac{M}{m_{b}}\sqrt{2gh}
      =\frac{1.96}{0.015}\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.138}
      \approx 2.15\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}\approx 215\;{\rm m/s},$$

i.e. $\approx 216\!-\!217\;{\rm m/s}$ when the $15\;{\rm g}$ of the
bullet is retained in the $M+m_{b}$ factor, $v_{b}\approx 2.17\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$, essentially the $ \sim 2\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$ normally quoted for the ballistic pendulum.

For a mass on a frictionless spring the mechanical energy is conserved

$$E_{tot}=E_{el}+E_{kin}=\frac12k x^{2}+\frac12 m v^{2}= {\rm const}$$

so that with the turning point $x=A$, $v=0$,

$$E_{tot}= \frac12kA^{2}$$

and at a general displacement $x$

$$\frac12kA^{2}= \frac12k x^{2}+\frac12 m v^{2}$$

i.e.

$$v(x)=\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}\Big[\,A^{2}-x^{2}\Big]}
      =\omega A\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{x}{A}\right)^{2}} $$

with $\displaystyle \omega=\sqrt{k/m}$.

Here

* $m=0.70\;{\rm kg}$
* $k=360\;{\rm N\,m^{-1}}$
* $A=17.6\;{\rm cm}=0.176\;{\rm m}$
* $x=13.4\;{\rm cm}=0.134\;{\rm m}$

$$\omega=\sqrt{\frac{360}{0.70}}= \sqrt{514.3}\approx 22.7\;{\rm rad\,s^{-1}}$$

$$v_{\max}= \omega A\approx 22.7\times0.176\approx 4.0\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$$

and

$$v(x)=v_{\max}\sqrt{1-(x/A)^{2}}
     =\sqrt{\frac{360}{0.70}\Big[0.176^{2}-0.134^{2}\Big]}$$

$$A^{2}-x^{2}=0.03098-0.01796=1.302\times10^{-2}\ {\rm m^{2}}$$

$$v\approx\sqrt{514.3\times1.302\times10^{-2}}
   \approx\sqrt{6.7}\approx2.6\;{\rm m/s}$$

in magnitude, about $2.5\!-\!2.6\;{\rm m/s}$ on its way through the
$13.4\;{\rm cm}$ position.  The total energy is $E_{tot}=\tfrac12kA^{2}\approx5.6\;{\rm J}$, of which $\tfrac12kx^{2}\approx3.2\;{\rm J}$ is elastic at $x=13.4\;{\rm cm}$, leaving $\approx2.3\;{\rm J}$ of kinetic energy.  The sign is opposite to the displacement, i.e. the mass is moving toward equilibrium.

The work done on the block in sliding a distance $s$ down the plane is the
work of the component of the weight down the plane minus the work of the
kinetic friction

$$
W_{g}=m g s\sin\theta ,\qquad 
W_{f}= -f_{k}s=-\mu_{k}N s=-\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta\,s ,
$$

so that with $K_{i}=0$

$$
\Delta K=K_{f}-K_{i}=W_{g}+W_{f}
      =mg s\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big] .
$$

Hence

$$
\frac12 m v^{2}=mg s\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]
$$

and the mass cancels,

$$
v(s)=\sqrt{\,2gs\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]\,}
$$

the familiar $a=g\big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\big]$ result
$v^{2}=v_{0}^{2}+2as$.

For $\theta=35^{\circ}$,

$$
\sin\theta=0.5736,\qquad \cos\theta=0.8192,
$$

$$
\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta
      =0.5736-0.24\times0.8192
      \approx 0.377 .
$$

The (constant) acceleration down the plane is

$$
a=g\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]
  \approx 9.81\times0.377\approx 3.70\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}} ,
$$

and for $s=2.3\;{\rm m}$ with $v_{0}=0$

$$
v=\sqrt{2as}=\sqrt{2gs\big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\big]}
  =\sqrt{2\times9.81\times2.3\times0.377}
  \approx\sqrt{1.70\times10^{1}}\;{\rm m/s}
  \approx 4.1\!-\!4.2\;{\rm m/s}
$$

down the plane, about $4.1\;{\rm m/s}$ in the usual $g=9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$
estimate, $v\approx4.12\;{\rm m/s}$ with the numbers quoted above.  This is
$v^{2}=2g s(\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta)$; with $a\approx3.70\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$
the familiar kinematic form $v=\sqrt{2as}$ is recovered.

In an insulated system the heat lost by the hot body is taken up by the cold
body

$$Q_{loss}=Q_{gain}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\Delta U_{Al}+\Delta U_{W}=0 $$

on the assumption that no work is done and that no phase change occurs

$$m_{Al}c_{Al}\big(T_{Al,i}-T_{f}\big)=m_{W}c_{W}\big(T_{f}-T_{W,i}\big) $$

so that

$$T_{f}=
\frac{m_{Al}c_{Al}T_{Al,i}+m_{W}c_{W}T_{W,i}}
     {m_{Al}c_{Al}+m_{W}c_{W}}  $$

is the common final temperature.  With

* $m_{Al}=0.71\;{\rm kg}$, $c_{Al}=900\;{\rm J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}$,
  $T_{Al,i}=176^{\circ}{\rm C}$,
* $m_{W}=0.98\;{\rm kg}$, $c_{W}=4186\;{\rm J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}$,
  $T_{W,i}=16.6^{\circ}{\rm C}$,

the heat capacities are

$$C_{Al}=m_{Al}c_{Al}=0.71\times900=6.39\times10^{2}\ {\rm J\,K^{-1}}$$
$$C_{W}=m_{W}c_{W}=0.98\times4186=4.10\times10^{3}\ {\rm J\,K^{-1}}$$

Hence

$$T_{f}=
\frac{C_{Al}T_{Al,i}+C_{W}T_{W,i}}{C_{Al}+C_{W}}
=
\frac{639\times176+4102.28\times16.6}{639+4102.28}
$$

$$T_{f}= \frac{1.12464\times10^{5}+6.8098\times10^{4}}{4.7413\times10^{3}}
      \approx 3.81\times10^{1}\ {\rm ^{\circ}C}$$

i.e. about $38\!-\!39^{\circ}{\rm C}$, $T_{f}\simeq 38.1^{\circ}{\rm C}$ on the
numbers quoted.  The aluminium therefore gives up

$$Q_{Al}=C_{Al}(176-T_{f})\approx 6.39\times10^{2}\times137.9\approx
8.8\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}$$

which is taken up by the water,
$Q_{W}=C_{W}(T_{f}-16.6)\approx 8.8\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}$, as required by
energy conservation in the insulated container.  With the usual
$ c_{W}\approx4.18\;{\rm kJ\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}$ this is $T_{f}\approx38^{\circ}{\rm C}$,
essentially the water temperature after equilibration.

In a ballistic pendulum the (essentially) instantaneous inelastic impact
is treated with linear momentum and the subsequent rise of the
pendulum is treated with mechanical energy.

Let

* $m$ = $15\;{\rm g}=1.5\times10^{-2}\ {\rm kg}$ the bullet
* $M$ = $1.96\;{\rm kg}$ the block
* $M_{t}=M+m$ the mass that goes up after the impact
* $h=13.8\;{\rm cm}=0.138\;{\rm m}$ the rise of the centre of mass
* $v_{0}$ the bullet speed before impact
* $v_{1}$ the speed of the $M_{t}$ system just after impact

Impact, $x$–momentum

The block is at rest before impact so that, neglecting external
impulses during the very short time of the impact,

$$m v_{0}=M_{t}v_{1}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
v_{1}= \frac{m}{M_{t}}v_{0}  $$

is the speed of the block+bullet immediately after the bullet is
embedded.

Swing

After the impact the kinetic energy of the $M_{t}$ system is turned
into gravitational potential.  With the zero of potential at the
lowest point

$$\frac12 M_{t}v_{1}^{2}=M_{t}g h $$

so that the speed just after impact is independent of the mass

$$v_{1}= \sqrt{2gh}$$

in the idealised pendulum.  With $g=9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$

$$v_{1}= \sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.138}
      =\sqrt{2.71}\approx1.6\!-\!1.7\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}} $$

about $1.65\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ at the bottom of the swing.

Hence from momentum

$$v_{0}= \frac{M_{t}}{m}v_{1}
      =\frac{M+m}{m}\sqrt{2gh}\;.$$

With the numbers as quoted

$$v_{0}= \frac{1.96+0.015}{0.015}\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.138}
      \approx 1.32\times10^{2}\times1.65\approx2.2\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$$

i.e. about $2.1\!-\!2.2\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$ in the ideal
frictionless limit.  Using $M_{t}\approx M$ the familiar textbook
estimate

$$v_{0}\approx\frac{M}{m}\sqrt{2gh}
      =\frac{1.96}{0.015}\sqrt{2gh}\approx2.15\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}
      \approx 215\;{\rm m/s},$$

$\approx 216\;{\rm m/s}$ with the $M+m$ mass kept in the momentum
balance, is the speed that will put the $1.96\;{\rm kg}$ pendulum up
$13.8\;{\rm cm}$.  The $m\ll M$ correction is $\sim0.8\%$ and is
usually neglected.

For a charge moving perpendicular to a uniform $B$ the magnetic Lorentz
force is the centripetal force

$$F_{B}=F_{c}$$

$$q\,v\,B=\frac{mv^{2}}{r}$$

so that the gyro–radius is

$$r=\frac{mv}{qB}$$

in SI units $r$ is in metres when $m$ is in kg, $v$ in m s$^{-1}$, $q$ in C
and $B$ in T.

* $m_{p}=1.673\times10^{-27}\ {\rm kg}$
* $q_{p}=1.602\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}$
* $v=9.8\times10^{6}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$
* $B=0.46\ {\rm T}$

$$ 
mv = 1.673\times10^{-27}\times 9.8\times10^{6}
     =1.6415\times10^{-20}\ {\rm kg\,m\,s^{-1}}
$$

$$
qB = 1.602\times10^{-19}\times0.46
    =7.37\times10^{-20}\ {\rm C\,T}
$$

Hence

$$
r=\frac{mv}{qB}
  =\frac{1.6415\times10^{-20}}{7.369\times10^{-20}}\ {\rm m}
  \approx 2.23\times10^{-1}\ {\rm m}
$$

$$
r\approx0.22\!-\!0.23\ {\rm m}\approx 2.2\times10^{2}\ {\rm mm}
$$

i.e. about $2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{2}\,$mm, $\approx 223\,$mm, for the
nominal constants.  With $m_{p}=1.67\times10^{-27}\,$kg this is
$r\approx0.222\,$m $\approx 222\,$mm, essentially the same $\sim 0.22$ m
circular orbit.

For the hanging mass and the disk the kinematics and the dynamics are

* No slip : $a = \alpha R$
* For the mass $m$

$$
m g -T = m a\tag{1}
$$

* For the disk about its central axis

$$
\tau = T R = I\alpha = I\frac{a}{R}
$$

so that

$$
T = \frac{I}{R^{2}}\,a\tag{2}
$$

For a uniform solid disc

$$
I=\frac12 MR^{2}
$$

so that

$$
\frac{I}{R^{2}}=\frac12M .
$$

Put (2) in (1)

$$
mg-\frac{I}{R^{2}}a = ma
$$

$$
a\left[m+\frac{I}{R^{2}}\right]=mg
$$

$$
a=\frac{mg}{\,m+I/R^{2}\,}
   =\frac{mg}{m+M/2}
   =\frac{g}{1+\displaystyle\frac{M}{2m}}
$$

For $M=4.17\;{\rm kg}$, $m=0.53\;{\rm kg}$, $R=0.25\;{\rm m}$

$$
m+\frac{M}{2}=0.53+\frac{4.17}{2}=0.53+2.085=2.615\;{\rm kg}
$$

$$
a=\frac{0.53\times 9.81}{2.615}\approx 1.9\!-\!2.0\;{\rm m/s^{2}}
$$

downward, about $2.0\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ down.  In the usual form

$$
a=\frac{g}{1+M/2m}\approx\frac{9.81}{4.93}\approx1.99\;{\rm m/s^{2}}
$$

down the string.  The corresponding angular acceleration of the disc is
$\alpha=a/R\approx1.99/0.25\approx7.9\;{\rm rad/s^{2}}$ in the sense of unwinding.

The work done on the block on the displacement $s$ down the plane is the
work of the component of the weight down the plane and the work of the
kinetic friction up the plane.

On the plane

* $N=mg\cos\theta$ 
* $f_{k}=\mu_{k}N=\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta$ up the plane

Hence the net force down the plane is

$$
F_{\parallel}=mg\sin\theta-f_{k}=mg\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]
$$

so that with $m$ cancelling

$$
a=g\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]
$$

is the (constant) acceleration down the plane.  For motion from rest

$$
v^{2}=v_{0}^{2}+2as=2gs\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big] ,
$$

which is the work–energy statement

$$
\Delta K =W_{g}+W_{f}=mg s\sin\theta-\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta\,s
      =\tfrac12mv^{2} .
$$

For $\theta=38^{\circ}$,

$$
\sin\theta=0.6157,\qquad \cos\theta=0.7880,
$$

$$
\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta
      =0.6157-0.23\times0.7880
      =0.6157-0.1813\approx0.4344 .
$$

Hence

$$
a=g\bigl[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\bigr]
  \approx9.81\times0.4344\approx4.26\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}
$$

down the plane and

$$
v=\sqrt{2as}
  =\sqrt{2g s\bigl[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\bigr]}
  =\sqrt{2\times9.81\times8.2\times0.4344}
  \approx\sqrt{69.9}\;{\rm m/s}
$$

$$
v\approx 8.3\!-\!8.4\;{\rm m/s}
$$

down the incline, about $8.36\;{\rm m/s}$ with the numbers quoted.
In closed form

$$
v(s)=\sqrt{2gs\bigl[\sin38^{\circ}-0.23\cos38^{\circ}\bigr]}
$$

which is $\approx 8.4\;{\rm m/s}$ after $8.2\;{\rm m}$ of slip.  The
motion is possible because $\sin\theta>\mu_{k}\cos\theta$, i.e. the
down-slope component of weight exceeds the limiting friction.

For a circular Kepler orbit

$$ \frac{mv^{2}}{r}=\frac{GM_{\oplus}m}{r^{2}}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
v^{2}=\frac{GM_{\oplus}}{r} $$

and $v=2\pi r/T$, so that

$$T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{GM_{\oplus}}}$$

is the Kepler period.  With

* $R_{\oplus}=6371\;{\rm km}$
* $h=663\;{\rm km}$

$$r=R_{\oplus}+h=6371+663=7034\;{\rm km}=7.034\times10^{6}\ {\rm m}$$

and $\mu\equiv GM_{\oplus}=3.986\times10^{14}\ {\rm m^{3}s^{-2}}$

$$ 
\frac{r^{3}}{\mu}=
\frac{(7.034\times10^{6})^{3}}{3.986\times10^{14}}
\approx\frac{3.48\times10^{20}}{3.986\times10^{14}}
\approx 8.73\times10^{5}\ {\rm s^{2}}
$$

$$ \sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{\mu}}\approx\sqrt{8.73\times10^{5}}\approx 9.34\times10^{2}\ {\rm s}$$

Hence

$$T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{\mu}}\approx2\pi(9.34\times10^{2}\ {\rm s})
\approx5.87\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}$$

$$T\approx\frac{5.87\times10^{3}}{60}\ {\rm min}\approx 9.8\times10^{1}\ {\rm min}$$

i.e. about $5.9\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}\approx 97\!-\!98\ {\rm min}$,
$\approx 1.6\ {\rm h}$, the familiar $\sim$ 100 min low-Earth-orbit period.
With the numbers quoted $T\approx 5.87\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}\approx97.8$ min,
essentially the $\approx 98$ min LEO period.  This is the usual
$\,T\approx2\pi\sqrt{r^{3}/\mu}$ estimate.

For a launch from and to the same height the time of flight is set by the
vertical motion

* $v_{0x}=v_{0}\cos\theta$ , $v_{0y}=v_{0}\sin\theta$

$$
v_{y}(t)=v_{0y}-gt\qquad v_{y}(t_{f})=0
$$

so that on the way up and down

$$
t_{up}= \frac{v_{0y}}{g}\qquad 
t_{f}=2t_{up}= \frac{2v_{0y}}{g}= \frac{2v_{0}\sin\theta}{g}
$$

and the horizontal displacement in that time is

$$
R=v_{0x}t_{f}=v_{0}\cos\theta\;\frac{2v_{0}\sin\theta}{g}
     =\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{g}\sin2\theta  ,
$$

the familiar level-ground range.

Here

* $v_{0}=38.1\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$
* $\theta =53^{\circ}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
v_{0x}&=v_{0}\cos53^{\circ}=38.1\times0.6018\approx 2.29\times10^{1}\ {\rm m/s}\\
v_{0y}&=v_{0}\sin53^{\circ}=38.1\times0.7986\approx 3.04\times10^{1}\ {\rm m/s}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
t_{f}= \frac{2v_{0y}}{g}= \frac{2\times30.4\;{\rm m/s}}{9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}}
      \approx 6.2\;{\rm s}
$$

Hence

$$
R=v_{0x}t_{f}\approx 22.9\;{\rm m/s}\times6.20\;{\rm s}\approx1.4\!-\!1.5\times10^{2}\ {\rm m}
$$

In closed form

$$
R=\frac{v_{0}^{2}\sin2\theta}{g}
  =\frac{(38.1)^{2}\sin106^{\circ}}{9.81}
  \approx\frac{1.45\times10^{3}\times0.961}{9.81}\ {\rm m}
  \approx 1.42\times10^{2}\ {\rm m}
$$

about $1.4\times10^{2}\,$m, $\approx 142\;{\rm m}$ on the level ground, 
$\,R\approx v_{0}^{2}\sin2\theta/g$.  With the usual $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is $\approx 143\;{\rm m}$, essentially the $ \sim 140\!-\!145\;{\rm m}$ range quoted in the literature.

linear acceleration be $a$.  For the disk

* $I_{c}= \dfrac12 MR^{2}$  about its central axle
* $\tau =TR = I_{c}\alpha$

and with no slip $a=R\alpha$,

$$
TR = I_{c}\frac{a}{R}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
T =\frac{I_{c}}{R^{2}}\,a =\frac12 Ma .
$$

For the hanging mass

$$
m g -T = m a .
$$

Hence

$$
m g -\frac12 M a = m a
$$

$$
m g = a\!\left(m+\frac{M}{2}\right)
$$

$$
a=\frac{m}{m+M/2}\;g
   =\frac{g}{1+M/2m}
$$

is the linear acceleration of the string and of the rim of the disk.
With

* $M=1.75\;{\rm kg}$ , $R=0.09\;{\rm m}$,
* $m=2.08\;{\rm kg}$,

$$
m+\frac{M}{2}=2.08+\frac{1.75}{2}=2.08+0.875=2.955\;{\rm kg}
$$

$$
a=\frac{2.08\times 9.81}{2.955}\;{\rm m/s^{2}}
  \approx 6.9\;{\rm m/s^{2}}
$$

downward, about $0.70\,g$.  In terms of the disk

$$
\alpha=\frac{a}{R}\approx\frac{6.9}{0.09}\approx7.7\times10^{1}\ {\rm rad/s^{2}}
$$

in the sense of unwinding the string.  The familiar form
$a=g\big/\big[1+M/2m\big]$ is $a\approx6.91\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ for
$g=9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$, essentially $6.9\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ downward.

The motion is the superposition of a uniform horizontal motion and a
free fall in the vertical.

* $v_{x0}=15.0\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}},\qquad v_{y0}=0$
* $v_{x}=v_{x0}=$ const.  in the absence of drag

In the vertical direction

$$y(t)=y_{0}-\frac12gt^{2}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
h=\frac12gt_{f}^{2}$$

so that the time of flight to the ground $y=0$ is

$$t_{f}=\sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}=\sqrt{\frac{2(20.1\;{\rm m})}{9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}}}
      \approx 2.02\;{\rm s}$$

The vertical component acquired in the fall is

$$v_{y,f}=g\,t_{f}=\sqrt{2gh}$$

$$v_{y,f}= \sqrt{2(9.81)(20.1)}\approx\sqrt{394.4}\approx 1.99\times10^{1}\ {\rm m/s}$$

downwards.  The horizontal component is unchanged,

$$v_{x,f}=v_{x0}=15.0\;{\rm m/s} .$$

Hence the magnitude of the velocity just before impact is

$$v_{f}=\sqrt{v_{x,f}^{2}+v_{y,f}^{2}}
     =\sqrt{v_{x0}^{2}+2gh}
     =\sqrt{(15.0)^{2}+2(9.81)(20.1)}\;{\rm m/s}$$

$$v_{f}\approx\sqrt{225+394.4}\approx\sqrt{619.4}\approx 2.5\times10^{1}\ {\rm m/s}$$

about $24\!-\!25\;{\rm m/s}$ .  In terms of components

$$v_{f}\approx 15.0\;{\rm m/s}\;\hat i+19.9\;{\rm m/s}\;\hat j_{\rm down},$$

i.e. $|\,v_{f}\,|\approx 24.9\;{\rm m/s}$ at

$$\theta=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{v_{y,f}}{v_{x,f}}\right)
      =\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{2gh}}{v_{x0}}\right)\approx
      52\!-\!53^{\circ}$$

below the horizontal, the familiar $ \sqrt{v_{x0}^{2}+2gh}$ free-fall
result.  With $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is $v_{f}\approx24.9\;{\rm m/s}$,
essentially $ \approx 25\;{\rm m/s}$ just before impact.

For a circular Kepler orbit

$$ \mu =GM_{\oplus},\qquad 
\omega^{2}r^{3}=\mu ,\qquad 
T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{\mu}} $$

with

$$r=R_{\oplus}+h=6371\;{\rm km}+1447\;{\rm km}=7818\;{\rm km}
      =7.818\times10^{6}\ {\rm m}$$

Hence

$$T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{GM}}
   =2\pi\sqrt{\frac{(7.818\times10^{6}\,{\rm m})^{3}}
                  {3.986\times10^{14}\ {\rm m^{3}s^{-2}}}} $$

$$r^{3}=4.78\times10^{20}\ {\rm m^{3}},\qquad 
\frac{r^{3}}{GM}\approx1.20\times10^{6}\ {\rm s^{2}} $$

$$\sqrt{r^{3}/GM}\approx1.09\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}$$

$$T\approx2\pi\times1.095\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}\approx6.9\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}$$

i.e.

$$T\approx\frac{6.88\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}}{60}\approx1.1\!-\!1.2\times10^{2}\ {\rm min}
\approx 1.15\times10^{2}\ {\rm min}$$

about $6.9\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}\simeq 114\!-\!115\;{\rm min}$,
$\approx 1.9\;{\rm h}$, the familiar $\sim$115 min low–Earth
period.  With the numbers quoted $T\approx 6.88\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}
\approx 114.6\;{\rm min}\approx115\;{\rm min}$, essentially the
$\sim$ 1 h 55 min LEO period.

In the absence of drag the horizontal motion is uniform and the vertical
motion is the free fall

* $x$ : $v_{x}(t)=v_{0x}=v_{0}$, $\qquad x(t)=v_{0}t$
* $y$ : $v_{y}(0)=0$, $\qquad a_{y}=-g$

$$
y(t)=y_{0}-\frac12gt^{2},\qquad v_{y}(t)=-gt
$$

The time of flight $T$ is obtained from the vertical drop $h=41.1\;{\rm m}$,
$y(T)-y_{0}=-h$,

$$
-h=-\frac12gT^{2}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
T=\sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}} .
$$

Hence on impact

$$
v_{x}(T)=v_{0},\qquad 
v_{y}(T)=-gT=-\,g\sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}=-\sqrt{2gh},
$$

the minus sign denoting the downward sense.  The magnitude of the
velocity is

$$
v_{f}=\sqrt{v_{x}^{2}+v_{y}^{2}}
     =\sqrt{v_{0}^{2}+2gh}\;,
$$

which is the familiar energy statement
$\tfrac12mv_{0}^{2}+mgh=\tfrac12mv_{f}^{2}$.

For $v_{0}=6.2\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ and $h=41.1\;{\rm m}$

$$
v_{y,f}= \sqrt{2gh}= \sqrt{2\times9.81\times41.1}
       =\sqrt{806.4}\approx 2.84\times10^{1}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

downwards, and

$$
v_{f}= \sqrt{v_{0}^{2}+v_{y,f}^{2}}
     =\sqrt{6.2^{2}+2\times9.81\times41.1}
     =\sqrt{38.44+806.38}
     =\sqrt{844.8}\approx 2.9\!-\!3.0\times10^{1}\ {\rm m/s}
$$

about $29\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ on impact.  In magnitude

$$
v_{f}\approx 29.1\;{\rm m/s}
$$

directed $\theta=\tan^{-1}\!\left(|v_{y}|/v_{x}\right)
      =\tan^{-1}\!\left(\sqrt{2gh}/v_{0}\right)\approx
      \tan^{-1}4.58\approx 77\!-\!78^{\circ}$
below the horizontal, the horizontal component remaining $v_{x}=6.2\;{\rm m/s}$.
The $v_{0}^{2}$ term is a $ \sim 4.5\%$ correction to the free-fall speed
$\sqrt{2gh}\approx28.4\;{\rm m/s}$.

In the impact the linear momentum of the bullet–block system is (to a very
good approximation) conserved, the kinetic energy taken up in the
inelastic embedding being afterwards converted into gravitational
potential energy of the rise.

Let

* $m=14\;{\rm g}=1.4\times10^{-2}\ {\rm kg}$ the bullet,
* $M=3.03\ {\rm kg}$ the block,
* $v_{0}$ the bullet speed before impact,
* $v_{1}$ the common speed of the $(M+m)$ system just after impact,
* $h=0.238\ {\rm m}$ the rise of the centre of mass.

Momentum, block initially at rest,

$$m v_{0}=(M+m)v_{1}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
v_{1}= \frac{m}{M+m}v_{0}  $$

After the impact the kinetic energy of the $(M+m)$ system is turned
into gravitational potential,

$$\frac12 (M+m)v_{1}^{2}=(M+m)gh ,$$

so that the speed immediately after the impact is the speed which
would give a rise $h$ in free fall,

$$v_{1}=\sqrt{2gh}\;.$$

Hence

$$v_{0}= \frac{M+m}{m}\,v_{1}
      =\frac{M+m}{m}\sqrt{2gh}\;.$$

With $M+m=3.044\;{\rm kg}$,

$$v_{1}= \sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.238}
      =\sqrt{4.67}\approx 2.16\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$$

and

$$v_{0}= \frac{3.044}{0.014}\times2.16\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      \approx 2.17\times10^{2}\times2.16\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      \approx 4.7\times10^{2}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}},$$

i.e. about $4.6\!-\!4.8\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$ in the usual
$ \approx 470\;{\rm m/s}$ estimate.  With $M\gg m$ this is often quoted
as $v_{0}\simeq (M/m)\sqrt{2gh}\approx 4.69\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$,
$\approx 470\;{\rm m/s}$ before impact, the $2.16\;{\rm m/s}$ being the
post-impact swing speed.  The $m$ in the numerator $M+m$ is normally
negligible, $v_{0}\approx M/m\sqrt{2gh}\approx 469\;{\rm m/s}$.

The stopping distance is the distance covered in the driver's reaction time
plus the distance covered while the brakes are on.

* $v_{0}=40\;{\rm km\,h^{-1}}=\dfrac{40\times10^{3}}{3600}=11.11\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      =\dfrac{100}{9}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$

Reaction

$$
d_{r}=v_{0}t_{r}
$$

$$
d_{r}=11.11\;{\rm m/s}\times0.62\;{\rm s}\approx 6.9\;{\rm m}
$$

is covered at essentially constant speed before the brakes are even applied.

Braking, $a=-5.6\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$

$$
0=v_{0}^{2}+2a d_{b}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
d_{b}=\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{2|a|}
$$

$$
d_{b}= \frac{(11.11)^{2}}{2\times5.6}
     =\frac{123.5}{11.2}\approx 1.10\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}
$$

about $11.0\!-\!11.3\;{\rm m}$ of pure braking.  In time

$$
t_{b}=v_{0}/|a|\approx 11.11/5.6\approx1.98\;{\rm s}
$$

so the mean speed under braking is $v_{0}/2$.

Total from the instant the hazard is seen

$$
d_{tot}=d_{r}+d_{b}=v_{0}t_{r}+\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{2|a|}
      \approx 6.9\;{\rm m}+11.0\;{\rm m}\approx 1.8\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}
$$

$\approx 17\!-\!18\;{\rm m}$ from the point of perception, $\approx 11\;{\rm m}$ of
which is actually under braking.  With $v_{0}=100/9\;{\rm m/s}$ exactly

$$
d_{tot}= \frac{100}{9}\Bigl[0.62+\frac{100}{9\times2\times5.6}\Bigr]
       \approx 17.9\;{\rm m}
$$

about $18\;{\rm m}$ in round numbers, the $ \approx 6.9\;{\rm m}$ reaction
run-out being the part that is often quoted as the “thinking distance’’.
The $ \approx 11.0\;{\rm m}$ is the conventional braking distance.

For a frictionless bank the normal reaction $N$ supplies the centripetal
force and the weight $mg$.

Resolve normal to the plane and parallel to the plane

* Normal : $N\cos\theta = mg$
* Parallel : $N\sin\theta = m v^{2}/r$

Hence

$$
\tan\theta=\frac{N\sin\theta}{N\cos\theta}=\frac{mv^{2}/r}{mg}
       =\frac{v^{2}}{rg}
$$

is the ideal banking angle.

$$
v =45\;{\rm km\,h^{-1}}=45\frac{1000}{3600}=12.5\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

$$
\tan\theta =\frac{v^{2}}{r g}
           =\frac{(12.5)^{2}}{247\times 9.81}
           =\frac{156.25}{2.42\times10^{3}}
           \approx 6.45\times10^{-2}
$$

$$
\theta =\arctan\!\left[\frac{v^{2}}{rg}\right]
       =\arctan 0.0645\approx 0.0644\;{\rm rad}
$$

$$
\theta\approx0.0644\times\frac{180}{\pi}\approx 3.6\!-\!3.7^{\circ}
$$

about $3.7^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, i.e. $\tan\theta\approx0.064$,
essentially $v^{2}/rg$.  With $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is
$\theta\approx3.70^{\circ}$, the familiar $ \theta\approx\arctan v^{2}/rg$
ideal bank.

For two like charges the fields can cancel only between them.  Put the
origin at $q_{1}$ and let the zero of the field be a distance $x$ towards
$q_{2}$ on the line of centres, $L=0.99\;{\rm m}$ being the separation.
Then

$$E_{1}(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{q_{1}}{x^{2}}\qquad 
{\rm towards\; }q_{2}$$
$$E_{2}(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{q_{2}}{(L-x)^{2}}\qquad 
{\rm towards\; }q_{1}$$

and $E_{1}=E_{2}$ on the line of centres, i.e.

$$\frac{q_{1}}{x^{2}}=\frac{q_{2}}{(L-x)^{2}}\;,$$

so that with the $+$ sign between the charges

$$\frac{L-x}{x}=\sqrt{\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}}\;.$$

Hence

$$x=\frac{L}{1+\sqrt{q_{2}/q_{1}}}$$

on the side of the smaller charge.  With $L=99\;{\rm cm}$,

$$\sqrt{\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}}=\sqrt{\frac{7.2}{2.2}}
      =\sqrt{\frac{36}{11}}=\frac{6}{\sqrt{11}}\approx1.81,$$

so that

$$x=\frac{99\;{\rm cm}}{1+\sqrt{7.2/2.2}}
   =\frac{99\,\sqrt{11}}{6+\sqrt{11}}\approx 3.5\!-\!3.6\times10^{1}\ {\rm cm}$$

towards $q_{2}$, i.e. about $35\!-\!36\;{\rm cm}$ from the $2.2\;\mu{\rm C}$
charge, $L-x\approx 99-35.2\approx 63.8\;{\rm cm}$ from the $7.2\;\mu{\rm C}$
charge.  In round numbers $x\approx 35\;{\rm cm}$ from $q_{1}$ on the
interior of the segment, $ \approx 35.3\;{\rm cm}$ with the numbers quoted
above, the familiar $x=L\big/\big[1+\sqrt{q_{2}/q_{1}}\big]$ result.  This
is the unique interior zero; outside the two like charges the fields add
and no zero exists.

For a reversible isothermal change of an ideal gas

$$w_{rev}= -\int_{V_{1}}^{V_{2}}P\,dV=-\int_{V_{1}}^{V_{2}}\frac{nRT}{V}dV
      =-nRT\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}} $$

is the work done on the gas in the chemistry sign convention.  The
magnitude of the work done by the gas is

$$|w_{by}|=nRT\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}} $$

on the $V_{2}/V_{1}$ ratio the units of $V$ cancel.  With

* $n=4.59\;{\rm mol}$
* $R=8.314\;{\rm J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$
* $T=499\;{\rm K}$
* $V_{2}/V_{1}=33.2/7.8=4.2564$

$$
nRT =4.59\times 8.314\times 499\approx 1.90\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}
$$

$$
\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}=\ln 4.2564\approx 1.45
$$

so that

$$
|w_{by}|\approx nRT\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}
      \approx 1.904\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}\times1.448\approx
      2.7\!-\!2.8\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}
$$

about $2.76\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}\approx 27\!-\!28\;{\rm kJ}$ of
expansion work is done by the gas.  In the usual chemistry sign
convention work done on the system is negative,

$$
w_{chem}= -\,nRT\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}\approx -2.8\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}
\approx -27.6\ {\rm kJ}
$$

the minus sign denoting work done by the system on the surroundings.
The magnitude often quoted as “work done by the gas’’ is $\approx
+2.8\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}$, $\approx 27.6\;{\rm kJ}$ of expansion work,
essentially $27.6\;{\rm kJ}$ done by the gas on the surroundings.  With
the numbers quoted above this is $w_{by}\simeq 2.76\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}$,
$w_{on}\simeq -2.76\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}$, about $27.6\;{\rm kJ}$ in
magnitude.

For the inelastic impact the linear momentum of the bullet–block system is
conserved in the instant of the impact and the kinetic energy which is
left in the system after the impact is turned into gravitational
potential in the swing.

Let

* $m=29\;{\rm g}=2.9\times10^{-2}\ {\rm kg}$ be the mass of the bullet,
* $M=3.75\ {\rm kg}$ be the mass of the block,
* $M_{t}=M+m$ the mass after the impact,
* $h=24.2\;{\rm cm}=0.242\;{\rm m}$ the rise of the centre of mass,
* $v_{0}$ the speed of the bullet before impact,
* $v_{1}$ the speed of the combined $M_{t}$ just after impact, at the
bottom of the swing.

Momentum in the impact

$$
m v_{0}=M_{t}v_{1}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
v_{0}=\frac{M_{t}}{m}v_{1}\;,
$$

the impact being taken as instantaneous so that the impulse of the
supporting strings can be neglected.

After the impact the $M_{t}v_{1}^{2}/2$ of kinetic energy at the bottom
is converted, to a very good approximation, into $M_{t}gh$ of
gravitational potential at the top of the swing,

$$
\frac12M_{t}v_{1}^{2}=M_{t}g\,h
$$

so that the speed just after impact is the ordinary free-fall speed
for a fall through $h$,

$$
v_{1}=\sqrt{2gh}\; .
$$

Hence

$$
v_{0}= \frac{M+m}{m}\sqrt{2gh}
$$

is the speed the bullet must have had before it struck the block.
With $g=9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$

$$
v_{1}= \sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.242}
     =\sqrt{4.75}\approx 2.18\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

is the speed of the $M+m$ system immediately after the bullet is
embedded.  The corresponding pre-impact bullet speed is

$$
v_{0}= \frac{3.75+0.029}{0.029}\;v_{1}
     \approx 1.30\times10^{2}\times2.18\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
     \approx 2.8\!-\!2.9\times10^{2}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}},
$$

about $2.8\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$ in the usual $M_{t}\approx M$
approximation.  Using $M_{t}=M+m$ explicitly,

$$
v_{0}\approx\frac{3.779}{0.029}\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.242}
      \approx 2.84\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}\approx 284\;{\rm m/s}
$$

in the direction of the swing.  Neglecting the $29\;{\rm g}$ in the
total mass, $v_{0}\approx(M/m)\sqrt{2gh}\approx 3.75/0.029\times2.18\approx
2.82\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}\approx 281\!-\!283\;{\rm m/s}$, essentially
the same result, i.e. of order $300\;{\rm m/s}$, the familiar rifle
range.  This is the speed required to raise the $3.75\;{\rm kg}$ block
$24.2\;{\rm cm}$ after a perfectly inelastic capture of the bullet.

The current which leaves the battery is the current in the series arm $R_{1}$.

The resistance of the $R_{2}\parallel R_{3}$ combination is

$$
R_{23}=R_{2}\parallel R_{3}=\frac{R_{2}R_{3}}{R_{2}+R_{3}}
      =\frac{38\times 45}{38+45}\;{\rm \Omega}
      =\frac{1710}{83}\;{\rm \Omega}\approx 20.6\;{\rm \Omega}
$$

Hence the total resistance seen by the ideal $V_{0}=11\;{\rm V}$ source is

$$
R_{T}=R_{1}+R_{23}=3+\frac{1710}{83}
     =\frac{1959}{83}\;{\rm \Omega}\approx 23.60\;{\rm \Omega}
$$

and the total current supplied by the battery, which is the current in $R_{1}$,
is

$$
I_{T}=\frac{V_{0}}{R_{T}}=\frac{11}{1959/83}
     =\frac{913}{1959}\;{\rm A}\approx 0.47\;{\rm A} .
$$

The voltage which appears across the parallel pair is

$$
V_{23}=V_{0}-I_{T}R_{1}=I_{T}R_{23}
      \approx 11-0.466\times3\approx 9.6\;{\rm V} .
$$

On the parallel branch the current divides in inverse proportion to the
resistances,

$$
I_{2}=I_{T}\,\frac{R_{3}}{R_{2}+R_{3}}
     =I_{T}\,\frac{45}{83},
$$

i.e. in closed form

$$
I_{2}=V_{0}\frac{R_{3}}{R_{1}(R_{2}+R_{3})+R_{2}R_{3}}
     =\frac{11\times45}{1959}\;{\rm A}
     =\frac{165}{653}\;{\rm A}\approx 2.5\times10^{-1}\ {\rm A},
$$

about $0.25\!-\!0.26\;{\rm A}$ flowing from the top node through $R_{2}$ to
the return.  In particular

$$
V_{23}\approx 9.6\;{\rm V},\qquad 
I_{2}=V_{23}/R_{2}\approx 9.60/38\approx0.25\;{\rm A},
$$

$I_{3}=V_{23}/R_{3}\approx0.21\;{\rm A}$, $I_{2}+I_{3}=I_{T}\approx0.47\;{\rm A}$,
as required.  Using the exact fractions $I_{2}=165/653\;{\rm A}\approx0.253\;{\rm A}$,
essentially $0.25\;{\rm A}$ in round numbers.

The work done on the block in going a distance $s$ down the plane is the
work of the component of the weight down the plane minus the work of the
kinetic friction

$$
W_{g}=mg\,s\sin\theta\qquad 
W_{f}=-f_{k}s=-\mu_{k}N s=-\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta\,s
$$

so that with $K_{i}=0$

$$
\Delta K=W_{g}+W_{f}=mg s\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]
      =\frac12 m v^{2}\;,
$$

the mass cancelling.  Hence

$$
v=\sqrt{\,2gs\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]\,}
$$

and the (constant) acceleration down the plane is

$$
a=g\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big] .
$$

For $\theta=43^{\circ}$

$$
\sin\theta=0.6820,\qquad \cos\theta=0.7314,
$$

$$
\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta
      =0.6820-0.17\times0.7314\approx0.558 .
$$

Hence

$$
a\approx g\times0.558\approx9.81\times0.558\approx5.47\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}
$$

down the plane and for $s=2.1\;{\rm m}$

$$
v=\sqrt{2as}=\sqrt{2gs\big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\big]}
  =\sqrt{2(9.81)(2.1)(0.5577)}\approx\sqrt{2.30\times10^{1}}
  \approx4.7\!-\!4.9\;{\rm m/s}
$$

down the incline, about $4.8\;{\rm m/s}$ in magnitude.  With the numbers
quoted above

$$
v\approx\sqrt{2\times9.81\times2.1\,
\big[\sin43^{\circ}-0.17\cos43^{\circ}\big]}\approx4.79\;{\rm m/s}
$$

down the plane, i.e. $\,v\approx4.8\;{\rm m/s}$ after $2.1\;{\rm m}$ of
sliding.  The corresponding constant acceleration is $a\approx5.5\;{\rm
m/s^{2}}$ down the plane.

For a reversible Carnot cycle

$$\eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}} = \frac{W}{Q_{H}} $$

with the absolute temperatures

* $T_{H}=474^{\circ}{\rm C}=474+273.15=747.15\;{\rm K}$
* $T_{C}=61^{\circ}{\rm C}=61+273.15=334.15\;{\rm K}$

Hence

$$\eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}
      =1-\frac{334.15}{747.15}
      \approx 1-0.447\approx 0.55 $$

i.e. about $55\%$ of the heat taken from the hot source can be turned into work in the ideal Carnot limit.

For a heat input per cycle

$$Q_{H}=5.6\;{\rm kJ}$$

the reversible work per cycle is

$$W=\eta_{C}Q_{H}= \left[1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}\right]Q_{H}$$

$$W\approx0.553\, \times 5.6\;{\rm kJ}\approx 3.0\!-\!3.1\;{\rm kJ}$$

per cycle.  With $T_{H}=747\;{\rm K}$, $T_{C}=334\;{\rm K}$,

$$W\approx\Bigl[1-\frac{334}{747}\Bigr]5.6\;{\rm kJ}\approx3.10\;{\rm kJ}$$

is the Carnot work, $Q_{C}=Q_{H}-W\approx2.5\;{\rm kJ}$ being rejected to the cold sink.  Using $273\;{\rm K}$ for the Celsius conversion $W\approx3.10\;{\rm kJ}\approx3.1\;{\rm kJ}$ per cycle, essentially $ \sim 3.1\;{\rm kJ}$ of mechanical work per cycle in the ideal limit.

The horizontal component is unchanged in free fall

$$v_{x}=v_{0x}=8.6\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$$

and the vertical component grows under gravity from rest

$$v_{y}(t)=g\,t\qquad{\rm with}\qquad 
h=\tfrac12gt^{2}$$

so that the time of fall from a height $h$ is

$$t_{f}=\sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}=
\sqrt{\frac{2\times 43.4}{9.81}}\approx 2.98\;{\rm s}$$

and

$$v_{y,f}=g t_{f}=\sqrt{2gh}
      =\sqrt{2\times9.81\times43.4}\approx 2.92\times10^{1}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$$

downwards.  The resultant speed on impact is

$$v_{f}=\sqrt{v_{x}^{2}+v_{y,f}^{2}}
     =\sqrt{v_{0x}^{2}+2gh}
     =\sqrt{(8.6)^{2}+2(9.81)(43.4)}\;{\rm m/s}$$

$$v_{f}\approx\sqrt{73.96+851.45}\approx\sqrt{9.25\times10^{2}}
      \approx 3.0\!-\!3.1\times10^{1}\ {\rm m/s}$$

about $30\!-\!31\;{\rm m/s}$ on impact, $\approx 30.4\;{\rm m/s}$,
directed $\theta=\tan^{-1}(v_{y,f}/v_{x})\approx\tan^{-1}(3.40)\approx
73\!-\!74^{\circ}$ below the horizontal.  The vertical part alone is
$\,v_{y,f}=\sqrt{2gh}\approx 29.2\;{\rm m/s}$.

*Remark:* $v_{f}=\sqrt{v_{0}^{2}+2gh}$ is the familiar energy result,
$ \tfrac12 m v_{f}^{2}= \tfrac12 m v_{0}^{2}+mgh$.

For an ideal Atwood the two masses have the same magnitude of acceleration
$a$ and the same tension $T$ in the inextensible string.

Take the heavy mass $m_{1}=3.01\;{\rm kg}$ down positive and the light mass
$m_{2}=1.60\;{\rm kg}$ up positive.

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_{1}g-T &= m_{1}a\\
T-m_{2}g &= m_{2}a
\end{aligned}
$$

so that

$$
a=\frac{m_{1}-m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\,g
$$

and

$$
T=m_{2}(g+a)=m_{1}(g-a)=\frac{2m_{1}m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\,g .
$$

With $m_{1}-m_{2}=1.41\;{\rm kg}$ and $m_{1}+m_{2}=4.61\;{\rm kg}$

$$
a=\frac{1.41}{4.61}\;g\approx0.3059\,g\approx
\frac{1.41\times9.81}{4.61}\approx3.0\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}
$$

down for the $3.01\;{\rm kg}$ mass and up for the $1.60\;{\rm kg}$ mass.
The common tension is then

$$
T=m_{2}(g+a)=1.60\bigl[\,9.81+3.00\,\bigr]\;{\rm N}
   \approx1.60\times12.81\;{\rm N}\approx2.0\!-\!2.1\times10^{1}\ {\rm N}
$$

$$
T=\frac{2m_{1}m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}g\approx
\frac{2\times3.01\times1.60}{4.61}\times9.81\approx20.5\;{\rm N}
$$

i.e. about $20\!-\!21\;{\rm N}$, $m_{1}g-T=m_{1}a$ and $T-m_{2}g=m_{2}a$
with the $3.01\;{\rm kg}$ mass accelerating downwards at $\approx3.0\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$.
In the ideal limit $T\to m_{1}m_{2}g/(m_{1}+m_{2})$ times two, $ \approx 20.5\;{\rm N}$,
essentially independent of the instantaneous speed, so long as the pulley remains
massless and frictionless.  With $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is $T\approx20.5\;{\rm N}$,
$\,a\approx3.00\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$, the familiar $T\approx m_{1}g-m_{1}a\approx m_{2}g+m_{2}a$.

In the short time of the impact the impulse of the external friction
and weight is negligible so that the linear momentum of the two blocks
is conserved in the impact

* Impact *

$$p_{i}=m_{1}v_{1}+m_{2}0=(m_{1}+m_{2})v_{f}$$

so that the common velocity just after the perfectly inelastic
sticking is

$$
v_{f}= \frac{m_{1}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\,v_{1}
$$

$$
v_{f}= \frac{2.68}{2.68+4.96}\times 3.7
     =\frac{2.68\times3.7}{7.64}
     =\frac{9.92}{7.64}\approx 1.30\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

in the direction of the incident block.  The kinetic energy lost in
the impact is

$$\Delta K =\tfrac12 m_{1}v_{1}^{2}-\tfrac12 (m_{1}+m_{2})v_{f}^{2} .$$

After the impact the only horizontal work is done by kinetic friction

$$F_{k}= \mu_{k}N=\mu_{k}(m_{1}+m_{2})g $$

on the mass $M=m_{1}+m_{2}$.  With $a_{k}=F_{k}/M$ the deceleration is
mass independent

$$a_{k}= \mu_{k}g $$

in the sense opposite to the motion.  From $v^{2}=v_{f}^{2}+2a_{s}s$
with $a_{s}=-a_{k}$,

$$0=v_{f}^{2}-2\mu_{k}g\,s_{stop}$$

i.e.

$$
s_{stop}= \frac{v_{f}^{2}}{2\mu_{k}g}

For a source moving with respect to a stationary observer the (non-relativistic)
Doppler shift is

* source toward observer

$$f_{o}=f_{s}\;\frac{v}{v-v_{s}} $$

$v$ is the speed of sound in the medium and $v_{s}>0$ is the component of the
source velocity toward the observer.  The denominator is smaller than $v$
so the observed frequency is up-shifted.

Here

* $f_{s}=967\;{\rm Hz}$
* $v=343\;{\rm m/s}$
* $v_{s}=20.6\;{\rm m/s}$ toward the observer

$$v-v_{s}=343-20.6=322.4\;{\rm m/s}$$

$$ \frac{v}{v-v_{s}}=\frac{343}{322.4}=1.0639 $$

Hence

$$f_{o}=967\times\frac{343}{322.4}\approx 967\times1.0639\approx
1.03\times10^{3}\ {\rm Hz}$$

about $1.03\;{\rm kHz}$, i.e. $\approx 1028\!-\!1029\;{\rm Hz}$,
$\approx 61\!-\!62\;{\rm Hz}$ higher than the emitted $967\;{\rm Hz}$.
In round numbers $f_{o}\simeq 1.03\,{\rm kHz}\approx 1029\;{\rm Hz}$ toward
the observer.  The up-shift is $\Delta f = f_{o}-f_{s}\approx 62\;{\rm Hz}$.

*Remark:*  With the usual sign convention $f_{o}=f_{s}v/(v\mp v_{s})$,
minus for approach, plus for recession.  For an observer moving toward a
stationary source $f_{o}=f_{s}(v+v_{o})/v$.

In an isolated system the heat lost by the hot body is taken up by the cold
body

$$Q_{loss}=Q_{gain}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\Delta U_{Cu}+\Delta U_{W}=0 $$

on the ideal calorimetric approximation

$$Q=m\,c\,\Delta T $$

with the sign convention $Q>0$ for a gain of heat.  For the copper

$$Q_{Cu}=m_{Cu}c_{Cu}\big(T_{f}-T_{Cu,0}\big)$$

and for the water

$$Q_{W}=m_{W}c_{W}\big(T_{f}-T_{W,0}\big)$$

so that in the adiabatic container

$$Q_{Cu}+Q_{W}=0$$

i.e.

$$m_{Cu}c_{Cu}\big(T_{f}-T_{Cu,0}\big)+m_{W}c_{W}\big(T_{f}-T_{W,0}\big)=0 .
$$

Hence

$$T_{f}\Big[m_{Cu}c_{Cu}+m_{W}c_{W}\Big]
      =m_{Cu}c_{Cu}T_{Cu,0}+m_{W}c_{W}T_{W,0}$$

and

$$
T_{f}= \frac{m_{Cu}c_{Cu}T_{Cu,0}+m_{W}c_{W}T_{W,0}}
            {m_{Cu}c_{Cu}+m_{W}c_{W}}
     =T_{W,0}+\frac{m_{Cu}c_{Cu}}{m_{Cu}c_{Cu}+m_{W}c_{W}}
       \big(T_{Cu,0}-T_{W,0}\big) ,
$$

the familiar weighted mean with the heat capacities
$C_{i}=m_{i}c_{i}$ as weights.

Now

* $C_{Cu}=m_{Cu}c_{Cu}=0.58\times385=2.23\times10^{2}\ {\rm J\,K^{-1}}$
* $C_{W}=m_{W}c_{W}=0.78\times4186=3.263\times10^{3}\ {\rm J\,K^{-1}}$

so that

$$
C_{Cu}+C_{W}=223.3+3263.1\approx 3.49\times10^{3}\ {\rm J\,K^{-1}} .
$$

The heat lost by the copper on cooling from $65.0^{\circ}{\rm C}$ to $T_{f}$ is

$$Q_{loss}=C_{Cu}\big(T_{Cu,0}-T_{f}\big)$$

and the heat taken up by the water is

$$Q_{gain}=C_{W}\big(T_{f}-T_{W,0}\big) .$$

Putting $Q_{loss}=Q_{gain}$,

$$
223.3\,(65.0-T_{f})=3263.1\,(T_{f}-29.7)
$$

$$
223.3\times65.0+3263.1\times29.7
      =T_{f}\,(223.3+3263.1)
$$

$$
T_{f}= \frac{1.451\times10^{4}+9.691\times10^{4}}{3.486\times10^{3}}
     \approx 3.20\times10^{1}\ {\rm ^{\circ}C},
$$

i.e. about $31.9\!-\!32.0^{\circ}{\rm C}$ on the usual calorimetric
approximation.  With the numbers quoted

$$
T_{f}\approx 31.96^{\circ}{\rm C}\approx 32^{\circ}{\rm C}
$$

above the initial water temperature by

$$\Delta T_{W}= \frac{C_{Cu}}{C_{Cu}+C_{W}}\,(T_{Cu,0}-T_{W,0})
          \approx 2.26\;{\rm K},$$

so that the copper cools by $\approx 33.0\;{\rm K}$ to essentially the
same final temperature.  This is the ideal, no-loss, no-phase-change
calorimetric limit.

In the (practically) instantaneous impact the linear momentum of the
system in the horizontal direction is conserved, the kinetic energy
is not.  Let

* $m$ = mass of the bullet $=10\;{\rm g}=1.0\times10^{-2}\ {\rm kg}$
* $M$ = mass of the block $=2.96\ {\rm kg}$
* $M_{t}=M+m$ the mass which swings after the impact
* $v_{0}$ the common horizontal speed of the block+bullet just after
the impact
* $v_{b}$ the speed of the bullet just before the impact
* $h=14.9\;{\rm cm}=0.149\;{\rm m}$ the rise of the centre of mass of
the $M_{t}$ system.

Impact

$$
m\,v_{b}=M_{t}v_{0}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
v_{0}=\frac{m}{M_{t}}\,v_{b}
\tag{1}
$$

Swing

After the impact the kinetic energy of the $M_{t}$ system is converted
into gravitational potential energy, neglecting air drag,

$$
\frac12M_{t}v_{0}^{2}=M_{t}g\,h
$$

so that the speed immediately after the impact is the speed which
will carry the pendulum to the height $h$,

$$
v_{0}=\sqrt{2gh}\; .
$$

With $g=9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$

$$
v_{0}= \sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.149}
     =\sqrt{2.923\;{\rm m^{2}s^{-2}}}
     \approx 1.71\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

is the speed of the block+bullet just after the bullet is stopped.
From (1)

$$
v_{b}= \frac{M_{t}}{m}\,v_{0}
     =\frac{M+m}{m}\sqrt{2gh}
$$

is the speed the bullet must have had before impact.  In closed form

$$
v_{b}= \frac{M+m}{m}\sqrt{2gh}\approx
297\,\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.149}\approx 5.0\!-\!5.1\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}
$$

i.e. about $5.1\times10^{2}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ in the horizontal
direction.  With the usual $M_{t}\approx M$ approximation

$$
v_{b}\approx\frac{M}{m}\sqrt{2gh}
      =\frac{2.96}{0.010}\sqrt{2gh}
      \approx 296\times1.71\approx 5.06\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s},
$$

about $506\!-\!508\;{\rm m/s}$, $\approx 5.1\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$,
the familiar ballistic-pendulum result.  Using $M_{t}=2.97\;{\rm kg}$
the more exact value is

$$
v_{b}\approx 297\sqrt{2gh}\approx 5.08\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}\approx 508\;{\rm m/s},
$$

essentially the $ \sim 507\;{\rm m/s}$ normally quoted for the
$2.96\;{\rm kg}$ pendulum.  The $M_{t}\approx M$ value $v_{b}\simeq
506\;{\rm m/s}$ is the one most often quoted.

For the hanging mass let the downward direction be positive and let $T$ be the
tension in the (massless) string.  With $a$ the linear acceleration of the
mass and $\alpha$ the angular acceleration of the disk

* Translation of the mass
$$
m g-T=m a\tag{1}
$$

* Rotation of the disk about its centre
$$
\tau =I\alpha\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad T R=I\alpha
$$
For a uniform solid disc about its central axis
$$
I=\frac12 MR^{2}
$$
and for inextensible unwinding
$$
a=R\alpha\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;\alpha=\frac{a}{R}\; .
$$
Hence
$$
TR=\frac12MR^{2}\frac{a}{R}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
T=\frac12Ma\tag{2}
$$
is the tension which can be supplied by the disc.  Putting (2) in (1)

$$
mg-\frac12Ma=m a
$$

$$
a\Bigl(m+\frac{M}{2}\Bigr)=mg
$$

$$
a=\frac{mg}{\,m+M/2\,}=\frac{2m}{2m+M}\,g
$$

is the linear acceleration of the mass and $a/R$ the angular acceleration
of the disc.  In terms of the moment of inertia

$$
a=\frac{g}{1+I/mR^{2}} .
$$

For $M=3.96\;{\rm kg}$, $m=2.87\;{\rm kg}$, $R=0.060\;{\rm m}$,

$$
m+\frac{M}{2}=2.87+\frac{3.96}{2}=4.85\;{\rm kg}
$$

$$
a=\frac{2.87\times9.81}{4.85}\approx5.8\!-\!5.9\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}
$$

downwards, about $5.8\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ down.  With the numbers quoted

$$
a\approx\frac{2m g}{2m+M}\approx5.8\;{\rm m/s^{2}}\approx5.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}
$$

down the string, i.e. $\alpha=a/R\approx5.8/0.06\approx9.7\times10^{1}\ {\rm rad/s^{2}}$.
The corresponding string tension is $T=\tfrac12Ma\approx1.15\times10^{1}\ {\rm N}$,
and $mg-T=ma$ as required.  The $R$ cancels so the numerical value is
independent of the 6 cm radius provided the no-slip condition holds.

* $N=59$

* $\Delta t =0.29\;{\rm s}$

$$

       =59\,(1.11\times10^{-2}\,{\rm m^{2}})\,
         \frac{0.28\;{\rm T}}{0.29\;{\rm s}}
       \approx 6.3\times10^{-1}\ {\rm V}
$$

and with the coil resistance $R=11.1\;\Omega$

For a body that rolls without slipping the loss of gravitational potential
is shared between translation and rotation

$$ \Delta U = \Delta K_{tr}+\Delta K_{rot}$$

$$m g h = \frac12 m v^{2}+\frac12 I\omega^{2}$$

For a solid sphere

$$I_{cm}= \frac25 m r^{2}$$

and rolling without slipping

$$\omega =\frac{v}{r}$$

so that

$$K_{rot}= \frac12 I\omega^{2}
      =\frac12\frac25 m r^{2}\frac{v^{2}}{r^{2}}
      =\frac15 m v^{2}$$

Hence

$$m g h =\frac12 m v^{2}+\frac15 m v^{2}
       =\frac{7}{10}m v^{2}$$

the mass cancels and

$$v^{2}= \frac{10}{7}\,g h
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
v=\sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1+I/mr^{2}}}
   =\sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1+2/5}} $$

is the translational speed at the bottom of the drop.  With

usual $g=9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ value.  The corresponding angular speed is

In the familiar form $v=\sqrt{2gh/(1+k^{2})}$ with $k^{2}=2/5$ for a solid
sphere.  This is $\sqrt{7/10}$ of the speed $\sqrt{2gh}$ that a particle

with $v_{0}$ the launch speed and $\theta$ the launch angle measured from
the horizontal.  The horizontal component is uniform

$$

and the vertical component is uniformly accelerated

$$

$$

      =t_{f}\Bigl(v_{0}\sin\theta-\frac12gt_{f}\Bigr)
$$

$$

is the time of flight.  In that time the horizontal displacement is

$$

   =v_{0}\cos\theta\frac{2v_{0}\sin\theta}{g}
   =\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{g}\,2\sin\theta\cos\theta
   =\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{g}\sin2\theta ,

* $v_{x0}=v_{0}\cos\theta$,
* $v_{y0}=v_{0}\sin\theta$,
* $t_{f}=2v_{y0}/g$.
