about $1.4\times10^{2}\,$m down range, $ \approx 142\;{\rm m}$ on the
$9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$ value of $g$.  With $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$
this is $R\approx 1.43\times10^{2}\,$m, essentially the $ \sim 140\!-\!145\;{\rm m}$ range usually quoted.  The maximum height reached in the same flight is $h_{\max}=v_{y0}^{2}/2g\approx47.3\,$m.

For a flat coil $\Phi = B A\cos\theta$ and for $\theta=0$

$${\cal E}= -N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}=-NA\frac{dB}{dt}$$

is the magnitude of the emf induced in the $N$ turns.  For a
steady change the average $dB/dt$ can be taken as $\Delta B/\Delta t$.

* Area per turn
$$
A = 283\;{\rm cm^{2}} = 283\times10^{-4}\;{\rm m^{2}} = 2.83\times10^{-2}\;{\rm m^{2}}
$$

* Rate of change of flux
$$
\Bigl|\frac{\Delta B}{\Delta t}\Bigr|
      =\frac{B_{i}-B_{f}}{\Delta t}
      =\frac{0.54-0.11}{0.08}\;{\rm T\,s^{-1}}
      =\frac{0.43}{0.08}=5.38\;{\rm T\,s^{-1}}
$$

Hence the magnitude of the induced emf in the $N=338$ turn winding is

$$
|{\cal E}| = N A \Bigl|\frac{\Delta B}{\Delta t}\Bigr|
          = 338\,(2.83\times10^{-2}\,{\rm m^{2}})\,
            \frac{0.43}{0.08}\;{\rm V}
          \approx 9.57\times5.38\;{\rm V}
          \approx 5.1\times10^{1}\ {\rm V}\approx 51\;{\rm V}
$$

in the sense which tries to keep the original flux.  With a total
circuit resistance $R=14.4\;\Omega$

$$
|I|=\frac{|{\cal E}|}{R}\approx\frac{51.4\;{\rm V}}{14.4\;\Omega}
     \approx 3.5\!-\!3.6\;{\rm A}
$$

about $3.6\;{\rm A}$ of current flowing so as to try to maintain the
decreasing $0.54\to0.11\;{\rm T}$ field.  The sign is opposite to the
sense of the applied $B$ decrease; in magnitude

$I\approx N A\Delta B/R\Delta t\approx3.6\;{\rm A}\approx3.57\;{\rm A}$

for the average over the $0.08\;{\rm s}$ interval.  The $-$ sign in
${\cal E}=-N d\Phi/dt$ is the Lenz sign.

For two equal sign charges the field can vanish only between them, where the
fields are opposite.  Put the origin at $q_{1}$ and let the point be a
distance $x$ from $q_{1}$ on the line $q_{1}q_{2}$ so that

$$r_{1}=x\qquad r_{2}=d-x\qquad d=99\;{\rm cm}$$

On the segment $q_{1}q_{2}$

$$E_{1}=k\frac{q_{1}}{r_{1}^{2}}\;\;\hbox{to the right},\qquad 
E_{2}=k\frac{q_{2}}{r_{2}^{2}}\;\;\hbox{to the left},$$

so that $E_{net}=0$ for

$$k\frac{q_{1}}{r_{1}^{2}}=k\frac{q_{2}}{r_{2}^{2}}\;,
\qquad 
\frac{r_{2}}{r_{1}}=\sqrt{\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}}\;.$$

Hence with $r_{1}+r_{2}=d$

$$r_{1}= \frac{d}{1+\sqrt{q_{2}/q_{1}}}
      =d\,\frac{\sqrt{q_{1}}}{\sqrt{q_{1}}+\sqrt{q_{2}}}\;.$$

With $q_{1}=2.4\;\mu{\rm C}$, $q_{2}=7.9\;\mu{\rm C}$ and $d=99\;{\rm cm}$

$$\sqrt{\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}}=\sqrt{\frac{7.9}{2.4}}\approx1.81,$$

so that

$$r_{1}= \frac{99\;{\rm cm}}{1+\sqrt{7.9/2.4}}
      \approx\frac{99}{2.814}\;{\rm cm}\approx 3.5\!-\!3.6\times10^{1}\ {\rm cm}$$

from the $2.4\;\mu{\rm C}$ charge, i.e. about $35\!-\!36\;{\rm cm}$ toward
the $7.9\;\mu{\rm C}$ charge.  In closed form

$$r_{1}=99\,\frac{\sqrt{2.4}}{\sqrt{2.4}+\sqrt{7.9}}\ {\rm cm}\approx
3.52\times10^{1}\ {\rm cm}$$

about $35.2\;{\rm cm}$ from $q_{1}$ and $99-35.2\approx63.8\;{\rm cm}$ from
$q_{2}$, on the side of the smaller charge between the two charges.  This
is the usual $r_{1}\approx35\;{\rm cm}$ quoted value, $r_{1}\simeq35.18\;{\rm cm}$ with the numbers given.

In the (practically) instantaneous impact the linear momentum in the
horizontal direction is conserved, the kinetic energy being lost in the
inelastic embedding.

Let

* $m=15\;{\rm g}=1.5\times10^{-2}\ {\rm kg}$ be the mass of the bullet,
* $M=2.22\ {\rm kg}$ the mass of the block,
* $V$ the common horizontal speed of the block+bullet immediately after
the impact,
* $v$ the speed of the bullet just before impact.

Momentum

$$
m v=(M+m)V\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
V=\frac{m}{M+m}\,v
\tag{1}
$$

After the impact the system rises to a height $h$ under gravity.  With
the loss of mechanical energy neglected in the swing,

$$
\frac12\,(M+m)V^{2}=(M+m)g\,h
$$

so that the speed immediately after impact is the speed which can raise
the centre of mass through $h$,

$$
V=\sqrt{2gh}\;,
$$

independent of the masses.  Hence from (1)

$$
v=\frac{M+m}{m}\sqrt{2gh}
$$

is the speed of the bullet before it strikes the pendulum.

For

$$
h=9.2\;{\rm cm}=9.2\times10^{-2}\ {\rm m},\qquad 
g=9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}},
$$

$$
V=\sqrt{2gh}=\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.092}\approx
\sqrt{1.805}\approx1.34\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

is the speed of the $(M+m)$ system just after impact.  With
$M+m=2.235\;{\rm kg}$,

$$
\frac{M+m}{m}=\frac{2.235}{0.015}=149
$$

so that

$$
v\approx149\,V\approx149\times1.34\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}\approx
2.0\times10^{2}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

i.e. about $2\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$ in the horizontal direction,
$\,v\approx 200\;{\rm m/s}$ on the usual $M/m\approx148$ approximation.
With $V=\sqrt{2gh}$ this is $v=(M+m)/m\sqrt{2gh}\approx 2.0\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$, about $200\;{\rm m/s}$ before impact, essentially the familiar ballistic-pendulum result.  Using $M/m$ alone gives $v\approx148\sqrt{2gh}\approx1.99\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$, the difference being the $m$ in the numerator.

For a parallel plate

$$C=\kappa\,\varepsilon_{0}\frac{A}{d}\qquad 
U=\frac12CV^{2}=\frac12\,\kappa\,\varepsilon_{0}\frac{A}{d}V^{2}$$

* $A=413\;{\rm cm^{2}}=413\times10^{-4}\;{\rm m^{2}}=4.13\times10^{-2}\;{\rm m^{2}}$
* $d=0.97\;{\rm mm}=0.97\times10^{-3}\;{\rm m}=9.7\times10^{-4}\;{\rm m}$
* $\kappa =5.4$, $V=26\;{\rm V}$

$$
\frac{\varepsilon_{0}A}{d}= 
\frac{8.854\times10^{-12}\times 4.13\times10^{-2}}{9.7\times10^{-4}}
\approx 3.77\times10^{-10}\ {\rm F}
$$

$$
C=\kappa\frac{\varepsilon_{0}A}{d}
   \approx5.4\times3.77\times10^{-10}\approx2.0\!-\!2.1\times10^{-9}\ {\rm F}
$$

about $2.0\;{\rm nF}$.

$$
U=\frac12CV^{2}
  =\frac12\,(2.04\times10^{-9}\,{\rm F})(26\,{\rm V})^{2}
  =\frac12\,(2.04\times10^{-9})(676)
  \approx6.9\times10^{-7}\ {\rm J}
$$

$$
U\approx6\!-\!7\times10^{-7}\ {\rm J}\approx0.6\!-\!0.7\;\mu{\rm J}
$$

i.e. $\,U\approx0.69\;\mu{\rm J}\approx 6.9\times10^{-7}\,{\rm J}$,
about $0.7\;\mu{\rm J}$ stored in the field.  With $\varepsilon_{0}=8.85\times10^{-12}$ this is $U\approx0.69\;\mu{\rm J}$, essentially $ \sim 0.7\;\mu{\rm J}$ on the quoted data.

For a string fixed at both ends the normal modes are standing waves

$$\lambda_{n}= \frac{2L}{n}\qquad n=1,2,\dots$$

so that with the wave speed on the string

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$$

$$f_{n}=\frac{v}{\lambda_{n}}=\frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} $$

is the $n$-th harmonic.  For the fundamental $n=1$

* $L=0.57\;{\rm m}$
* $T=69\;{\rm N}$
* $\mu =2.9\;{\rm g\,m^{-1}}=2.9\times10^{-3}\;{\rm kg\,m^{-1}}$

The phase speed on the string is

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}
   =\sqrt{\frac{69\;{\rm N}}{2.9\times10^{-3}\;{\rm kg\,m^{-1}}}}
   =\sqrt{2.38\times10^{4}\;{\rm m^{2}s^{-2}}}
   \approx 1.54\times10^{2}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}} $$

The fundamental wavelength for a string fixed at both ends is

$$\lambda_{1}=2L=2\times0.57\;{\rm m}=1.14\;{\rm m}$$

Hence

$$f_{1}=\frac{v}{\lambda_{1}}=\frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}
     =\frac{1}{1.14\;{\rm m}}\sqrt{\frac{69}{2.9\times10^{-3}}}
     \approx\frac{154.3}{1.14}\ {\rm Hz}
     \approx 1.3\!-\!1.4\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}$$

about $1.35\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}$, i.e. $\approx 135\;{\rm Hz}$ for the
$n=1$ mode.  The $n$-th mode is $f_{n}=n\,f_{1}$.

*Remark:* $f_{1}\approx 135\;{\rm Hz}$ with the numbers quoted.  Using
$\mu=0.0029\;{\rm kg/m}$ the often quoted value is $f_{1}\simeq 1.35\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}\approx 135\!-\!136\;{\rm Hz}$, essentially the musical note E3.

For the hanging mass let down be positive and let $T$ be the tension in the string.

* Translation of the mass
$$
m g -T = m a\qquad 1
$$

* Rotation of the disk
The string does not slip so that
$$
a = R\,\alpha
$$
and for a uniform solid disk about its central axis
$$
I = \frac12 M R^{2}
$$

The torque on the disk is $ \tau = T R$ so that
$$
\tau = I\alpha
$$
$$
T R = \frac12 M R^{2}\frac{a}{R}
$$
$$
T = \frac12 M a
$$

Put this in 1
$$
m g -\frac12 M a = m a
$$
$$
a\left(m+\frac{M}{2}\right)=m g
$$
$$
a = \frac{m}{m+M/2}\;g
      =\frac{g}{1+I/mR^{2}}
$$

For the numbers
$$
m+\frac{M}{2}=0.24\;{\rm kg}+\frac{4.50}{2}\;{\rm kg}=0.24+2.25=2.49\;{\rm kg}
$$

$$
a = \frac{0.24\times 9.81}{2.49}\approx 0.94\!-\!0.95\;{\rm m/s^{2}}
$$

down the string.  With $g=9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$

$$
a\approx 9.46\times10^{-1}\ {\rm m/s^{2}}\approx0.95\;{\rm m/s^{2}}
$$

downward, i.e. about $g/10.4$.  The corresponding angular acceleration of the disk is $\alpha=a/R\approx0.946/0.13\approx7.3\;{\rm rad/s^{2}}$ in the sense of unwinding.  With $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is $a\approx0.94\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$.

For a reversible Carnot cycle

$$ \eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}\qquad 
W_{cyc}= \eta_{C}Q_{H}=Q_{H}-Q_{C} $$

with the absolute temperatures

* $T_{H}=291^{\circ}{\rm C}=291+273.15\simeq 5.64\times10^{2}\ {\rm K}$
* $T_{C}= 80^{\circ}{\rm C}= 80+273.15\simeq 3.53\times10^{2}\ {\rm K}$

Hence

$$
\eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}
      =1-\frac{353.15}{564.15}
      =1-0.626\approx 0.374
$$

i.e. about $37\!-\!38\%$ of the heat taken in from the hot
reservoir can be turned into work in the reversible limit.  With
$Q_{H}=10.6\;{\rm kJ}$ per cycle

$$
W_{cyc}= \eta_{C}Q_{H}\approx0.374\times10.6\;{\rm kJ}\approx
3.9\!-\!4.0\;{\rm kJ}
$$

per cycle, about $3.96\;{\rm kJ}$ on the $273.15\;{\rm K}$ scale.
In the usual textbook $T({\rm K})=t(^{\circ}{\rm C})+273$ convention
$T_{H}=564\;{\rm K}$, $T_{C}=353\;{\rm K}$,

$$
\eta_{C}=1-\frac{353}{564}=0.373\;,
\qquad 
W_{cyc}\approx0.373\times10.6\approx3.95\;{\rm kJ}
$$

per cycle, $Q_{C}=Q_{H}-W_{cyc}\approx6.6\;{\rm kJ}$ being rejected to
the cold sink.  This is the reversible Carnot limit; any real engine
will give a smaller work output.

For a stationary observer the Doppler shift for a moving source is

$$f' = f_{0}\,\frac{v}{v\mp v_{s}} $$

the minus sign being used for a source moving towards the observer.
With $v_{o}=0$

$$f' = f_{0}\frac{v}{v-v_{s}}$$

is the observed frequency.  Here

* $f_{0}=605\;{\rm Hz}$,
* $v=343\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$,
* $v_{s}=32.1\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ towards the observer,

so that

$$
f' = 605\;\frac{343}{343-32.1}
     = 605\;\frac{343}{310.9}
     \approx 6.67\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}
$$

i.e. about $6.7\times10^{2}\,$Hz, $\approx 667\!-\!668\;{\rm Hz}$, an
up-shift of $\Delta f\approx 62\;{\rm Hz}$ from the emitted $605\;{\rm Hz}$.
In round numbers $f'\simeq 6.7\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}\approx 667\;{\rm Hz}$,
about $667.5\;{\rm Hz}$ with the numbers quoted.

The motion is the sum of a uniform motion during the reaction time and a
uniformly decelerated motion after the brakes are applied.

* Speed at the instant the obstacle is seen

$$
v_{0}=45\;{\rm km\,h^{-1}}=45\frac{1000}{3600}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      =12.5\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

Reaction distance

During the reaction time $t_{r}$ the car continues at $v_{0}$,

$$
s_{r}=v_{0}t_{r}
$$

$$
s_{r}=12.5\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}\times1.40\;{\rm s}=17.5\;{\rm m}
$$

is covered before the brakes actually begin to act.

Braking distance

After the brakes are on

$$
v^{2}=v_{0}^{2}+2a s_{b},\qquad v=0,\;\;a=-a_{b}
$$

with $a_{b}=6.7\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$

$$
s_{b}=\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{2a_{b}}
     =\frac{(12.5)^{2}}{2\times6.7}
     =\frac{156.25}{13.4}\approx 1.17\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}
$$

$$
s_{b}\approx 11.7\;{\rm m}
$$

is the distance covered while the brakes are acting.

Total stopping distance from the instant the obstacle is first seen

$$
s_{\rm tot}=s_{r}+s_{b}=v_{0}t_{r}+\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{2a_{b}}
$$

$$
s_{\rm tot}\approx 17.5\;{\rm m}+11.7\;{\rm m}\approx 2.9\!-\!3.0\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}
$$

about $29\;{\rm m}$ from the point where the driver first sees the obstacle, $\approx 17.5\;{\rm m}$ of which is travelled during the $1.40\;{\rm s}$ reaction time and $\approx 11.7\;{\rm m}$ under braking.  With the numbers quoted this is $s_{\rm tot}\simeq 29.2\;{\rm m}$, essentially $ \sim 29\;{\rm m}$ of stopping distance.

For the hanging mass let the downward direction be positive and let the
string be inextensible so that

* $a$ is the linear acceleration of the mass
* $\alpha$ is the angular acceleration of the disk

$$a = R\,\alpha\qquad {\rm no\; slip}$$

For the hanging mass

$$ \sum F_{y}=m a $$
$$ m g -T = m a\tag{1}$$

For the disk the only external torque about the axle is that of the
string

$$ \sum \tau = I\alpha $$

$$ T R = I_{\rm disk}\,\alpha $$

For a uniform solid disk about its central axis

$$ I_{\rm disk}= \frac12 M R^{2} $$

so that

$$ T R = \frac12 M R^{2}\,\frac{a}{R} $$

$$ T = \frac12 M\,a\tag{2}$$

Eliminate $T$ between (1) and (2)

$$ m g -\frac12 M a = m a $$

$$ m g = a\left(m+\frac{M}{2}\right) $$

$$ a = \frac{m}{m+M/2}\;g
     =\frac{g}{1+I/(mR^{2})}
     =\frac{g}{1+M/2m} $$

in the downward sense.  With

* $M = 4.17\;{\rm kg}$
* $m = 0.53\;{\rm kg}$
* $R =0.25\;{\rm m}$
* $g =9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$

$$ m+\frac{M}{2}=0.53+\frac{4.17}{2}=0.53+2.085=2.615\;{\rm kg}$$

$$ a = \frac{0.53\times 9.81}{2.615}\approx 1.9\!-\!2.0\;{\rm m/s^{2}} $$

downward, about $1.99\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ down.  The corresponding string
tension is

$$T=\frac{M}{2}a\approx2.085\times1.99\approx4.1\!-\!4.2\;{\rm N},$$

and the angular acceleration of the disk is $\alpha=a/R\approx
1.99/0.25\approx7.95\;{\rm rad/s^{2}}$.

With $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is $a\approx1.98\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$
down, essentially $ \approx 2.0\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ down, i.e. about
$1/5\,g$ because the disk has to be spun up as well as the mass
accelerated.

In the inelastic impact the linear momentum in the horizontal direction is
conserved

$$m_{b}v_{b}=(m_{b}+M)v_{0}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
v_{0}=\frac{m_{b}}{m_{b}+M}v_{b} ,$$

where $v_{0}$ is the velocity of the $(m_{b}+M)$ system immediately after
the impact.  After the impact the kinetic energy of the system is
converted into gravitational potential

$$\frac12\,(m_{b}+M)v_{0}^{2}=(m_{b}+M)g\,h ,$$

so that the velocity immediately after impact is the velocity which will
carry the pendulum to the height $h$,

$$v_{0}=\sqrt{2gh}\;.$$

Hence

$$v_{b}=\frac{m_{b}+M}{m_{b}}\,v_{0}
      =\frac{m_{b}+M}{m_{b}}\sqrt{2gh}
      =\left[1+\frac{M}{m_{b}}\right]\sqrt{2gh}\;.$$

With $m_{b}=12\;{\rm g}=1.20\times10^{-2}\ {\rm kg}$,
$M=2.53\ {\rm kg}$ and $h=13.2\ {\rm cm}=0.132\ {\rm m}$,

$$v_{0}=\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.132}\approx\sqrt{2.59}\approx1.61\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$$

and

$$\frac{m_{b}+M}{m_{b}}=\frac{2.542}{0.012}\approx2.12\times10^{2},$$

so that

$$v_{b}\approx 2.118\times10^{2}\times1.61\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      \approx 3.4\!-\!3.5\times10^{2}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}},$$

i.e. about $3.4\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$ in the horizontal direction,
$\,v_{0}\approx1.6\ {\rm m/s}$ for the combined pendulum.  With the
numbers quoted this is

$$v_{b}\simeq\frac{2.53+0.012}{0.012}\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.132}
      \approx 3.4\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}\approx 341\ {\rm m/s},$$

about $340\;{\rm m/s}$ before impact, the $1.61\;{\rm m/s}$ being the
post-impact swing speed which rises $h$ under gravity.  This is the
usual ballistic-pendulum estimate; using $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ gives
$v_{b}\approx 3.41\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$, essentially the same result.

For a coil the induced emf is the rate of change of the magnetic flux
linkage

$$\mathcal E = -N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}=-N A\frac{dB}{dt}$$

for a field normal to the plane of the turns.  In magnitude

$$|\mathcal E| = N A\frac{|\Delta B|}{\Delta t}$$

with

* $N=28$
* $A=156\;{\rm cm^{2}}=156\times10^{-4}\;{\rm m^{2}}=1.56\times10^{-2}\;{\rm m^{2}}$
* $|\Delta B|=|B_{f}-B_{i}|=|0.93-1.32|\;{\rm T}=0.39\;{\rm T}$
* $\Delta t =0.17\;{\rm s}$

Hence

$$
|\mathcal E| = 28\,(1.56\times10^{-2}\,{\rm m^{2}})\,
\frac{0.39\;{\rm T}}{0.17\;{\rm s}}
      \approx 1.0\;{\rm V}
$$

about $1.00\;{\rm V}$ of emf is induced in the $N$ turns.  With a total
resistance $R=3.2\;\Omega$

$$
|I|=\frac{|\mathcal E|}{R}
    =\frac{N A|\Delta B|/ \Delta t}{R}
    \approx\frac{1.00\;{\rm V}}{3.2\;\Omega}
    \approx 3.1\times10^{-1}\ {\rm A}
$$

i.e. $\approx 0.31\!-\!0.32\;{\rm A}$ in magnitude, $\,I\approx0.31\;{\rm A}$,
the sign being given by Lenz’s law.  Using the numbers as quoted

$|\mathcal E|\simeq1.00\;{\rm V}$ and $|I|\simeq1.00/3.2\simeq0.313\;{\rm A}$,
about $0.3\;{\rm A}$ induced in the coil.

For two like charges the fields point away from each charge so that between
them the two fields are opposite.  The zero is where the magnitudes are the
same

$$E_{1}=E_{2}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\frac{kq_{1}}{r_{1}^{2}}=\frac{kq_{2}}{r_{2}^{2}} $$

on the line joining them.  Put the origin at $q_{1}$ and let the zero be a
distance $r_{1}=x$ from $q_{1}$ on the way to $q_{2}$.  Then

$$r_{2}=L-x $$

with $L=75\;{\rm cm}$ the separation, and

$$\frac{q_{1}}{x^{2}}=\frac{q_{2}}{(L-x)^{2}} $$

so that

$$\frac{\sqrt{q_{1}}}{x}=\frac{\sqrt{q_{2}}}{L-x}\;, \qquad
\frac{L-x}{x}=\sqrt{\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}}\;.$$

Hence

$$L-x = x\sqrt{\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
x\Bigl[\,1+\sqrt{q_{2}/q_{1}}\,\Bigr]=L
$$

$$x=\frac{L}{\,1+\sqrt{q_{2}/q_{1}}\,}$$

on the $q_{1}\to q_{2}$ side.  With $q_{1}=2.9\;\mu{\rm C}$,
$q_{2}=7.3\;\mu{\rm C}$ and $L=75\;{\rm cm}$

$$\sqrt{\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}}=\sqrt{\frac{7.3}{2.9}}
      =\sqrt{2.517}\approx1.59 $$

$$x=\frac{75\;{\rm cm}}{1+1.5866}\approx\frac{75}{2.587}\approx
2.9\times10^{1}\ {\rm cm}$$

from the $2.9\;\mu{\rm C}$ charge, i.e. about $29\;{\rm cm}$ toward the
$7.3\;\mu{\rm C}$ charge.  The complementary distance to $q_{2}$ is

$$r_{2}=L-x\approx75-29\approx46\;{\rm cm},$$

and indeed $kq_{1}/x^{2}\approx kq_{2}/r_{2}^{2}$, so the net $E$ vanishes
between the charges, closer to the smaller charge as expected.  This is
$\approx 46\;{\rm cm}$ from the $7.3\;\mu{\rm C}$ charge.

In the (essentially) horizontal impact the horizontal linear momentum is
conserved.  For a perfectly plastic impact

$$p_{i}=p_{f}$$

$$m_{1}v_{1}= (m_{1}+m_{2})v^{\prime}$$

so that immediately after the impact

$$v^{\prime}= \frac{m_{1}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\,v_{1}$$

is the common velocity of the stuck pair.  With

* $m_{1}=0.90\;{\rm kg}$ , $v_{1}=9.1\;{\rm m/s}$
* $m_{2}=3.79\;{\rm kg}$

$$M=m_{1}+m_{2}=0.90+3.79=4.69\;{\rm kg}$$

$$p_{i}=m_{1}v_{1}=0.90\times 9.1=8.19\;{\rm kg\,m/s}$$

$$v^{\prime}= \frac{8.19}{4.69}\approx 1.7\!-\!1.8\;{\rm m/s}$$

about $1.75\;{\rm m/s}$ in the direction of the incident block.  The
kinetic energy left in the pair is

$$K^{\prime}= \tfrac12 M v^{\prime 2}
      =\tfrac12\frac{m_{1}^{2}v_{1}^{2}}{M}\;.$$

After the impact the pair is brought to rest by kinetic friction

$$F_{f}= \mu_{k}N=\mu_{k}Mg $$

so that the (constant) deceleration of the centre of mass is

$$a_{f}= \frac{F_{f}}{M}= \mu_{k}g  $$

and the work–energy balance for the sliding after impact is

$$K^{\prime}=W_{f}=F_{f}s=\mu_{k}Mg\,s $$

i.e.

$$s=\frac{v^{\prime 2}}{2\mu_{k}g}
   =\frac{1}{2\mu_{k}g}\left[\frac{m_{1}v_{1}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\right]^{2} .
$$

With $\mu_{k}=0.50$

$$a_{f}= \mu_{k}g\approx0.50\times9.81=4.90\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$$

and

$$s=\frac{v^{\prime 2}}{2a_{f}}
  =\frac{(1.746\,{\rm m/s})^{2}}{2\times0.50\times9.81}
  \approx\frac{3.05}{9.81}\approx 3.1\times10^{-1}\ {\rm m}$$

about $0.30\!-\!0.32\;{\rm m}$ of sliding from the point of impact,
$\approx 31\;{\rm cm}$, reached in

$$t_{s}=v^{\prime}/a_{f}\approx1.75/4.90\approx0.36\;{\rm s}$$

after the impact.  The $0.31\;{\rm m}$ is the distance travelled by the
combined $4.69\;{\rm kg}$ mass after it has stuck together; the
$0.90\;{\rm kg}$ block has of course travelled a little farther in
reaching the point of impact.  With $g\approx9.8\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is
$s\approx0.31\;{\rm m}$, essentially $ \sim 30\;{\rm cm}$ of post-impact
slide.

In projectile motion with no drag the horizontal component is constant
and the vertical component is free fall from rest.

* $v_{x0}=v_{x}=10.4\;{\rm m/s}$  constant
* $v_{y0}=0$

Fall time from a height $h$

$$h = v_{y0}t+\tfrac12gt^{2}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
t_{f}= \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}$$

$$t_{f}= \sqrt{\frac{2\times 35.8\;{\rm m}}{9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}}}
      =\sqrt{7.30\;{\rm s^{2}}}\approx 2.70\;{\rm s}$$

Vertical speed on arrival

$$v_{y}=v_{y0}+gt_{f}=gt_{f}=\sqrt{2gh}$$

$$v_{y}= \sqrt{2\times9.81\times35.8}\approx\sqrt{702.4}\approx 2.65\times10^{1}\ {\rm m/s}$$

downwards.  In magnitude

$$v_{y}\approx 26.5\;{\rm m/s}\;\;{\rm down}$$

The horizontal speed is unchanged

$$v_{x}=10.4\;{\rm m/s}$$

so the speed magnitude on impact is

$$v=\sqrt{v_{x}^{2}+v_{y}^{2}}
   =\sqrt{v_{x}^{2}+2gh}
   =\sqrt{10.4^{2}+2\times9.81\times35.8}$$

$$v=\sqrt{108.2+702.4}\approx\sqrt{810.6}\approx 2.8\!-\!2.9\times10^{1}\ {\rm m/s}$$

$\approx 28\!-\!29\;{\rm m/s}$ , about $28.5\;{\rm m/s}$ in the forward-downward
direction.  The direction is

$$\theta =\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{v_{y}}{v_{x}}\right)
       =\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{2gh}}{10.4}\right)
       \approx \tan^{-1}(2.55)\approx 68\!-\!69^{\circ}$$

below the horizontal, i.e. $v\approx10.4\,\hat i-26.5\,\hat j\;{\rm m/s}$ on
impact.  With $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is $v\approx28.4\;{\rm m/s}$,
essentially the same.

The escape speed from a spherical body is

$$v_{e}=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}} $$

so that for the Earth

$$v_{e,E}= \sqrt{\frac{2GM_{E}}{R_{E}}}$$

and for the planet

$$v_{e,p}= \sqrt{\frac{2GM_{p}}{R_{p}}}
      =\sqrt{\frac{2G\,2.74M_{E}}{1.32R_{E}}}
      =\sqrt{\frac{2.74}{1.32}}\;
        \sqrt{\frac{2GM_{E}}{R_{E}}}
      =\sqrt{\frac{2.74}{1.32}}\;v_{e,E} .$$

For the Earth

$$
v_{e,E}= \sqrt{\frac{2(6.674\times10^{-11}{\rm \;Nm^{2}kg^{-2}})
(5.972\times10^{24}{\rm \;kg})}{6.371\times10^{6}{\rm \;m}}}
      =\sqrt{1.25\times10^{8}\ {\rm m^{2}s^{-2}}}
      \approx 1.12\times10^{4}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      \approx 11.2\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}},
$$

the familiar $11.18\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$.

Hence

$$
\frac{v_{e,p}}{v_{e,E}}=\sqrt{\frac{2.74}{1.32}}
      =\sqrt{2.08}\approx 1.44 .
$$

$$
v_{e,p}\approx1.44\,v_{e,E}\approx1.44\times11.2\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}
      \approx 1.6\times10^{4}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}\approx 16\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}},
$$

about $16.1\!-\!16.3\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ with the numbers quoted, i.e. $\approx 16\;{\rm km/s}$ on the planet, $\sim 44\%$ larger than the terrestrial escape speed.  Using $v_{e,E}=11.186\;{\rm km/s}$,

$$v_{e,p}\approx\sqrt{2.0788}\times11.186\;{\rm km/s}\approx16.1\;{\rm km/s},$$

essentially $ \sim 1.6\times10^{1}\ {\rm km/s}$ from the surface.

For an RC charge

$$V_{C}(t)=V_{\infty}\Bigl[\,1-e^{-t/RC}\Bigr]\qquad 
\tau\equiv RC$$

is the charging time constant.  With $V_{C}(t_{1/2})=V_{\infty}/2$

$$\frac12 =1-e^{-t_{1/2}/\tau}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
e^{-t_{1/2}/\tau}= \frac12 $$

so that

$$t_{1/2}= \tau\ln 2 = RC\ln 2 $$

is the $50\%$ charging time.  In the present case

$$\tau =RC=(24.0\times10^{3}\,\Omega)(64.0\times10^{-6}\,{\rm F})
      =1.536\;{\rm s}$$

Hence

$$t_{1/2}= \tau\ln2\approx1.536\times0.6931\;{\rm s}\approx1.0\!-\!1.1\;{\rm s}$$

about $1.06\;{\rm s}$ after the switch is closed, i.e. $t_{1/2}=RC\ln2$
$\approx 1.5\,\ln2\;{\rm s}$.  With $\ln2\approx0.693$ this is often quoted
as $t_{50\%}\approx0.693\,\tau\approx1.06\;{\rm s}$, essentially the
$0.693$ time constant.

For a charge moving perpendicular to a uniform $B$ the magnetic Lorentz
force provides the centripetal force

$$q v B=\frac{mv^{2}}{r}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
r=\frac{mv}{qB}$$

for $v\perp B$.  With

* $m_{p}=1.673\times10^{-27}\ {\rm kg}$
* $q_{p}=1.602\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}$
* $v=2.2\times10^{5}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$
* $B=1.33\ {\rm T}$

the (non-relativistic) cyclotron radius is

$$
r=\frac{m_{p}v}{q_{p}B}
   =\frac{\,1.673\times10^{-27}\times2.2\times10^{5}\,}
          {\,1.602\times10^{-19}\times1.33\,}\ {\rm m}
$$

$$
m_{p}v =3.68\times10^{-22}\ {\rm kg\,m/s},\qquad 
q_{p}B =2.13\times10^{-19}\ {\rm N\,s/C}
$$

$$
r\approx\frac{3.68\times10^{-22}}{2.13\times10^{-19}}\ {\rm m}
   \approx1.7\!-\!1.8\times10^{-3}\ {\rm m}
$$

i.e.

$$
r\approx1.7\times10^{-3}\ {\rm m}\approx1.7\!-\!1.8\ {\rm mm}
$$

about $1.73\;{\rm mm}$ on the usual constants, $r\approx mv/qB$.  This is
the radius of the non-relativistic helical/circular motion in the
$1.33\;{\rm T}$ field.

For a body that rolls without slipping the loss of gravitational potential
is shared between translation of the centre of mass and rotation about the
centre of mass.

Loss of potential on the drop $h$

$$\Delta U = m g h$$

is the kinetic energy at the bottom

$$K = K_{tr}+K_{rot}= \frac12 m v^{2}+\frac12 I\omega^{2}$$

For a solid cylinder about its central axis

$$I_{cm}= \frac12 m r^{2}$$

and rolling without slipping

$$v = \omega r\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \omega =\frac{v}{r}$$

so that

$$K_{rot}= \frac12 I_{cm}\omega^{2}
       =\frac12\left(\frac12 m r^{2}\right)\frac{v^{2}}{r^{2}}
       =\frac14 m v^{2}$$

Hence

$$K = \frac12 m v^{2}+\frac14 m v^{2}= \frac34 m v^{2}$$

Energy conservation, $K_{i}=0$,

$$m g h = \frac34 m v^{2}$$

the mass cancels and

$$v = \sqrt{\frac{4}{3}g h}
   =\sqrt{\frac{2g h}{1+I/mr^{2}}}$$

is the centre-of-mass speed.  For a solid cylinder $I/mr^{2}=1/2$.

In numbers

$$v =\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}\,9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}\times1.36\;{\rm m}}
   =\sqrt{17.79\;{\rm m^{2}/s^{2}}}
   \approx 4.2\!-\!4.3\;{\rm m/s}$$

about $4.22\;{\rm m/s}$ down the incline, the corresponding angular
speed being $\omega=v/r$.  The familiar form $v=\sqrt{4gh/3}$ is often
quoted.  With $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is $v\approx4.22\;{\rm m/s}$,
essentially $4.2\;{\rm m/s}$ translational speed at the bottom.

For a string fixed at both ends the standing wave condition is

$$L=n\frac{\lambda_{n}}{2}\qquad n=1,2,\dots$$

so that

$$f_{n}= \frac{v}{\lambda_{n}}=\frac{n}{2L}v $$

with the transverse wave speed on the string

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$$

The linear density in SI is

$$\mu =2.9\;{\rm g\,m^{-1}}=2.9\times10^{-3}\ {\rm kg\,m^{-1}}$$

Hence

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}=\sqrt{\frac{69\ {\rm N}}{2.9\times10^{-3}\ {\rm kg\,m^{-1}}}}
      =\sqrt{2.38\times10^{4}\ {\rm m^{2}s^{-2}}}
      \approx 1.54\times10^{2}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$$

The fundamental $n=1$ is

$$f_{1}= \frac{v}{2L}= \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$$

$$f_{1}= \frac{1}{2(0.57\;{\rm m})}\sqrt{\frac{69}{2.9\times10^{-3}}}
      =\frac{154\;{\rm m/s}}{1.14\;{\rm m}}
      \approx 1.3\!-\!1.4\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}$$

i.e. about $1.35\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}$, $\approx 135\;{\rm Hz}$, the $n$-th harmonic being $f_{n}=n f_{1}$.  This is the usual $f_{1}\approx v/2L$ estimate for a string fixed at both ends.

For two like charges the fields can cancel only on the line between them.
Put the origin at $q_{1}$ and $q_{2}$ at $L=78\;{\rm cm}$ on the $+x$ axis.
For a point $x$ between the charges, $0<x<L$,

* $E_{1}$ is away from $q_{1}$ : $E_{1}=kq_{1}/x^{2}$ to the right,
* $E_{2}$ is away from $q_{2}$ : $E_{2}=kq_{2}/(L-x)^{2}$ to the left.

Cancellation $E_{1}=E_{2}$ in magnitude gives

$$
\frac{kq_{1}}{x^{2}}=\frac{kq_{2}}{(L-x)^{2}}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\frac{L-x}{x}=\sqrt{\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}}\; .
$$

Hence, on the segment $q_{1}q_{2}$,

$$
x=\frac{L}{1+\sqrt{q_{2}/q_{1}}}\;,
\qquad L-x=\frac{L\sqrt{q_{2}/q_{1}}}{1+\sqrt{q_{2}/q_{1}}}\; .
$$

With $q_{1}=5.3\;\mu{\rm C}$, $q_{2}=8.4\;\mu{\rm C}$ and $L=78\;{\rm cm}$

$$
\sqrt{\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}}=\sqrt{\frac{8.4}{5.3}}=\sqrt{1.585}\approx1.26
$$

so that

$$
x_{0}= \frac{78\;{\rm cm}}{1+\sqrt{8.4/5.3}}
      \approx\frac{78}{2.259}\;{\rm cm}\approx 3.4\!-\!3.5\times10^{1}\ {\rm cm}
$$

from $q_{1}$ toward $q_{2}$, i.e. about $34\!-\!35\;{\rm cm}$ between the
charges.  In terms of the distance to $q_{2}$

$$
L-x_{0}=78-x_{0}\approx78-34.5\approx43.5\;{\rm cm},
$$

the zero being nearer the smaller charge $q_{1}$ as required.  This is
the unique interior zero; no zero exists on the exterior of the two
like charges.  With the usual rounding $x_{0}\simeq 34.5\;{\rm cm}\approx
35\;{\rm cm}$ from $q_{1}$, $43.5\;{\rm cm}$ from $q_{2}$, on the
$q_{1}q_{2}$ segment.

The induced emf in a coil is the rate of change of the total magnetic flux
linking the $N$ turns

$$\mathcal E = N\left|\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}\right|
      = N A\left|\frac{\Delta B}{\Delta t}\right| $$

for a field normal to the area of each turn.

* $N = 364$
* $A = 64\;{\rm cm^{2}} = 64\times10^{-4}\;{\rm m^{2}} = 6.4\times10^{-3}\;{\rm m^{2}}$
* $\Delta B = B_{2}-B_{1}=0.40-0.18 = 0.22\;{\rm T}$
* $\Delta t = 0.66\;{\rm s}$

The flux change per turn is

$$\Delta\Phi = A\,\Delta B = 6.4\times10^{-3}\times0.22
           =1.41\times10^{-3}\ {\rm Wb}$$

and for the $N$ turns

$$N\Delta\Phi = 364\times1.41\times10^{-3}\approx 0.513\ {\rm Wb}$$

Hence

$$\mathcal E = \frac{N\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}
          =\frac{364\,(6.4\times10^{-3}\,{\rm m^{2}})(0.22\,{\rm T})}{0.66\,{\rm s}}
          \approx 7.8\times10^{-1}\ {\rm V}\approx0.78\ {\rm V}$$

in magnitude.  With the coil resistance $R=3.5\;\Omega$

$$I=\frac{|\mathcal E|}{R}
  =\frac{N A |\Delta B|/ \Delta t}{R}
  \approx\frac{0.777\ {\rm V}}{3.5\;\Omega}
  \approx 2.2\times10^{-1}\ {\rm A}$$

about $0.22\;{\rm A}$ of induced current, the sign being given by Lenz’s law.  This is $\approx 0.22\!-\!0.23\;{\rm A}$ $\approx 0.222\;{\rm A}$ with the numbers quoted.

For the motion down the plane put $x$ down the plane.  The forces
parallel to the plane are

* $W_{\parallel}=mg\sin\theta$ down the plane
* $F_{f}= \mu_{k}N=\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta$ up the plane

so that with $m$ the mass of the block

$$m a = mg\sin\theta-\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta $$

i.e.

$$a=g\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big] $$

is the (constant) acceleration down the plane, provided
$\sin\theta>\mu_{k}\cos\theta$.  With

$$\theta =25^{\circ},\qquad \mu_{k}=0.28,\qquad 
\sin\theta =0.4226,\qquad \cos\theta =0.9063,$$

$$\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta
=0.4226-0.28\times0.9063=0.1689,$$

and

$$a=g\bigl[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\bigr]
\approx 9.81\times0.1689\approx1.66\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}} $$

down the plane.  For constant $a$ and $u=0$

$$v^{2}=u^{2}+2as=2as,$$

so that on the work–energy form

$$\frac12mv^{2}=mg s\sin\theta-\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta\,s
=mgs\bigl[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\bigr],$$

i.e.

$$v=\sqrt{\,2gs\bigl[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\bigr]\,}$$

down the plane.  For $s=7.8\;{\rm m}$

$$v=\sqrt{2\times9.81\times7.8\,
\bigl[\sin25^{\circ}-0.28\cos25^{\circ}\bigr]}
      =\sqrt{25.84}\;{\rm m/s}\approx5.0\!-\!5.1\;{\rm m/s}$$

down the incline, about $5.1\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$ in magnitude, 
$ \approx 18\;{\rm km\,h^{-1}}$, the familiar $v\approx\sqrt{2as}$ with
$a\approx1.66\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$.  With the quoted numbers $v\approx5.08\;{\rm m/s}$,
essentially $5\;{\rm m/s}$ down the plane.  The sign is taken positive
down the plane; the magnitude is the speed quoted above.

For a reversible Carnot cycle the thermal efficiency is the
fraction of the heat taken from the hot reservoir that can be turned
into work

$$\eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}} $$

with the absolute temperatures.  The temperatures have to be in
kelvin

* $T_{H}=527^{\circ}{\rm C}=527+273.15\simeq 8.00\times10^{2}\ {\rm K}$
* $T_{C}= 76^{\circ}{\rm C}= 76+273.15\simeq 3.49\times10^{2}\ {\rm K}$

Hence

$$\eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}
      =1-\frac{349.15}{800.15}\approx 1-0.436\approx0.56\!-\!0.57 $$

In the often used $T[K]=T[^{\circ}{\rm C}]+273$ approximation

$$\eta_{C}\approx1-\frac{349}{800}= \frac{451}{800}=0.5638\approx56.4\% $$

is the maximum fraction of $Q_{H}$ that can appear as work in a
cycle.  With a heat intake per cycle

$$Q_{H}=12.9\;{\rm kJ}$$

the Carnot work per cycle is

$$W_{C}= \eta_{C}Q_{H}
      =\left[1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}\right]Q_{H}
      \approx0.564\times12.9\;{\rm kJ}\approx7.2\!-\!7.3\;{\rm kJ}$$

per cycle, about $56\%$ of the heat taken in.  With the $273.15$ K
conversion

$$W_{C}\approx0.5636\times12.9\;{\rm kJ}\approx7.27\;{\rm kJ}$$

is obtained, i.e. $\approx 7.3\;{\rm kJ}$ of mechanical work per cycle.
The remainder

$$Q_{C}=Q_{H}-W_{C}\approx12.9-7.27\approx5.6\;{\rm kJ}$$

is rejected to the cold reservoir per cycle.  This is the ideal
Carnot limit; any real engine operating between the same two
temperatures will do less work.

In an insulated system the heat lost by the hot aluminium is taken up by the
cold water

$$Q_{Al}=Q_{W}$$

$$m_{Al}c_{Al}\big(T_{Al,i}-T_{f}\big)=m_{W}c_{W}\big(T_{f}-T_{W,i}\big)$$

so that

$$T_{f}=
\frac{m_{Al}c_{Al}T_{Al,i}+m_{W}c_{W}T_{W,i}}
     {m_{Al}c_{Al}+m_{W}c_{W}}  $$

is the common final temperature.

$$ 
m_{Al}c_{Al}=0.44\times 900=3.96\times10^{2}\ {\rm J\,K^{-1}}
$$

$$
m_{W}c_{W}=0.83\times4186=3.474\times10^{3}\ {\rm J\,K^{-1}}
$$

Hence

$$
T_{f}=
\frac{396(141.0)+3474.38(26.9)}{396+3474.38}
     =\frac{55\,836+93\,461}{3\,870.4}
     \approx 3.86\times10^{1}\ {\rm^{\circ}C}
$$

i.e. about $3.8\!-\!3.9\times10^{1}\,^{\circ}{\rm C}$, $\approx 38\!-\!39^{\circ}{\rm C}$,
about $38.6^{\circ}{\rm C}$ on the numbers quoted, the aluminium cooling
from $141^{\circ}{\rm C}$ and the water warming from $26.9^{\circ}{\rm C}$ to
essentially the water-weighted temperature.  With the usual $c_{Al}\approx
900\;{\rm J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}$ this is $T_{f}\simeq 38.5\!-\!38.6^{\circ}{\rm C}$,
essentially $ \sim 39^{\circ}{\rm C}$ in round figures.

and
