For a charge moving perpendicular to a uniform $B$ the magnetic Lorentz
force provides the centripetal force

$$F_{c}=F_{B}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \frac{mv^{2}}{r}=qvB $$

so that, for $v\perp B$,

$$r=\frac{mv}{qB}$$

is the Larmor radius of the motion.  In the non-relativistic limit
$v/c\simeq 3.3\times10^{-2}$ the classical expression is adequate.

$$ 
r=\frac{m_{p}v}{eB}
   =\frac{\,1.673\times10^{-27}\ {\rm kg}\times 9.8\times10^{6}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}\,}
          {\,1.602\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}\times0.46\ {\rm T}\,}
$$

$$ 
mv =1.673\times9.8\times10^{-21}=1.64\times10^{-20}\ {\rm kg\,m\,s^{-1}}
$$

$$ 
qB =1.602\times0.46\times10^{-19}=7.37\times10^{-20}\ {\rm N\,s\,C^{-1}\,m^{-1}}
$$

Hence

$$
r=\frac{1.6415\times10^{-20}}{7.369\times10^{-20}}\ {\rm m}
  \approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{-1}\ {\rm m}
$$

$$
r\approx 0.22\;{\rm m}\approx 2.2\times10^{2}\ {\rm mm}
$$

i.e. about $2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{2}\ {\rm mm}$, $\approx 223\;{\rm mm}$ on the
numbers quoted, $r\approx0.223\;{\rm m}$ in SI.  With the usual
$m_{p}=1.6726\times10^{-27}\,$kg this is $r\approx0.222\;{\rm m}\approx222\;{\rm mm}$, essentially the same $\sim 0.22\;{\rm m}$ cyclotron radius.

For a projectile launched from and landing on the same horizontal level

* $v_{0x}=v_{0}\cos\theta$ , $v_{0y}=v_{0}\sin\theta$

* $y(t)=v_{0y}t-\tfrac12gt^{2}=0$ for the return to $y=0$

so that, apart from $t=0$,

$$t_{f}=\frac{2v_{0y}}{g}=\frac{2v_{0}\sin\theta}{g}$$

is the time of flight.  The horizontal motion is uniform

$$x(t)=v_{0x}t=v_{0}\cos\theta\,t $$

Hence on the level ground

$$R=v_{0}\cos\theta\,t_{f}
   =v_{0}\cos\theta\frac{2v_{0}\sin\theta}{g}
   =\frac{v_{0}^{2}}{g}\sin2\theta  $$

is the familiar range formula.

Here

* $v_{0}=37.1\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$
* $\theta =15^{\circ}$,
* $2\theta =30^{\circ}$,
* $g=9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$.

$$v_{0x}=v_{0}\cos15^{\circ}=37.1\times0.9659\approx 3.58\times10^{1}\ {\rm m/s}$$
$$v_{0y}=v_{0}\sin15^{\circ}=37.1\times0.2588\approx 9.60\ {\rm m/s}$$

Time of flight

$$t_{f}=\frac{2v_{0y}}{g}=\frac{2\times9.60}{9.81}\approx1.96\ {\rm s}$$

and

$$R=v_{0x}t_{f}\approx 35.84\times1.96\approx 7.0\times10^{1}\ {\rm m}$$

In closed form

$$R=\frac{v_{0}^{2}\sin2\theta}{g}
   =\frac{(37.1)^{2}\sin30^{\circ}}{9.81}
   =\frac{1.376\times10^{3}\times0.50}{9.81}\approx 7.0\!-\!7.1\times10^{1}\ {\rm m},$$

about $70\;{\rm m}$, $ \approx 70.1\!-\!70.3\;{\rm m}$ with the numbers quoted, $\,R\approx 70.2\;{\rm m}$ on the $g=9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ convention.  This is the $v_{0}^{2}\sin2\theta/g$ result, $R\approx 70\;{\rm m}$ horizontally for the $15^{\circ}$ launch.

For two like charges the fields point away from each charge so that between
them the two fields are opposite in direction and can cancel.

Put the origin at $q_{1}$ and let the $x$-axis be the line joining the two
charges.  With $q_{1}$ on the left and $q_{2}$ on the right

* $E_{1}$ at a point a distance $r_{1}$ to the right of $q_{1}$ is to the
right,
$E_{1}=kq_{1}/r_{1}^{2}$,
* $E_{2}$ at the same point a distance $r_{2}=L-r_{1}$ to the left of
$q_{2}$ is to the left,
$E_{2}=kq_{2}/r_{2}^{2}$,

where $L=69\;{\rm cm}$ is the separation.  The net field on the line is

$$E(r_{1})= \frac{kq_{1}}{r_{1}^{2}}-\frac{kq_{2}}{(L-r_{1})^{2}} $$

and $E=0$ for

$$\frac{q_{1}}{r_{1}^{2}}=\frac{q_{2}}{r_{2}^{2}}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\frac{r_{2}}{r_{1}}=\sqrt{\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}}\;.$$

Hence with $r_{2}=L-r_{1}$

$$\frac{L-r_{1}}{r_{1}}=\sqrt{\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}}$$

so that

$$r_{1}= \frac{L}{1+\sqrt{q_{2}/q_{1}}}$$

is the zero-field point between the charges, on the side of the smaller
charge.

Here

$$\sqrt{\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}}= \sqrt{\frac{8.0}{4.5}}
      =\sqrt{\frac{16}{9}}=\frac{4}{3}=1.33$$

and

$$r_{1}= \frac{69\;{\rm cm}}{1+4/3}= \frac{69}{7/3}\;{\rm cm}
      =\frac{207}{7}\;{\rm cm}\approx 2.96\times10^{1}\ {\rm cm}$$

from $q_{1}$ toward $q_{2}$.  That is $r_{2}=L-r_{1}\approx69-29.6\approx
39.4\;{\rm cm}$ from $q_{2}$, i.e. about $30\;{\rm cm}$ from the $4.5\;\mu{\rm C}$
charge, the zero being closer to the smaller charge as expected.  The
symmetric point $r_{1}\approx 39.4\;{\rm cm}$ from $q_{1}$ is the zero on the
other side of the larger charge and is not between the two charges.

For a series $R-C$ charge the capacitor voltage is

$$V_{C}(t)=V_{0}\Big[\,1-e^{-t/RC}\,\Big] \qquad V_{C}(0)=0$$

so that the fraction of the final value $V_{0}$ reached at time $t$ is

$$f(t)=\frac{V_{C}(t)}{V_{0}}=1-e^{-t/RC} .$$

For $f=1/2$

$$\frac12 =1-e^{-t_{1/2}/RC}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
e^{-t_{1/2}/RC}= \frac12 $$

$$-\frac{t_{1/2}}{RC}= \ln\frac12=-\ln2$$

$$t_{1/2}=RC\;\ln2 $$

The $RC$ time constant is

$$RC = 24\times10^{3}\ {\rm \Omega}\times 64\times10^{-6}\ {\rm F}
     =1.536\ {\rm s}$$

Hence

$$t_{1/2}=1.536\,\ln2\;{\rm s}\approx1.536\times0.6931\;{\rm s}
       \approx1.0\!-\!1.1\;{\rm s}$$

about $1.06\;{\rm s}$ for the voltage to be one half of its asymptotic
value $V_{0}$.  In particular $t_{1/2}=0.693\,RC$ is independent of the
magnitude of the ideal source voltage.  With the usual $RC\ln2$ value
this is $t_{1/2}\approx1.06\!-\!1.07\;{\rm s}$, $\approx1.64\;{\rm s}$ for
$63.2\%$ etc.

For the motion while the mass is still on the spring the mechanical
energy

$$E={\rm E_{el}}+{\rm E_{g}}+{\rm E_{k}}$$

is conserved, the spring being taken as massless.  Put the zero of
gravitational potential at the release point $y=0$ and let $s$ be the
instantaneous compression measured positive downwards from the
unstressed length, $s_{0}=0.123\;{\rm m}$ at release.  While the mass
is in contact

$$E(s)=\frac12k s^{2}+m g\,(s_{0}-s)+\frac12m\dot s^{2}={\rm const.}$$

The elastic energy which is available at release is

$$E_{el,0}=\frac12k s_{0}^{2}
      =\frac12(712\;{\rm N/m})(0.123\;{\rm m})^{2}
      \approx 5.4\;{\rm J}  $$

in the idealised $E_{el}\to m g h$ estimate.  If the spring is allowed
to come back to its natural length before the mass leaves, the whole
$E_{el,0}$ can be turned into gravitational potential $m g h_{0}$ in the
limit $v\to0$,

$$h_{0}\simeq\frac{E_{el,0}}{m g}
      =\frac{\,k s_{0}^{2}/2\,}{m g}
      =\frac{712(0.123)^{2}}{2(0.47)(9.81)}\approx1.1\!-\!1.2\;{\rm m}$$

above the release point, i.e. about $h_{0}-s_{0}\approx1.05\;{\rm m}$
above the unstressed length of the spring.  In round numbers

$$h_{0}\approx\frac{kx^{2}}{2mg}\approx1.2\;{\rm m}$$

above the compressed position, $\approx 1.0\;{\rm m}$ above the free
length of the spring.

*Remark on the loss of contact.*  In reality the normal reaction
vanishes when $k s_{\rm sep}=mg$,

$$s_{\rm sep}=\frac{mg}{k}=\frac{0.47\times9.81}{712}\approx6.5\times10^{-3}\ {\rm m},$$

so the mass actually leaves the spring $s_{0}-s_{\rm sep}=0.1165\;{\rm m}$
above the release point with

$$\frac12m v_{\rm sep}^{2}= \frac12k s_{0}^{2}-\frac12k s_{\rm sep}^{2}
      -mg\,(s_{0}-s_{\rm sep})\approx4.83\;{\rm J},$$

i.e. $v_{\rm sep}\approx4.5\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$.  Free flight thereafter
gives an additional rise

$$\Delta h_{f}=v_{\rm sep}^{2}/2g\approx1.05\;{\rm m},$$

so that the true maximum height measured from the release point is

$$h^{*}=s_{0}-s_{\rm sep}+\frac{v_{\rm sep}^{2}}{2g}\approx0.117+1.05\approx1.16\;{\rm m}$$

above the point of release, $h^{*}-s_{0}\approx1.04\;{\rm m}$ above the
natural length of the spring.  The $s_{\rm sep}$ correction is
$\,{\cal O}(mg/k)\ll s_{0}$ and the familiar $k x^{2}/2mg$ estimate
$h_{0}\approx1.17\;{\rm m}$ is the one normally quoted.

For a reversible change the (PV) work is

$$ \delta w_{rev}=-P_{ext}dV=-P\,dV\qquad{\rm (chem.\,sign)}$$

and for an ideal gas $P=nRT/V$ so that for an isothermal
reversible change

$$w_{rev}=-\int_{V_{1}}^{V_{2}}P\,dV
      =-nRT\int_{V_{1}}^{V_{2}}\frac{dV}{V}
      =-nRT\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}  $$

is the work done on the gas.  The work done by the gas on the
surroundings is the opposite sign,

$$w_{by}=+nRT\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}\;.$$

In magnitude

* $nRT =4.62\;{\rm mol}\times 8.314\;{\rm J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\times393\;{\rm K}
      =1.51\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}$

* $\displaystyle \ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}
      =\ln\frac{42.8}{9.1}=\ln 4.7055\approx1.55$

Hence

$$|w|\approx nRT\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}
      \approx 1.5095\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}\times1.5487
      \approx 2.3\!-\!2.4\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}$$

about $2.34\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}\approx 23\!-\!24\;{\rm kJ}$ of
expansion work.  In the usual chemical sign convention the work
done on the system is

$$w_{rev}=-nRT\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}\approx-2.3\!-\!2.4\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}
\approx -23.4\ {\rm kJ}$$

the minus sign denoting work done by the system on the surroundings.
The magnitude of the reversible isothermal work of expansion is
$\,|w|\simeq 2.34\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}$ , i.e. $\approx 23.4\;{\rm kJ}$
done by the gas, $w_{chem}\approx-23.4\;{\rm kJ}$ on the conventional
chemistry sign convention.  This is the $+23.4\;{\rm kJ}$ often quoted
as “work done by the gas”.

For an ideal Atwood the two masses have the same magnitude of acceleration
$a$ and the same string tension $T$.

Take the heavy mass $m_{1}=1.61\;{\rm kg}$ down positive and the light mass
$m_{2}=0.97\;{\rm kg}$ up positive.

* Heavy side
$$
m_{1}g-T=m_{1}a\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad T=m_{1}g-m_{1}a
$$

* Light side
$$
T-m_{2}g=m_{2}a\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad T=m_{2}g+m_{2}a
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates $T$,

$$
(m_{1}-m_{2})g=(m_{1}+m_{2})a
$$

so that

$$
a=g\,\frac{m_{1}-m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}
  =9.81\;\frac{1.61-0.97}{1.61+0.97}\;{\rm m/s^{2}}
  =9.81\;\frac{0.64}{2.58}\;{\rm m/s^{2}}
  \approx 2.4\!-\!2.5\;{\rm m/s^{2}}
$$

about $2.43\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ down for $m_{1}$ and up for $m_{2}$.

The common tension can be written in closed form as

$$
T=\frac{2m_{1}m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\,g
  =m_{1}\!\left(g-a\right)=m_{2}\!\left(g+a\right)
$$

i.e.

$$
T=\frac{2(1.61)(0.97)}{1.61+0.97}\;9.81
  =\frac{3.1234}{2.58}\;9.81\;{\rm N}
  \approx 1.19\times10^{1}\ {\rm N}
$$

$$
T\approx 1.19\times10^{1}\ {\rm N}\;\approx\;11.9\;{\rm N}
$$

about $11.9\;{\rm N}$ on each side of the ideal string, $m_{1}g-T=m_{1}a$
and $T-m_{2}g=m_{2}a$ with the $a\approx2.43\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ quoted above.
With $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is $T\approx11.86\;{\rm N}\approx12\;{\rm N}$,
essentially the average of the two weights.

For a charge moving perpendicular to a uniform $B$ the magnetic Lorentz
force provides the centripetal force

$$F_{c}=F_{B}$$

$$\frac{mv^{2}}{r}=qvB\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
r=\frac{mv}{qB}$$

for $v\perp B$.

* $m_{p}=1.673\times10^{-27}\ {\rm kg}$
* $q_{p}=1.602\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}$
* $v=9.0\times10^{6}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$
* $B=1.53\ {\rm T}$

$$ 
r=\frac{m_{p}v}{q_{p}B}
   =\frac{\,1.673\times10^{-27}\ {\rm kg}\times9.0\times10^{6}\ {\rm m/s}\,}
          {\,1.602\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}\times1.53\ {\rm T}\,}
$$

$$ 
m_{p}v =1.5057\times10^{-20}\ {\rm kg\,m/s}
$$

$$ 
q_{p}B =2.45\times10^{-19}\ {\rm N\,s/C\,m}
$$

$$
r=\frac{1.5057\times10^{-20}}{2.451\times10^{-19}}\ {\rm m}
  \approx 6.1\times10^{-2}\ {\rm m}
$$

$$
r\approx 0.061\ {\rm m}\approx 6.1\ {\rm cm}\approx 61\ {\rm mm}
$$

about $6\times10^{-2}\,$m of curvature, i.e. $\sim 61\!-\!62\,$mm radius
for the $9.0\times10^{6}\ {\rm m/s}$ proton in a $1.53\,$T field.  With the
usual $m_{p}=1.67\times10^{-27}\,$kg, $q=1.60\times10^{-19}\,$C this is
$r\approx 6.13\times10^{-2}\,$m $\approx 61.3\,$mm.

For the hanging mass let the tension in the string be $T$ and take down as
positive.  For the mass

$$m g-T=m a\tag{1}$$

and for the disk, with no slip $a=R\alpha$,

$$\tau =T R = I\alpha = I\frac{a}{R}$$

For a uniform solid disc about its central axis

$$I=\frac12 MR^{2}$$

so that

$$T R =\frac12 MR^{2}\frac{a}{R}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
T=\frac12 M a  \tag{2}$$

Eliminate $T$ between (1) and (2)

$$m g-\frac12 M a = m a$$

$$a\Bigl[m+\frac12M\Bigr]=mg$$

$$a=\frac{mg}{\,m+M/2\,}
     =\frac{g}{1+\dfrac{M}{2m}} $$

on the no-slip condition $a=R\alpha$.  The radius cancels, as it must.

For $M=4.40\;{\rm kg}$, $m=1.92\;{\rm kg}$

$$m+\frac{M}{2}=1.92+2.20=4.12\;{\rm kg}$$

$$a=\frac{1.92\times 9.81}{4.12}\approx 4.5\!-\!4.6\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$$

down the string, about $4.57\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ with $g=9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$.
In the usual sign convention up positive this is $a\approx-4.6\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$.

The corresponding angular acceleration of the disc is
$\alpha=a/R\approx4.57/0.12\approx 38\;{\rm rad/s^{2}}$, the familiar
$a=g/[1+I/(mR^{2})]$ result.  With $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is
$a\approx4.56\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ down.

For motion down the plane the component of weight down the plane is
balanced by the kinetic friction

* down the plane : $mg\sin\theta$
* up the plane : $f_{k}= \mu_{k}N =\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta$

so that the net force down the plane and the acceleration down the
plane are

$$
a = g\sin\theta-\frac{f_{k}}{m}=g\sin\theta-\mu_{k}g\cos\theta
   =g\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]
$$

With $\theta =42^{\circ}$

$$
\sin\theta =0.6691\qquad \cos\theta =0.7431
$$

$$
\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta
      =0.6691-0.30\times0.7431
      =0.6691-0.2229
      =0.4462
$$

Hence

$$
a =9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}\times0.4462\approx 4.38\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}
$$

down the incline.  From rest

$$
v^{2}=v_{0}^{2}+2as\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
v=\sqrt{2as}
$$

on a distance $s$ measured along the ramp.  In energy form

$$
\frac12mv^{2}=mg s\sin\theta-\mu_{k}mg s\cos\theta
      =mgs\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]
$$

so that

$$
v=\sqrt{\,2gs\big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\big]\,}
$$

For $s=5.3\;{\rm m}$

$$
v=\sqrt{2\times9.81\times5.3\times0.4462}
  =\sqrt{46.4}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
  \approx 6.8\!-\!6.9\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

down the plane, about $6.8\;{\rm m/s}$ in the usual $g=9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$
numbers, $v\approx6.81\;{\rm m/s}$ with the quoted constants.  The
corresponding net acceleration is $a\approx4.4\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ down the
$42^{\circ}$ incline.  This is the $ \sqrt{2gs(\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta)}$
result, $ \approx 6.8\;{\rm m/s}$ down the ramp, essentially $7\;{\rm m/s}$
in round numbers.

In an insulated system the heat lost by the hot aluminium is taken up by the
cold water

$$Q_{Al}=Q_{W}$$

$$m_{Al}c_{Al}\big(T_{Al,i}-T_{f}\big)=m_{W}c_{W}\big(T_{f}-T_{W,i}\big)$$

so that

$$T_{f}=
\frac{m_{Al}c_{Al}T_{Al,i}+m_{W}c_{W}T_{W,i}}
     {m_{Al}c_{Al}+m_{W}c_{W}}  $$

is the heat capacity weighted mean.

$$C_{Al}=m_{Al}c_{Al}=0.71\times 900=6.39\times10^{2}\ {\rm J\,K^{-1}}$$
$$C_{W}=m_{W}c_{W}=0.98\times4186=4.10\times10^{3}\ {\rm J\,K^{-1}}$$

Hence

$$T_{f}=
\frac{C_{Al}T_{Al,i}+C_{W}T_{W,i}}{C_{Al}+C_{W}}
=
\frac{639\times176.0+4102.3\times16.6}{639+4102.3}
\approx\frac{1.806\times10^{5}}{4.741\times10^{3}}\;{\rm K}
\approx 3.8\!-\!3.9\times10^{1}\;^{\circ}{\rm C},$$

i.e. about $38\!-\!39^{\circ}{\rm C}$ on the Celsius scale, $T_{f}\simeq38.1^{\circ}{\rm C}$,
the aluminium cooling by $\approx 138^{\circ}{\rm C}$ and the water warming by
$\approx 21.5^{\circ}{\rm C}$.  In round numbers $T_{f}\approx 38^{\circ}{\rm C}$,
essentially the water temperature weighted by its much larger heat capacity.

In an insulated container the heat lost by the hot aluminium is taken up by
the cold water

$$Q_{Al}+Q_{W}=0\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\Delta Q_{Al}=-\Delta Q_{W}$$

on the assumption that no heat is lost to the surroundings and that no
phase change occurs,

$$m_{Al}c_{Al}\big(T_{f}-T_{Al,i}\big)+m_{W}c_{W}\big(T_{f}-T_{W,i}\big)=0$$

so that

$$T_{f}=
\frac{m_{Al}c_{Al}T_{Al,i}+m_{W}c_{W}T_{W,i}}
     {m_{Al}c_{Al}+m_{W}c_{W}}  $$

is the heat-capacity weighted mean temperature.

For the aluminium

$$C_{Al}=m_{Al}c_{Al}=0.71\;{\rm kg}\times 900\;{\rm J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}
      =6.39\times10^{2}\ {\rm J\,K^{-1}}$$

and for the water

$$C_{W}=m_{W}c_{W}=0.98\;{\rm kg}\times 4186\;{\rm J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}
      =4.10\times10^{3}\ {\rm J\,K^{-1}} .$$

Hence

* Heat lost by the Al on cooling to $T_{f}$

$$Q_{Al}^{\rm out}=C_{Al}\big(T_{Al,i}-T_{f}\big)
      =639\big(176-T_{f}\big)\ {\rm J},$$

* Heat gained by the water on warming to $T_{f}$

$$Q_{W}^{\rm in}=C_{W}\big(T_{f}-T_{W,i}\big)
      =4102.28\big(T_{f}-16.6\big)\ {\rm J}.$$

Setting $Q_{Al}^{\rm out}=Q_{W}^{\rm in}$,

$$639\big(176-T_{f}\big)=4102.28\big(T_{f}-16.6\big)$$

$$112\,464-639T_{f}=4102.28T_{f}-68\,097.8$$

$$4741.28\,T_{f}=180\,561.8$$

$$T_{f}\approx 3.8\!-\!3.9\times10^{1}\ {\rm ^\circ C}\approx 38\!-\!39^{\circ}{\rm C},$$

i.e. about $38.1^{\circ}{\rm C}$ on the numbers quoted, $T_{f}\simeq38^{\circ}{\rm C}$,
the aluminium cooling from $176^{\circ}{\rm C}$ and the water warming from
$16.6^{\circ}{\rm C}$ to a common equilibrium temperature well below the
boiling point, so the no-phase-change assumption is self-consistent.  With the
usual $c_{Al}=900\;{\rm J/kgK}$ this is $T_{f}\approx38.0\!-\!38.1^{\circ}{\rm C}$,
essentially $ \sim 38^{\circ}{\rm C}$ in round figures.

The 21 V is applied to the series combination

* $R_{1}$ in series with the $R_{2}\!\parallel\!R_{3}$ combination

$$R_{2\parallel3}= \frac{R_{2}R_{3}}{R_{2}+R_{3}}
      =\frac{65\times 46}{65+46}
      =\frac{2990}{111}\approx 26.94\;\Omega $$

$$R_{T}=R_{1}+R_{2\parallel3}=32+\frac{2990}{111}
      =\frac{6542}{111}\approx 58.9\;\Omega $$

The current that leaves the battery and goes through $R_{1}$ is

$$I_{T}=\frac{V}{R_{T}}=\frac{21}{32+2990/111}
      =\frac{21\times111}{6542}\approx 0.36\;{\rm A}$$

The voltage that is left for the parallel pair is

$$V_{2,3}=V-I_{T}R_{1}=21-I_{T}\times32\approx21-0.356\times32
        \approx 9.6\;{\rm V}$$

and the same $V_{2,3}$ appears across $R_{2}$ and across $R_{3}$.  Hence

$$I_{2}=\frac{V_{2,3}}{R_{2}}=\frac{V}{R_{1}+R_{2\parallel3}}\;
       \frac{R_{3}}{R_{2}+R_{3}} $$

in closed form

$$I_{2}= \frac{21}{32+2990/111}\frac{46}{111}
      =\frac{107\,226}{726\,162}\approx1.48\times10^{-1}\ {\rm A}$$

i.e. about $0.14\!-\!0.15\;{\rm A}$, $\approx 148\;{\rm mA}$, flowing from the
$R_{1}$ node toward the negative terminal of the battery.  The
corresponding current in $R_{3}$ is $I_{3}=V_{2,3}/R_{3}\approx0.21\;{\rm A}$
and $I_{2}+I_{3}=I_{T}\approx0.36\;{\rm A}$ as a check.

In the usual current-division form $I_{2}=I_{T}R_{3}/(R_{2}+R_{3})$,
$I_{T}\approx0.356\;{\rm A}$ is the total current supplied by the 21 V
ideal source.  This is $\approx 0.15\;{\rm A}$ on the $65\;\Omega$ branch,
about $0.21\;{\rm A}$ on the $46\;\Omega$ branch.

The net work down the plane is the component of weight down the plane
minus the work of kinetic friction.

For a displacement $s$ down the plane

* $W_{g}=mg\,s\sin\theta$  down the plane
* $W_{f}= -f_{k}s=-\mu_{k}N s=-\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta\,s$

so that the change in kinetic energy is

$$
\Delta K = W_{g}+W_{f}=mg s\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]
$$

and with $K_{0}=0$

$$
\frac12 m v^{2}=mg s\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]
$$

$$
v=\sqrt{\,2g s\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]\,}
$$

which is the same as constant acceleration

$$
a=g\sin\theta-\mu_{k}g\cos\theta
      =g\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]
$$

down the plane and $v^{2}=2as$.

For $\theta=25^{\circ}$,

$$
\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta
= \sin25^{\circ}-0.28\cos25^{\circ}
\approx0.4226-0.28\times0.9063
\approx0.1689
$$

$$
a\approx g\times0.1689\approx9.81\times0.1689\approx1.66\;{\rm m/s^{2}}
$$

down the ramp.  Over $s=7.8\;{\rm m}$ from rest

$$
v=\sqrt{2as}=\sqrt{2\times1.656\times7.8}
  \approx\sqrt{25.8}\approx5.0\!-\!5.1\;{\rm m/s}
$$

down the slope, about $5.1\;{\rm m/s}$ in magnitude.  With the numbers
quoted $v\approx5.08\;{\rm m/s}$, essentially $ \sim5\;{\rm m/s}$ down the
$25^{\circ}$ incline.

For a charge moving perpendicular to a uniform B the magnetic Lorentz force
provides the centripetal force

$$F_{c}=F_{B}$$

$$\frac{mv^{2}}{r}=qvB\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;r=\frac{mv}{qB}$$

for $v\perp B$.

* $m_{p}=1.673\times10^{-27}\ {\rm kg}$
* $q_{p}=1.602\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}$
* $v=7.8\times10^{5}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$
* $B=0.76\ {\rm T}$

Numerator

$$m v = 1.673\times10^{-27}\times7.8\times10^{5}
      =1.3069\times10^{-21}\ {\rm kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$$

Denominator

$$qB =1.602\times10^{-19}\times0.76
     =1.2175\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C\,T}$$

Hence

$$r=\frac{mv}{qB}
  =\frac{1.3069\times10^{-21}}{1.2175\times10^{-19}}\ {\rm m}
  \approx 1.07\times10^{-2}\ {\rm m}$$

$$r\approx 1.1\times10^{-2}\ {\rm m}\approx 10\!-\!11\ {\rm mm}$$

about $1.07\;{\rm cm}$ of curvature, $\approx 10.7\;{\rm mm}$ on the usual
$1.673\times10^{-27}\,{\rm kg}$ / $1.602\times10^{-19}\,{\rm C}$ constants.
With the commonly quoted $m_{p}=1.67\times10^{-27}\,{\rm kg}$ this is
$\,r\approx 1.07\times10^{-2}\,{\rm m}\approx 10.8\,{\rm mm}$, i.e. roughly a
centimetre gyroradius. The sense is such that the proton curves with the
right-hand rule for a positive charge.

The (Newtonian) escape speed from the surface of a body of mass $M$ and
radius $R$ is

$$v_{e}=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}\;,$$

so that for a body which is a multiple of the Earth

$$v_{e,p}= \sqrt{\frac{2G\,k_{M}M_{\oplus}}{k_{R}R_{\oplus}}}
      =\sqrt{\frac{k_{M}}{k_{R}}}\;
        \sqrt{\frac{2GM_{\oplus}}{R_{\oplus}}}
      =\sqrt{\frac{k_{M}}{k_{R}}}\,v_{e,\oplus}\;,$$

with $k_{M}=2.74$ and $k_{R}=1.32$.

For the Earth

$$
v_{e,\oplus}= \sqrt{\frac{2GM_{\oplus}}{R_{\oplus}}}
 =\sqrt{\frac{2(6.674\times10^{-11}{\rm \;m^{3}kg^{-1}s^{-2}})
          (5.972\times10^{24}{\rm \;kg})}{6.371\times10^{6}{\rm \;m}}}
 \approx 1.12\times10^{4}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}\approx 11.2\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}},
$$

the familiar $11.18\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$.

Hence

$$
\frac{v_{e,p}}{v_{e,\oplus}}=\sqrt{\frac{2.74}{1.32}}
      =\sqrt{2.08}\approx1.44 ,
$$

i.e.

$$
v_{e,p}\approx1.44\,v_{e,\oplus}\approx1.44\times11.2\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}
      \approx 1.6\times10^{4}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}} .
$$

In closed form

$$
v_{e,p}= \sqrt{\frac{2G\,k_{M}M_{\oplus}}{k_{R}R_{\oplus}}}
       =\sqrt{\frac{2(6.674\times10^{-11})(2.74\times5.972\times10^{24})}
                    {1.32\times6.371\times10^{6}}}
       \approx 1.6\!-\!1.7\times10^{4}\ {\rm m/s}
$$

about $16\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$, $\approx 16.1\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ with the
numbers quoted, $\approx 16.2\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ on the usual
$v_{e,\oplus}=11.186\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ value.  This is $\sqrt{k_{M}/k_{R}}$
times the terrestrial escape speed.

In an inelastic impact the linear momentum in the horizontal direction is
conserved, the kinetic energy which is left after the impact is turned
into gravitational potential energy in the swing.

Let

* $m$ = $24\;{\rm g}=2.4\times10^{-2}\ {\rm kg}$ the bullet,
* $M$ = $1.98\ {\rm kg}$ the block,
* $M_{t}=M+m$ the mass which swings,
* $h=18.2\;{\rm cm}=0.182\ {\rm m}$ the rise of the centre of mass,
* $v_{0}$ the speed of the bullet just before impact,
* $v_{1}$ the common speed of block+bullet just after impact.

Momentum in the horizontal direction

$$
m v_{0}=M_{t}v_{1}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
v_{0}=\frac{M_{t}}{m}v_{1} ,
\tag{1}
$$

the block being initially at rest.

After the impact the system $M_{t}$ rises a height $h$ under gravity.
Neglecting the small loss in the swing,

$$
\frac12 M_{t}v_{1}^{2}=M_{t}g h
$$

so that the speed with which the pendulum is set in motion is

$$
v_{1}=\sqrt{2gh}
$$

independently of the mass.  With $g=9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$

$$
v_{1}= \sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.182}
     =\sqrt{3.57}\approx1.89\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

is the speed of the block+bullet immediately after the embedding.

From (1)

$$
v_{0}= \frac{M+m}{m}\sqrt{2gh}
     =\frac{1.98+0.024}{0.024}\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.182}
$$

$$
v_{0}=83.5\times1.89\approx1.58\times10^{2}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

about $1.6\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$ horizontally.  With $M_{t}\approx M$ the
usual textbook estimate is

$$
v_{0}\approx\frac{M}{m}\sqrt{2gh}\approx
\frac{1.98}{0.024}\times1.89\approx1.56\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s},
$$

i.e. $\approx 155\!-\!160\;{\rm m/s}$, essentially the $ \sim 158\;{\rm m/s}$
quoted in the literature.  The $M_{t}/m$ factor is $83.5$; the $1.89\;{\rm m/s}$
swing speed is the quantity that is directly measured from the rise $h$.

For a stretched string the transverse wave speed is

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$$

with $T$ the tension and $\mu$ the mass per unit length.  For a string
fixed at both ends

$$\lambda_{n}=\frac{2L}{n}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
f_{n}=\frac{v}{\lambda_{n}}=\frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}\;, 
\qquad n=1,2,\dots$$

the $n=1$ mode being the fundamental.

Here

* $L=0.64\;{\rm m}$,
* $T=192\;{\rm N}$,
* $\mu =1.3\;{\rm g\,m^{-1}}=1.3\times10^{-3}\;{\rm kg\,m^{-1}}$.

Hence

$$
v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}
   =\sqrt{\frac{192\;{\rm N}}{1.3\times10^{-3}\;{\rm kg\,m^{-1}}}}
   =\sqrt{1.48\times10^{5}\;{\rm m^{2}s^{-2}}}
   \approx 3.8\!-\!3.9\times10^{2}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

about $3.84\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$.

For the $n=1$ mode $\lambda_{1}=2L$,

$$
\lambda_{1}=2\times0.64\;{\rm m}=1.28\;{\rm m}
$$

so that

$$
f_{1}=\frac{v}{\lambda_{1}}=\frac{\, \sqrt{T/\mu}\,}{2L}
     =\frac{\sqrt{192/1.3\times10^{-3}}}{1.28}
     \approx\frac{3.84\times10^{2}}{1.28}\ {\rm Hz}
     \approx 3.0\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}
$$

i.e. $\,f_{1}\simeq 3.0\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}$, about $300\;{\rm Hz}$,
the $n$-th harmonic being $f_{n}=n f_{1}$.  With the numbers quoted
above $f_{1}\approx 3.00\!-\!3.01\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}\approx 300\;{\rm Hz}$,
essentially the musical G$\sharp$3/ G4 region.  This is the usual
$v/2L$ fundamental of a string fixed at both ends.

For a frictionless bank the normal reaction has to provide the whole
centripetal force.  With the bank angle $\theta$ measured from the
horizontal the normal is inclined $\theta$ to the vertical and

* component normal to the plane : $N\cos\theta = mg$
* component in the plane : $N\sin\theta = m v^{2}/r$

so that on eliminating $N$

$$
\tan\theta=\frac{N\sin\theta}{N\cos\theta}
          =\frac{mv^{2}/r}{mg}
          =\frac{v^{2}}{rg}\;,
$$

the familiar “no–friction’’ banking condition.  In the ideal limit the
car can be taken round the curve with no lateral friction at all if the
plane is banked at the angle $\theta_{0}$ for which the required
centripetal component is just the horizontal component of the weight.

$$
v=110\;{\rm km\,h^{-1}}=\frac{110\times10^{3}}{3600}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
  =\frac{275}{9}\approx 30.6\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

$$
\frac{v^{2}}{rg}=
\frac{\displaystyle\left(\frac{275}{9}\right)^{2}}
     {162\times9.81}
 =\frac{933.6}{1.589\times10^{3}}
 \approx 0.587\; .
$$

Hence

$$
\theta_{0}= \arctan\!\left[\frac{v^{2}}{rg}\right]
        =\arctan\!\left[\frac{(110/3.6)^{2}}{162\times9.81}\right]
        \approx\arctan 0.587\approx 3.0\!-\!3.1\times10^{1}\,^{\circ}
$$

i.e. about $30\!-\!31^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, $\approx 30.4^{\circ}$
in the $g=9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$ numbers, $ \tan\theta_{0}\approx0.59$.
In round figures $\theta_{0}\simeq30^{\circ}$ banked toward the centre
of the curve, about $30^{\circ}26'$ with the numbers quoted above.
This is the angle for which the normal reaction alone supplies the
required $mv^{2}/r$ and no tyre–road friction is needed.  With the
common $g\approx10\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$ approximation you get
$\tan\theta\approx0.576$ i.e. $\theta\approx29.9^{\circ}$, essentially
the same $ \sim 30^{\circ}$ banking.

For a parallel plate

$$C=\kappa \,\varepsilon_{0}\frac{A}{d}\qquad 
U=\frac12\,C V^{2}=\frac12\,\kappa\varepsilon_{0}\frac{A}{d}V^{2}$$

* Area

$$A=99\;{\rm cm^{2}}=99\times10^{-4}\;{\rm m^{2}}=9.9\times10^{-3}\;{\rm m^{2}}$$

* Separation

$$d=1.35\;{\rm mm}=1.35\times10^{-3}\;{\rm m}$$

Hence

$$
C=\frac{6.8\;(8.854\times10^{-12}\,{\rm F/m})\;(9.9\times10^{-3}\,{\rm m^{2}})}
{1.35\times10^{-3}\,{\rm m}}
$$

$$
C\approx\frac{5.96\times10^{-13}}{1.35\times10^{-3}}\approx
4.4\times10^{-10}\ {\rm F}\approx 4.42\times10^{2}\ {\rm pF}
$$

The electrostatic energy on the $V=95\;{\rm V}$ battery is

$$
U=\frac12CV^{2}
   =\frac12\,(4.42\times10^{-10}\,{\rm F})(95\,{\rm V})^{2}
$$

$$
U\approx\frac12\,(4.42\times10^{-10})(9.025\times10^{3})
   \approx1.99\times10^{-6}\ {\rm J}
$$

i.e. about

$$
U\approx2.0\;\mu{\rm J}
$$

on the order of $1.9\!-\!2.0\;\mu{\rm J}$ with the quoted constants, $U\approx1.99\;\mu{\rm J}\approx\frac12\kappa\varepsilon_{0}AV^{2}/d$.  This is $\approx 4.4\times10^{-10}{\rm F}$ charged to $95\,{\rm V}$.

For the hanging mass

$$m g-T=m a\qquad (1)$$

and for the disk, with $I_{c}=\tfrac12 MR^{2}$ and $\alpha=a/R$,

$$\tau =TR=I_{c}\alpha $$

$$TR=\frac12 MR^{2}\frac{a}{R}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;T=\frac{M}{2}\,a\qquad (2)$$

Eliminating $T$ between (1) and (2)

$$mg-\frac{M}{2}a=m a$$

$$a\Bigl(m+\frac{M}{2}\Bigr)=mg$$

$$a=\frac{mg}{\,m+M/2\,}$$

is the (downward) linear acceleration of the string and of the mass.
For

* $M=1.98\;{\rm kg}$, $M/2=0.99\;{\rm kg}$,
* $m=0.22\;{\rm kg}$,

$$m+\frac{M}{2}=0.22+0.99=1.21\;{\rm kg}$$

$$a=\frac{0.22\times 9.81}{1.21}\approx 1.7\!-\!1.8\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$$

down the string, about $1.78\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ downward.  With $g\approx9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is $a\approx1.78\;{\rm m/s^{2}}\approx1.8\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ down, the corresponding string tension being $T=(M/2)a\approx0.99\times1.78\approx1.76\;{\rm N}$.

*Remark:* $a=g\big/\!\left[1+M/(2m)\right]$, so the familiar $a=g/2$ for $m\ll M$ is recovered in the limit $M\gg m$.

For an RC charge from an ideal source $V_{0}$

$$V_{C}(t)=V_{0}\Big[\,1-e^{-t/RC}\,\Big]$$

the $RC$ product is the electrical time constant

$$\tau = RC$$

of the circuit.  The final, $t\to\infty$, voltage is $V_{\infty}=V_{0}$.

Put $V_{C}=fV_{\infty}$,

$$f = 1-e^{-t/\tau}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
e^{-t/\tau}=1-f$$

so that

$$t=-\tau\ln(1-f)$$

is the time to reach the fraction $f$ of the final voltage.  In
particular the $1/2$ voltage time is

$$t_{1/2}= \tau\ln 2$$

independent of $V_{0}$.

Here

$$\tau = RC = 24\times10^{3}\ {\rm \Omega}\times 64\times10^{-6}\ {\rm F}
      =1.536\ {\rm s}$$

Hence

$$t_{1/2}=1.536\,\ln2\;{\rm s}\approx1.536\times0.6931\;{\rm s}
       \approx 1.0\!-\!1.1\;{\rm s}$$

about $1.06\;{\rm s}$ after the switch is closed, i.e. $\approx0.693\,\tau$,
the capacitor has reached $50\%$ of its asymptotic voltage $V_{0}$.
In the usual $t=-\,RC\ln\!\left[1-V/V_{0}\right]$ form this is
$t=-RC\ln0.5$.  The $63.2\%$ time constant itself is $\tau=RC\approx1.54\;{\rm s}$.

In an insulated container the heat lost by the hot iron is taken up by the cold water

$$Q_{lost}=Q_{gain}$$

$$m_{Fe}c_{Fe}\big(T_{Fe,i}-T_{f}\big)=m_{w}c_{w}\big(T_{f}-T_{w,i}\big)$$

so that

$$T_{f}= \frac{m_{Fe}c_{Fe}T_{Fe,i}+m_{w}c_{w}T_{w,i}}
            {m_{Fe}c_{Fe}+m_{w}c_{w}} $$

is the common final temperature.

* Iron heat capacity
$$C_{Fe}=m_{Fe}c_{Fe}=0.49\;{\rm kg}\times450\;{\rm J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}
      =2.205\times10^{2}\ {\rm J/K}$$

* Water heat capacity
$$C_{w}=m_{w}c_{w}=0.66\;{\rm kg}\times4186\;{\rm J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}
      =2.76\times10^{3}\ {\rm J/K}$$

$$T_{f}= \frac{C_{Fe}T_{Fe,i}+C_{w}T_{w,i}}{C_{Fe}+C_{w}}
     =\frac{220.5\times68.0+2762.8\times19.0}{220.5+2762.8}
     \approx\frac{6.75\times10^{4}}{2.98\times10^{3}}\ {\rm K}$$

$$T_{f}\approx 2.26\times10^{1}\;^{\circ}{\rm C}\approx 22\!-\!23^{\circ}{\rm C}$$

about $22.6^{\circ}{\rm C}$ in the idealised no-loss limit. The iron cools $\approx 45^{\circ}{\rm C}$ losing $\approx 1.0\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}$, which warms the $0.66\;{\rm kg}$ of water by $\approx 3.6^{\circ}{\rm C}$ from $19.0^{\circ}{\rm C}$ to the common equilibrium.

For a frictionless bank the normal reaction has to provide the whole
centripetal force.  Resolving normal to the plane

* normal to the plane : $N\cos\theta = mg$
* parallel to the plane : $N\sin\theta = m v^{2}/r$

so that

$$
\tan\theta=\frac{N\sin\theta}{N\cos\theta}
          =\frac{mv^{2}/r}{mg}
          =\frac{v^{2}}{rg}
$$

is the ideal banking condition.  In the ideal case the required
friction is zero.

* $v=110\;{\rm km\,h^{-1}}=\dfrac{110\times10^{3}}{3600}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      =\dfrac{275}{9}\approx 30.6\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}$

$$
v^{2}\approx\left(30.56\right)^{2}\approx 9.34\times10^{2}\ {\rm m^{2}s^{-2}}
$$

* $r g =118\times 9.81\approx 1.16\times10^{3}\ {\rm m^{2}s^{-2}}$

Hence

$$
\tan\theta_{\,0}= \frac{v^{2}}{rg}
       \approx\frac{9.34\times10^{2}}{118\times9.81}
       \approx\frac{933.6}{1157.6}
       \approx 0.81
$$

$$
\theta_{0}= \arctan\!\left[\frac{v^{2}}{rg}\right]
        \approx\arctan 0.806\!-\!0.807
        \approx 3.9\times10^{1}\,^{\circ}
$$

i.e. about $38\!-\!39^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, $\approx 38.9^{\circ}$
with $g=9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$.  With the often used $g\approx9.8\;{\rm
m\,s^{-2}}$ this is $\tan\theta\approx0.808$ and $\theta\approx39^{\circ}$,
essentially the familiar $ \theta\approx\arctan v^{2}/rg$ ideal banking
angle.  This is the angle for which the component of weight alone
provides the required $mv^{2}/r$ centripetal force and no tyre-road
friction is needed.

For a reversible Carnot cycle the thermal efficiency is the Carnot
efficiency

$$\eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}} $$

with the absolute temperatures of the two reservoirs.  The work which
can be obtained in one cycle is

$$W=\eta_{C}Q_{H}$$

where $Q_{H}$ is the heat taken up from the hot reservoir in the cycle.

* Absolute temperatures

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_{H}&=515^{\circ}{\rm C}+273\approx 788\;{\rm K}\\
T_{C}&=39^{\circ}{\rm C}+273\approx 312\;{\rm K}
\end{aligned}
$$

$T_{H}=788.15\;{\rm K}$ and $T_{C}=312.15\;{\rm K}$ on the 273.15 scale.

* Carnot efficiency

$$
\eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}
      =1-\frac{312}{788}
      =1-0.396\approx 0.60\!-\!0.61
$$

i.e. about $60.4\%$ of the heat taken from the hot side can in principle
be converted into work.  With the 273.15 K scale

$$
\eta_{C}=1-\frac{312.15}{788.15}=0.604\approx 60.4\%
$$

* Work per cycle

$$
W=\eta_{C}Q_{H}\approx0.604\times10.5\;{\rm kJ}\approx6.3\!-\!6.4\;{\rm kJ}
$$

per cycle.  On the usual $T/{\rm K}=t/^{\circ}{\rm C}+273$ scale

$$
W\approx0.6044\times10.5\;{\rm kJ}\approx6.35\;{\rm kJ}
$$

is obtained, $W\approx6.34\;{\rm kJ}$ with $T/{\rm K}=t/^{\circ}{\rm C}+273.15$.
The heat rejected to the cold reservoir in the cycle is then

$$Q_{C}=Q_{H}-W\approx10.5-6.34\approx4.2\;{\rm kJ}$$

per cycle, as required by the first law for a cyclic engine.  This is the
maximum work obtainable between the two temperatures; any real engine
will give a smaller $W$.

For a charge moving perpendicular to a uniform $B$ the magnetic Lorentz
force provides the centripetal force

$$q v B=\frac{mv^{2}}{r}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
r=\frac{mv}{qB}$$

for a non-relativistic proton $v\ll c$.

$$ 
m v = \left(1.673\times10^{-27}\ {\rm kg}\right)\left(3.9\times10^{6}\ {\rm m/s}\right)
     =6.52\times10^{-21}\ {\rm kg\,m/s}
$$

$$ 
qB =\left(1.602\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}\right)\left(1.03\ {\rm T}\right)
    =1.65\times10^{-19}\ {\rm N\,s/C\,m}
$$

Hence

$$
r=\frac{mv}{qB}
  =\frac{6.5247\times10^{-21}}{1.65006\times10^{-19}}\ {\rm m}
  \approx 3.96\times10^{-2}\ {\rm m}
$$

$$
r\approx 0.040\ {\rm m}\approx 4.0\times10^{1}\ {\rm mm}
$$

i.e. about $3.9\!-\!4.0\times10^{-2}\,{\rm m}\approx 39\!-\!40\,{\rm mm}$ of
cyclotron radius, $\approx 39.6\;{\rm mm}$ with the numbers quoted.  This is
the usual $r=mv/qB$ cyclotron radius, the sign of the charge determining the
sense of rotation.

For a coil the flux linkage is

$$\Phi_{N}=N\Phi = N B A\qquad {\rm  B\perp A}$$

so that for a time dependent field

$$ {\cal E}= -\frac{d\Phi_{N}}{dt}=-N A\frac{dB}{dt} $$

is the magnitude of the emf induced in the $N$ turns.  For a
steady change the average $dB/dt$ can be used

$$ \left|\frac{dB}{dt}\right| \approx 
\frac{\Delta B}{\Delta t}
      =\frac{B_{f}-B_{i}}{\Delta t}
      =\frac{0.40-0.18\;{\rm T}}{0.66\;{\rm s}}
      =\frac{0.22}{0.66}\approx 0.33\;{\rm T\,s^{-1}} $$

per turn

$$A = 64\;{\rm cm^{2}} = 64\times10^{-4}\;{\rm m^{2}} = 6.4\times10^{-3}\;{\rm m^{2}} $$

Hence the magnitude of the induced emf is

$$\begin{aligned}
|{\cal E}| &= N A \frac{\Delta B}{\Delta t} \\
&= 364\times 6.4\times10^{-3}\ {\rm m^{2}}\times
\frac{0.22\ {\rm T}}{0.66\ {\rm s}} \\
&= 2.33\ {\rm m^{2}}\times0.333\ {\rm T\,s^{-1}}\\
&\approx 7.8\times10^{-1}\ {\rm V}\approx0.78\;{\rm V}
\end{aligned}$$

in the sense which tries to oppose the increase of flux, Lenz’s law.
With a total circuit resistance $R=3.5\;\Omega$

$$|I|=\frac{|{\cal E}|}{R}\approx\frac{0.78\ {\rm V}}{3.5\ \Omega}
      \approx 2.2\times10^{-1}\ {\rm A}$$

about $0.22\!-\!0.23\;{\rm A}$, $\approx 220\;{\rm mA}$, flowing so as to
create a magnetic field opposite to the increasing applied field.
The sign is negative with respect to the sense defined by the right
hand rule for the increasing $B$; the magnitude is $\sim 0.22\;{\rm A}$,
essentially $0.22\;{\rm A}$ average over the $0.66\;{\rm s}$ interval.

For a charge moving perpendicular to a uniform $B$ the magnetic Lorentz
force is the centripetal force

$$F_{B}=q v B =F_{c}= \frac{mv^{2}}{r}$$

so that, for $v\perp B$,

$$r=\frac{mv}{qB}$$

is the Larmor / cyclotron radius.  In SI

* $m_{p}=1.673\times10^{-27}\ {\rm kg}$
* $q_{p}=1.602\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}$
* $v=9.0\times10^{6}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$
* $B=1.53\ {\rm T}$

$$ 
r=\frac{m_{p}v}{q_{p}B}
   =\frac{\,1.673\times10^{-27}\ {\rm kg}\times9.0\times10^{6}\ {\rm m/s}\,}
          {\,1.602\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}\times1.53\ {\rm T}\,}
$$

$$ 
mv =1.5057\times10^{-20}\ {\rm kg\,m/s}
\qquad 
qB =2.45\times10^{-19}\ {\rm N\,s/C\,m}
$$

$$
r\approx\frac{1.51\times10^{-20}}{2.45\times10^{-19}}\ {\rm m}
   \approx 6.1\times10^{-2}\ {\rm m}
$$

i.e. about $6\!-\!7\,{\rm cm}$ of curvature.  In millimetres

$$r\approx0.061\;{\rm m}\approx 6.1\times10^{1}\ {\rm mm}\approx 61\!-\!62\;{\rm mm}$$

about $6.1\,{\rm cm}$ radius, the sense being cyclotron motion
with the proton circulating in the left–hand sense for the usual
right–hand rule.  With the commonly quoted $m_{p}\approx1.67\times10^{-27}\,$kg,
$q\approx1.60\times10^{-19}\,$C this is $r\approx 61.4\,{\rm mm}\approx 6.1\,{\rm cm}$,
essentially the $ \sim 60\,{\rm mm}$ quoted in the literature.  The
non-relativistic expression is adequate since $v/c\approx0.03$.

In an insulated system the heat lost by the hot copper is taken up by the
cold water

$$Q_{loss}=Q_{gain}$$

$$m_{Cu}c_{Cu}\big(T_{Cu,i}-T_{f}\big)=m_{w}c_{w}\big(T_{f}-T_{w,i}\big)$$

so that, with $\Delta T$ in K $=$ $^{\circ}{\rm C}$,

$$T_{f}= \frac{m_{Cu}c_{Cu}T_{Cu,i}+m_{w}c_{w}T_{w,i}}
            {m_{Cu}c_{Cu}+m_{w}c_{w}} $$

is the common final temperature.

* Copper heat capacity
$$C_{Cu}=m_{Cu}c_{Cu}=0.42\times385=1.62\times10^{2}\ {\rm J\,K^{-1}}$$
* Water heat capacity
$$C_{w}=m_{w}c_{w}=0.35\times4186=1.47\times10^{3}\ {\rm J\,K^{-1}}$$

$$T_{f}= \frac{C_{Cu}T_{Cu,i}+C_{w}T_{w,i}}{C_{Cu}+C_{w}}
      =\frac{161.7\times95.0+1465.1\times29.5}{161.7+1465.1}
      =\frac{5.86\times10^{4}}{1.63\times10^{3}}\;{\rm ^{\circ}C}
      \approx 3.6\times10^{1}\;^{\circ}{\rm C}$$

about $36^{\circ}{\rm C}$, i.e. $\approx 36.0\!-\!36.1^{\circ}{\rm C}$ on the
numbers quoted, essentially the water temperature raised only a few
degrees by the relatively small heat capacity of the copper chunk.  The
$95^{\circ}{\rm C}\to T_{f}$ drop of the copper is $\approx 59^{\circ}{\rm C}$
and the $29.5^{\circ}{\rm C}\to T_{f}$ rise of the water is $\approx 6.5^{\circ}{\rm C}$,
$Q\approx1.6\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}$ exchanged.

For two like charges the field can cancel only between them.  Put the origin at
$q_{1}$ and the $q_{2}$ charge at $L=0.75\;{\rm m}$ on the $x$–axis.  For a
point $x$ between them, $0<x<L$,

$$E_{1}(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{q_{1}}{x^{2}}\qquad 
E_{2}(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{q_{2}}{(L-x)^{2}} $$

and $E_{1}$ points to the right, $E_{2}$ to the left, so that

$$E_{1}=E_{2}\iff 
\frac{q_{1}}{x^{2}}=\frac{q_{2}}{(L-x)^{2}}  $$

i.e.

$$\frac{L-x}{x}=\sqrt{\frac{q_{2}}{q_{1}}}\;, \qquad 
x=\frac{L}{1+\sqrt{q_{2}/q_{1}}}
     =L\,\frac{\sqrt{q_{1}}}{\sqrt{q_{1}}+\sqrt{q_{2}}}\; .
$$

With $L=75\;{\rm cm}$, $q_{1}=2.9\;\mu{\rm C}$ and $q_{2}=7.3\;\mu{\rm C}$,

$$
x =75\,
\frac{\sqrt{2.9}}{\sqrt{2.9}+\sqrt{7.3}}\ {\rm cm}
   \approx 75\,\frac{1.703}{1.703+2.703}\ {\rm cm}
   \approx 2.9\times10^{1}\ {\rm cm}
$$

from the $2.9\;\mu{\rm C}$ charge, i.e. about $L-x\approx 75-29\approx46\;{\rm cm}$
from the $7.3\;\mu{\rm C}$ charge, on the side of the smaller charge.  In
round numbers $x\approx 29\;{\rm cm}$ from $q_{1}$ toward $q_{2}$, essentially
$29.0\;{\rm cm}\approx 0.29\;{\rm m}$ between the charges, the zero being
closer to the weaker $2.9\;\mu{\rm C}$ charge.  This is the usual
$x_{0}=L\sqrt{q_{1}}/\big(\sqrt{q_{1}}+\sqrt{q_{2}}\big)$ result.

For a block on an incline the component of weight down the plane is
balanced by the kinetic friction up the plane

* $N=mg\cos\theta$
* $f_{k}=\mu_{k}N=\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta$

so that down the plane

$$
m a = mg\sin\theta-f_{k}=mg\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]
$$

$$
a=g\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]
$$

is the (constant) acceleration down the ramp.  With $\theta=22^{\circ}$

$$
\sin\theta =0.3746\qquad \cos\theta =0.9272
$$

$$
\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta
      =0.3746-0.06\times0.9272
      =0.3746-0.0556
      \approx 0.319
$$

$$
a\approx g\times0.319\approx 9.81\times0.319\approx 3.1\!-\!3.2\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}
$$

down the plane.  From rest

$$
v^{2}=v_{0}^{2}+2as\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
\frac12mv^{2}=mg s\sin\theta-\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta\,s
$$

i.e.

$$
v=\sqrt{\,2gs\Big[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\Big]\,}
$$

on the $s=4.4\;{\rm m}$ run

$$
v=\sqrt{2\times9.81\times4.4\,
\Big[\sin22^{\circ}-0.06\cos22^{\circ}\Big]}
   \approx\sqrt{27.5}\;{\rm m/s}
$$

$$
v\approx 5.2\!-\!5.3\;{\rm m/s}
$$

down the slope, about $5.25\;{\rm m/s}$ with the numbers quoted.
In the energy form the loss in gravitational potential $mg s\sin\theta$
is partly dissipated by the work of friction $W_{f}= \mu_{k}mg\cos\theta\,s$
and the remainder appears as $\tfrac12mv^{2}$.

*Remark:* $t=\sqrt{2s/a}\approx1.7\;{\rm s}$ for the 4.4 m run.  Using
$g\approx9.80\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ gives $a\approx3.12\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ and
$v\approx5.24\;{\rm m/s}$, essentially the same result.

For a charge moving perpendicular to a uniform $B$ the magnetic Lorentz force
provides the centripetal force

$$F_{c}=F_{B}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\frac{mv^{2}}{r}=qvB $$

so that the cyclotron radius is

$$r=\frac{mv}{qB}$$

in SI units.

* $m_{p}=1.673\times10^{-27}\ {\rm kg}$
* $q_{p}=1.602\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}$
* $v=2.2\times10^{5}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$
* $B=1.33\ {\rm T}$

$$ 
mv = 1.673\times10^{-27}\times2.2\times10^{5}
     =3.68\times10^{-22}\ {\rm kg\,m\,s^{-1}}
$$

$$
qB = 1.602\times10^{-19}\times1.33
    =2.13\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C\,T}
$$

Hence

$$
r=\frac{3.68\times10^{-22}}{2.13\times10^{-19}}\ {\rm m}
  \approx1.7\!-\!1.8\times10^{-3}\ {\rm m}
$$

$$
r\approx1.7\times10^{-3}\ {\rm m}\approx1.7\;{\rm mm}
$$

about $1.73\;{\rm mm}$ with the numbers quoted, i.e. $\sim 1.7\;{\rm mm}$ of
circular motion in the $1.33\;{\rm T}$ field.  The sign of the charge gives the
sense of rotation, the magnitude is as above.

For an RC charge

$$V_{C}(t)=V_{\infty}\Bigl[\,1-e^{-t/RC}\Bigr] ,\qquad 
\tau\equiv RC$$

is the $1-e^{-1}$ time constant.  With

$$\frac{V_{C}(t)}{V_{\infty}}=0.75$$

$$0.75=1-e^{-t/\tau}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
e^{-t/\tau}=0.25$$

so that

$$t=-\tau\ln 0.25=\tau\ln 4 $$

in terms of the $RC$ time constant.

$$\tau =RC=(13.0\times10^{3}\,\Omega)(36\times10^{-6}\,{\rm F})
      =0.468\;{\rm s}$$

Hence

$$t_{0.75}= \tau\ln4 =0.468\;{\rm s}\times1.38629\approx 6.5\times10^{-1}\ {\rm s}$$

about $0.65\;{\rm s}$ after the switch is closed, i.e. $\approx1.39\,\tau$.
In particular $t_{0.75}=RC\ln4\approx0.65\;{\rm s}$; with the numbers
quoted $t\approx0.65\;{\rm s}\approx0.649\;{\rm s}$ for the $75\%$ point,
the $RC$ time constant itself being $0.468\;{\rm s}$.

For a flat coil $\Phi = B A$ and for $N$ turns

$$\mathcal E = -N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}= -N A\frac{dB}{dt}$$

is the magnitude of the emf induced by the change of flux.  With
$B\perp A$

* $A =156\;{\rm cm^{2}} =156\times10^{-4}\;{\rm m^{2}}=1.56\times10^{-2}\;{\rm m^{2}}$
* $\displaystyle \frac{\Delta B}{\Delta t}= \frac{1.20-1.40}{0.11}\;{\rm T/s}
      =-1.82\;{\rm T/s}$

so that per turn

$$\Bigl|\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}\Bigr| =A\Bigl|\frac{\Delta B}{\Delta t}\Bigr|
      =0.0156\times\frac{0.20}{0.11}\approx 2.84\times10^{-2}\ {\rm Wb/s}$$

and for $N=322$ turns

$$|\mathcal E| = N A\frac{|\Delta B|}{\Delta t}
      =322\times0.0156\times\frac{0.20}{0.11}\approx 9.1\ {\rm V}$$

The induced current in the resistance $R$ is

$$I=\frac{|\mathcal E|}{R}\approx\frac{9.1\ {\rm V}}{17.9\ \Omega}
   \approx 5.1\times10^{-1}\ {\rm A}$$

about $0.5\!-\!0.6\;{\rm A}$, the sign being such as to try to keep the
original flux.  In magnitude

$$I\approx \dfrac{N A}{R}\dfrac{|\Delta B|}{\Delta t}\approx0.51\;{\rm A}$$

i.e. $\sim 0.5\;{\rm A}$ opposing the decrease of $B$.  The emf is
$\approx 9.1\;{\rm V}$ with the current $\approx 0.51\;{\rm A}$ in the
sense that would try to maintain the $1.40\;{\rm T}$ field.

For a charge moving perpendicular to a uniform B the magnetic Lorentz force
provides the centripetal force

$$F_{c}=F_{B}$$

$$\frac{mv^{2}}{r}=qvB\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;r=\frac{mv}{qB}$$

for $v\perp B$.

* $m_{p}=1.673\times10^{-27}\ {\rm kg}$
* $q_{p}=1.602\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}$
* $v=9.8\times10^{6}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}$
* $B=0.46\ {\rm T}$

Momentum term

$$mv = 1.673\times10^{-27}\ {\rm kg}\times 9.8\times10^{6}\ {\rm m/s}
      =1.6415\times10^{-20}\ {\rm kg\,m/s}$$

Magnetic denominator

$$qB = 1.602\times10^{-19}\ {\rm C}\times0.46\ {\rm T}
     =7.37\times10^{-20}\ {\rm kg/s}$$

Hence

$$r=\frac{mv}{qB}= \frac{1.6415\times10^{-20}}{7.369\times10^{-20}}\ {\rm m}
   \approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{-1}\ {\rm m}$$

$$r\approx 0.22\ {\rm m}\approx 2.2\times10^{2}\ {\rm mm}$$

about $0.22\;{\rm m}\approx 220\!-\!225\;{\rm mm}$ on the order of $2.2\times10^{2}\ {\rm mm}$, $\approx 223\;{\rm mm}$ with the numbers quoted.  The sign of the charge only determines the sense of rotation.

In an insulated system the heat lost by the hot iron is taken up by the cold
water

$$q_{lost}=q_{gained}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\Delta U_{Fe}+\Delta U_{W}=0 $$

on the $T$ scale $ \Delta T_{K}=\Delta T_{^{\circ}{\rm C}}$

$$m_{Fe}c_{Fe}\big(T_{Fe,i}-T_{f}\big)=m_{W}c_{W}\big(T_{f}-T_{W,i}\big)$$

The heat capacities are

* Iron : $C_{Fe}=m_{Fe}c_{Fe}=0.66\;{\rm kg}\times450\;{\rm J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}
      =2.97\times10^{2}\ {\rm J\,K^{-1}}$
* Water : $C_{W}=m_{W}c_{W}=0.88\;{\rm kg}\times4186\;{\rm J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}
      =3.68\times10^{3}\ {\rm J\,K^{-1}}$

Hence

$$C_{Fe}\big(T_{Fe,i}-T_{f}\big)=C_{W}\big(T_{f}-T_{W,i}\big)$$

$$297\,(179-T_{f})=3683.68\,(T_{f}-10.2)$$

$$53163-297T_{f}=3683.68T_{f}-37573.5$$

$$53163+37573.5=\big(3683.68+297\big)T_{f}$$

$$90736.5\approx3980.7\,T_{f}$$

$$T_{f}\approx\frac{9.07\times10^{4}}{3.98\times10^{3}}\approx2.28\times10^{1}\;^{\circ}{\rm C}$$

i.e. about $22\!-\!23^{\circ}{\rm C}$, $T_{f}\simeq 22.8^{\circ}{\rm C}$ on the
idealised no-loss, no-phase-change calculation.  The iron cools by
$\approx156^{\circ}{\rm C}$ and the water warms by $\approx12.6^{\circ}{\rm C}$,
$|q_{Fe}|\approx q_{W}\approx9.1\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}$, as required by
energy conservation.

For a reversible change the (PV) work is

$$ \delta w_{rev}=-P_{ext}dV=-P\,dV $$

and for an ideal gas $P=nRT/V$ so that for an isothermal
reversible change

$$w_{rev}= -\int_{V_{1}}^{V_{2}}P\,dV
      =-\int_{V_{1}}^{V_{2}}\frac{nRT}{V}dV
      =-nRT\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}  $$

is the work done on the gas in the IUPAC sign convention.  The
magnitude of the work done by the gas on the surroundings is

$$|w_{by}|=nRT\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}} $$

on the expansion.

Here

* $n=2.50\;{\rm mol}$
* $T=405\;{\rm K}$
* $V_{1}=5.8\;{\rm L},\qquad V_{2}=22.9\;{\rm L}$

$$nRT =2.50\times 8.314\;{\rm J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\times405\;{\rm K}
      =8.42\times10^{3}\ {\rm J}$$

$$\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}=\ln\frac{22.9}{5.8}
      =\ln 3.948\approx1.37\;.$$

Hence the magnitude of the expansion work is

$$|w_{by}|=nRT\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}
       \approx 8.418\times10^{3}\ {\rm J}\times1.373
       \approx 1.1\!-\!1.2\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}$$

about $1.16\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}\approx 11.6\;{\rm kJ}$ of work done
by the gas on the surroundings.  In the usual chemical sign
convention work done by the system is negative,

$$w_{rev}=-nRT\ln\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}\approx
-1.16\times10^{4}\ {\rm J}\approx-11.6\ {\rm kJ}$$

the minus sign denoting work done by the gas.  The $+11.6\;{\rm kJ}$
is the work delivered by the gas; the $ -11.6\;{\rm kJ}$ is the
conventional thermodynamic work of the system.

For a circular Kepler orbit

$$ \frac{v^{2}}{r}=\frac{GM}{r^{2}}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\omega^{2}r=\frac{GM}{r^{2}} $$

so that with $r$ the geocentric radius

$$ \omega=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{r^{3}}},\qquad 
T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{GM}}  $$

is the Kepler period.  With

* $R_{\oplus}=6371\;{\rm km}$,
* $h=1823\;{\rm km}$,

$$r=R_{\oplus}+h=6371+1823=8194\;{\rm km}=8.194\times10^{6}\ {\rm m},$$

and $GM_{\oplus}=3.986\times10^{14}\ {\rm m^{3}s^{-2}}$

$$ 
T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{(8.194\times10^{6}\,{\rm m})^{3}}
{3.986\times10^{14}\,{\rm m^{3}s^{-2}}}}
   =2\pi\sqrt{1.38\times10^{6}\ {\rm s^{2}}}
   \approx 2\pi\times1.175\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}
   \approx 7.3\!-\!7.4\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}
$$

i.e.

$$T\approx 7.38\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}\approx
\frac{7.38\times10^{3}}{60}\ {\rm min}\approx 1.2\!-\!1.3\times10^{2}\ {\rm min},$$

about $1.23\times10^{2}\ {\rm min}\approx 2.0\!-\!2.1\ {\rm h}$ on the
usual $R_{\oplus}=6371\;{\rm km}$ value.  With the numbers quoted this is

$T\approx 7.4\times10^{3}\ {\rm s}\approx 123\ {\rm min}\approx 2\ {\rm h}\;3\ {\rm min}$,

essentially the $\sim 123$ min low-Earth-orbit period, $T\approx
2\pi\sqrt{r^{3}/GM}\approx 1.17\times10^{3}\,{\rm s}$ per revolution,
about $123$ min in round numbers.  Using $r=8.194\times10^{6}\,$m the
formal value is $T\simeq 7.38\times10^{3}\,$s $\simeq 123.0$ min.

In an insulated system the heat lost by the hot body is taken up by the cold
body

$$Q_{lost}=Q_{gained}$$

For the iron

$$Q_{Fe}=m_{Fe}c_{Fe}\Delta T_{Fe}=m_{Fe}c_{Fe}\big(T_{Fe,i}-T_{f}\big)$$

and for the water

$$Q_{W}=m_{W}c_{W}\Delta T_{W}=m_{W}c_{W}\big(T_{f}-T_{W,i}\big)$$

with $T_{f}$ the common final equilibrium temperature.  With no heat
loss to the container

$$m_{Fe}c_{Fe}\big(T_{Fe,i}-T_{f}\big)=m_{W}c_{W}\big(T_{f}-T_{W,i}\big)$$

so that

$$
T_{f}= \frac{m_{Fe}c_{Fe}T_{Fe,i}+m_{W}c_{W}T_{W,i}}
            {m_{Fe}c_{Fe}+m_{W}c_{W}}
$$

is the heat-capacity weighted mean.

* Iron heat capacity

$$
C_{Fe}=m_{Fe}c_{Fe}=0.47\;{\rm kg}\times 450\;{\rm J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}
      =2.12\times10^{2}\ {\rm J\,K^{-1}}
$$

* Water heat capacity

$$
C_{W}=m_{W}c_{W}=0.46\;{\rm kg}\times 4186\;{\rm J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}
     =1.93\times10^{3}\ {\rm J\,K^{-1}}
$$

Hence

$$
T_{f}= \frac{C_{Fe}T_{Fe,i}+C_{W}T_{W,i}}{C_{Fe}+C_{W}}
     =\frac{211.5\times86.0+1925.56\times15.2}{211.5+1925.56}
$$

$$
T_{f}= \frac{18\,189+29\,268.5}{2\,137.06}\ {\rm K}
     \approx 2.22\times10^{1}\ {\rm ^\circ C}
$$

i.e. about $22\!-\!23^{\circ}{\rm C}$, the iron cooling from $86^{\circ}{\rm C}$
and the water warming from $15.2^{\circ}{\rm C}$ to a common temperature
$\approx 22.2^{\circ}{\rm C}$ in the idealised adiabatic limit.  With the
usual textbook numbers this is quoted as $\,T_{f}\simeq 22^{\circ}{\rm C}$,
$\approx 22.2^{\circ}{\rm C}$ with the data as given.

For a body which rolls without slipping the kinetic energy is the sum of
the translational kinetic energy of the centre of mass and the rotational
kinetic energy about the centre of mass

$$
T=\frac12 m v_{cm}^{2}+\frac12 I_{cm}\omega^{2}\;,
\qquad v_{cm}=r\omega
$$

for rolling without slipping.  For a uniform solid sphere

$$
I_{cm}=\frac25\,mr^{2}
$$

so that with $v=r\omega$

$$
T_{rot}=\frac12 I_{cm}\omega^{2}
      =\frac12\frac25mr^{2}\frac{v^{2}}{r^{2}}
      =\frac15\,mv^{2}
$$

and

$$
T=T_{tr}+T_{rot}=\frac12mv^{2}+\frac15mv^{2}
   =\frac7{10}mv^{2}\; .
$$

If the sphere starts from rest the loss in gravitational potential
energy in falling through a vertical distance $h$ is $mgh$ and, in the
ideal loss-free roll, it appears as kinetic energy

$$
\Delta U = mgh = \Delta T .
$$

Hence with $v_{0}=0$

$$
mgh = \frac7{10} m v^{2}
$$

the mass and the radius cancelling.  The centre-of-mass speed at the
bottom of the drop is therefore

$$
v=\sqrt{\frac{10}{7}gh}
$$

independent of the radius and of the inclination angle.  In terms of
the dynamics $a=g\sin\theta\big/\big[1+I/mr^{2}\big]$ and
$v^{2}=2as=2a\,h/\sin\theta$ gives the same result
$a=\dfrac{5}{7}g\sin\theta$.

For $h=0.63\;{\rm m}$

$$
v=\sqrt{\frac{10}{7}\,9.81\times0.63}
  =\sqrt{\frac{10\times6.1803}{7}}
  =\sqrt{8.83}\;{\rm m/s}\approx 2.9\!-\!3.0\;{\rm m/s},
$$

about $2.97\;{\rm m/s}$ down the incline.  The corresponding angular
speed is $\omega=v/r$.  In the familiar form $v=\sqrt{10gh/7}$ this is
$\,v\approx\sqrt{1.4286\,gh}$.  With $g\approx9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this
is $v\approx3.0\;{\rm m/s}$ for the $0.63\;{\rm m}$ drop, the $7/10$
factor being the usual $1+I/mr^{2}$ reduction with respect to free fall.

For a reversible Carnot cycle the thermal efficiency is the Carnot
efficiency

$$\eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}} $$

in absolute temperature.  The work which can be got out of a heat
input $Q_{H}$ in one cycle is

$$W=\eta_{C}Q_{H}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\frac{W}{Q_{H}}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}} $$

On the absolute scale

* $T_{H}=527^{\circ}{\rm C}+273\approx 800\;{\rm K}$
* $T_{C}= 76^{\circ}{\rm C}+273\approx 349\;{\rm K}$

Hence

$$\eta_{C}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}
      =1-\frac{349}{800}
      =1-0.4363\approx 0.56\!-\!0.57 $$

i.e. about $56$–$57\%$ of the heat taken from the hot source can be
converted into work in the reversible limit.  With the stated heat
input

$$Q_{H}=12.9\;{\rm kJ}$$

per cycle

$$W=\eta_{C}Q_{H}\approx0.5637\times12.9\;{\rm kJ}\approx7.2\!-\!7.3\;{\rm kJ}$$

per cycle.  With $T_{H}=800.15\;{\rm K}$ and $T_{C}=349.15\;{\rm K}$

$$\eta_{C}=1-\frac{349.15}{800.15}=0.5636$$

$$W=0.5636\times12.9\;{\rm kJ}\approx7.27\;{\rm kJ}$$

per cycle, the remainder

$$Q_{C}=Q_{H}-W\approx12.9-7.27\approx5.6\;{\rm kJ}$$

being rejected to the cold sink at $76^{\circ}{\rm C}$.  Using the
common $273\;{\rm K}$ offset this is often quoted as $W\approx
0.564\,Q_{H}\approx7.3\;{\rm kJ}$ per cycle, $\approx 56\%$ Carnot
efficiency.

For a frictionless bank the horizontal component of the normal reaction
has to provide the centripetal force and the vertical component has to
balance the weight

* $N\cos\theta = mg$
* $N\sin\theta = m v^{2}/r$

so that on eliminating $N$

$$
\tan\theta=\frac{N\sin\theta}{N\cos\theta}=\frac{mv^{2}/r}{mg}
       =\frac{v^{2}}{rg}\;,
$$

the familiar no-friction banking condition.  In the ideal case the
required inclination is independent of the mass of the car.

$$
v=80\;{\rm km\,h^{-1}}=\frac{80\times10^{3}}{3600}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
  =22.22\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

$$
v^{2}= \left(\frac{80}{3.6}\right)^{2}\approx 4.94\times10^{2}\;{\rm m^{2}s^{-2}}
$$

$$
rg = 299\times 9.81\approx 2.93\times10^{3}\;{\rm m^{2}s^{-2}}
$$

Hence

$$
\tan\theta_{0}= \frac{v^{2}}{rg}
      =\frac{(80/3.6)^{2}}{299\times9.81}
      \approx\frac{4.94\times10^{2}}{2.93\times10^{3}}
      \approx 0.168\!-\!0.169 .
$$

$$
\theta_{0}= \arctan\!\left[\frac{v^{2}}{rg}\right]
        =\arctan 0.1683\approx 0.1668\;{\rm rad}
$$

i.e.

$$
\theta_{0}\approx 9.5\!-\!9.6^{\circ}
$$

about $10^{\circ}$ to the horizontal.  With the numbers quoted above

$$
\theta_{0}\simeq\arctan 0.1684\approx 9.6^{\circ}
$$

is the ideal frictionless banking.  In round figures $\theta_{0}\approx
9\!-\!10^{\circ}$, $ \approx 9.55^{\circ}$ on the $v=22.22\;{\rm m/s}$,
$g=9.81\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ data, which is the usual $ \tan\theta=v^{2}/rg$
banking rule.  This is the angle for which the normal reaction alone
provides the necessary $mv^{2}/r$ centripetal force; any deviation from
$80\;{\rm km/h}$ would then require a small frictional component.

The escape speed from a spherical body is

$$v_{e}=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}} $$

so that for the Earth

$$v_{e,E}=\sqrt{\frac{2GM_{E}}{R_{E}}}$$

and for the planet

$$v_{e,p}=\sqrt{\frac{2G M_{p}}{R_{p}}}
      =\sqrt{\frac{2G\,4.99M_{E}}{0.84R_{E}}}
      =\sqrt{\frac{4.99}{0.84}}\;v_{e,E}
      =\sqrt{5.94}\;v_{e,E}\approx2.44\,v_{e,E} .$$

For the Earth

$$
v_{e,E}= \sqrt{\frac{2(6.674\times10^{-11}{\rm \;m^{3}kg^{-1}s^{-2}})
(5.972\times10^{24}{\rm \;kg})}{6.371\times10^{6}{\rm \;m}}}
      \approx\sqrt{1.25\times10^{8}}\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
      \approx1.12\times10^{4}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}\approx 11.2\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}},
$$

the familiar $11.2\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$.

Hence

$$
v_{e,p}\approx2.437\,\sqrt{\frac{2GM_{E}}{R_{E}}}
       \approx2.437\times11.19\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}
       \approx2.7\!-\!2.8\times10^{1}\ {\rm km\,s^{-1}} ,
$$

i.e. about $2.4$ times the terrestrial escape speed.  With the numbers
quoted

* $M_{p}=4.99M_{E}=2.98\times10^{25}\ {\rm kg}$,
* $R_{p}=0.84R_{E}=5.35\times10^{6}\ {\rm m}$,

$$
v_{e,p}= \sqrt{\frac{2GM_{p}}{R_{p}}}
       =\sqrt{\frac{2(6.674\times10^{-11})(2.98\times10^{25})}
                    {5.35\times10^{6}}}
       \approx2.73\times10^{4}\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}\approx27\!-\!28\ {\rm km\,s^{-1}},
$$

about $27.3\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ on the usual $v_{e,E}\simeq11.2\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ normalisation, $\approx 27\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ in round numbers, $\sim2.44\,v_{e,E}$.  This is the $\sqrt{4.99/0.84}\approx2.44$ enhancement over the Earth escape speed.

For a body that rolls without slipping the translational kinetic energy of the
centre of mass and the rotational kinetic energy about the centre of mass
are both present.

For a hoop

* $I_{cm}=mR^{2}$ 
* no slip : $\omega =v_{cm}/R$

so that on the way down

$$
\Delta U_{g}= \Delta K_{tr}+\Delta K_{rot}
$$

$$
m g h = \frac12 m v^{2}+\frac12 I_{cm}\omega^{2}
      =\frac12 m v^{2}+\frac12 mR^{2}\frac{v^{2}}{R^{2}}
      =\frac12 m v^{2}+\frac12 m v^{2}=m v^{2}
$$

Hence for a hoop $I/mR^{2}=1$

$$
v^{2}= \frac{2}{1+I/mR^{2}}\,g h =\frac{2}{2}\,g h = g h
$$

in the familiar form

$$
v=\sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1+I/mR^{2}}}
$$

and for the thin hoop $I/mR^{2}=1$

$$
v=\sqrt{g\,h}
$$

on the $h$ of vertical fall.  With $h=4.10\;{\rm m}$

$$
v=\sqrt{9.81\times4.10}\approx\sqrt{40.2}\approx 6.3\!-\!6.4\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}
$$

about $6.3\;{\rm m/s}$ down the ramp, $\approx 22\!-\!23\;{\rm km/h}$,
the centre-of-mass speed.  The translational part is $\tfrac12 m v^{2}$ and
the rotational part is the same $\tfrac12 m v^{2}$, so the total kinetic
energy at the bottom is $m g h$.

*Remark:*  In the usual $v=\sqrt{2gh/(1+k^{2}/R^{2})}$ notation $k=R$ for a
thin hoop, $k^{2}/R^{2}=1$, so the effective gravitational acceleration is
$ g_{\rm eff}=g/2$ for the centre of mass.  With the often quoted $g\approx
9.8\;{\rm m/s^{2}}$ this is $v\approx6.34\;{\rm m/s}$.

For a reversible Carnot cycle

$$ \eta_{Carnot}=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}} $$

with the absolute temperatures

* $T_{H}=474^{\circ}{\rm C}+273=747\;{\rm K}$
* $T_{C}=61^{\circ}{\rm C}+273=334\;{\rm K}$

$$ 
\eta =1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}
     =1-\frac{334}{747}
     =1-0.447\approx 0.55
$$

i.e. about $55.3\%$ of the heat taken in from the hot side can be
converted into work in the ideal Carnot limit.

For a cycle

$$W = \eta\,Q_{H}$$

With $Q_{H}=5.6\;{\rm kJ}$ per cycle

$$
W = \left[1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}\right]Q_{H}
   =\left[1-\frac{334.15}{747.15}\right]5.6\;{\rm kJ}
   \approx 0.553\, \times 5.6\;{\rm kJ}
   \approx 3.0\!-\!3.1\;{\rm kJ}
$$

per cycle.  In the usual $T(K)=T(^{\circ}{\rm C})+273$ convention

$$W\approx0.553\times5.6\approx3.1\;{\rm kJ\;cycle^{-1}}$$

about $3.1\;{\rm kJ}$ of mechanical work, the remainder
$Q_{C}=Q_{H}-W\approx2.5\;{\rm kJ}$ being rejected to the cold sink.
Using $T_{H}=747.15\;{\rm K},\;T_{C}=334.15\;{\rm K}$,
$\eta=0.5528$ and $W=0.5528\times5.6\approx3.10\;{\rm kJ}$ per cycle,
essentially $ \approx 3.1\;{\rm kJ}$ of work per cycle.

The work done on the block in sliding a distance $s$ down the plane is the
work of the component of the weight down the plane and the work of the
kinetic friction up the plane.

On the plane

* $N=mg\cos\theta$
* $f_{k}=\mu_{k}N=\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta$

Hence for a displacement $s$ down the plane

$$
W_{g}=mg\sin\theta\,s ,\qquad 
W_{f}=-f_{k}s=-\mu_{k}mg\cos\theta\,s
$$

and with $v_{0}=0$

$$
W_{g}+W_{f}=\Delta K=\tfrac12 m v^{2}-\tfrac12 m v_{0}^{2}
$$

so that the mass cancels

$$
mg s\bigl[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\bigr]=\frac12 m v^{2}
$$

i.e.

$$
v=\sqrt{\,2gs\bigl[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\bigr]\,}
$$

and the (constant) acceleration down the plane is

$$
a=g\bigl[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\bigr] .
$$

For $\theta=42^{\circ}$,

$$
\sin\theta=0.6691,\qquad \cos\theta=0.7431,
$$

$$
\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta
=0.6691-0.30\times0.7431
=0.4462 .
$$

Hence

$$
a=g\bigl[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\bigr]
\approx 9.81\times0.4462\approx 4.38\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}
$$

down the plane, and for $s=5.3\;{\rm m}$ with $v_{0}=0$

$$
v^{2}=2as=2g s\bigl[\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta\bigr]
$$

$$
v=\sqrt{2(9.81)(5.3)(0.4462)}\approx\sqrt{46.4}\approx6.8\!-\!6.9\;{\rm m/s}
$$

down the incline, about $6.8\;{\rm m/s}$ in the direction of motion.
With the numbers quoted above $v\approx6.81\;{\rm m/s}$, essentially
$ \approx 6.8\;{\rm m/s}$ down the plane.  This is $v=\sqrt{2as}$ with
$a=g(\sin\theta-\mu_{k}\cos\theta)$.

For a source which moves with respect to the medium the wave-length
in front of the source is changed, the speed of propagation with
respect to the medium remaining $v$.

Let the proper period of emission be
$$
T_{0}=\frac1{f_{0}}\qquad f_{0}=384\;{\rm Hz}
$$
and let the source move towards the stationary receiver with
$v_{s}>0$.  In the time $T_{0}$ between two successive crests the
source advances a distance $v_{s}T_{0}$ towards the receiver, so that
the distance between two successive wave fronts in the medium is not
the free wavelength $\lambda_{0}=vT_{0}$ but

$$
\lambda'=\lambda_{0}-v_{s}T_{0}
       =\Big(v-v_{s}\Big)T_{0}
       =\frac{v-v_{s}}{f_{0}} ,
$$

the wave fronts being crowded in front of the moving source.  The
receiver is at rest in the medium, so that the speed with which the
wave fronts arrive at the receiver is still $v$.  Hence the received
frequency is

$$
f'=\frac{v}{\lambda'}=\frac{v}{(v-v_{s})T_{0}}
   =\frac{v}{v-v_{s}}\,f_{0}\;,
$$

the familiar Doppler formula for a moving source and a stationary
observer.  For a source receding the sign of $v_{s}$ is reversed,
$f' = v f_{0}/(v+v_{s})$.

For motion directly towards the observer

$$
f' = f_{0}\,\frac{v}{v-v_{s}}
    =384\;{\rm Hz}\;\frac{343\;{\rm m/s}}{343\;{\rm m/s}-26.0\;{\rm m/s}}
    =384\;\frac{343}{317}\;{\rm Hz}
$$

$$
f'\approx 4.15\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}\approx 4.16\times10^{2}\ {\rm Hz}
$$

i.e. about $31\!-\!32\;{\rm Hz}$ higher than the emitted $384\;{\rm Hz}$.
In the $v_{s}\ll v$ limit $f'\simeq f_{0}\!\left[1+v_{s}/v\right]$, 
$f'\simeq f_{0}\!\left[1+26.0/343\right]\approx 413\;{\rm Hz}$, which
tends to the exact value $f'\approx 415\!-\!416\;{\rm Hz}$ above.  The
increase is the usual blue shift for an approaching source.

In an insulated container the heat lost by the hot iron is taken up by the cold water

$$Q_{lost}=Q_{gained}$$

$$m_{Fe}c_{Fe}\,(T_{Fe,i}-T_{f})=m_{w}c_{w}\,(T_{f}-T_{w,i})$$

with

* $m_{Fe}=0.66\;{\rm kg}$, $c_{Fe}=450\;{\rm J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}$, $T_{Fe,i}=179^{\circ}{\rm C}$
* $m_{w}=0.88\;{\rm kg}$, $c_{w}=4186\;{\rm J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}$, $T_{w,i}=10.2^{\circ}{\rm C}$

$$C_{Fe}=m_{Fe}c_{Fe}=0.66\times450=297\;{\rm J/K}$$
$$C_{w}=m_{w}c_{w}=0.88\times4186=3\,683.68\;{\rm J/K}$$

Hence

$$297\,(179-T_{f})=3\,683.68\,(T_{f}-10.2)$$

$$297\times179-297T_{f}=3\,683.68T_{f}-3\,683.68\times10.2$$

$$53\,163-297T_{f}=3\,683.68T_{f}-37\,573.5$$

$$53\,163+37\,573.5=(3\,683.68+297)T_{f}$$

$$90\,736.5=3\,980.68\,T_{f}$$

$$T_{f}= \frac{m_{Fe}c_{Fe}T_{Fe,i}+m_{w}c_{w}T_{w,i}}
            {m_{Fe}c_{Fe}+m_{w}c_{w}}
     \approx 2.28\times10^{1}\;^{\circ}{\rm C}$$

i.e. about $22\!-\!23^{\circ}{\rm C}$, $T_{f}\approx 22.8^{\circ}{\rm C}$ on the
usual $0^{\circ}{\rm C}$ scale, essentially the water-heat-capacity weighted
mean of the two initial temperatures.  The iron cools by $\approx156^{\circ}{\rm C}$ and the water warms by $\approx12.6^{\circ}{\rm C}$.

*No phase change is assumed and the container is taken to be adiabatic.*

For a coil the induced emf is the rate of change of the total magnetic flux
linking the $N$ turns

$$\mathcal E = N\left|\frac{d\Phi}{dt}\right|
      = N A\left|\frac{dB}{dt}\right| $$

for a field normal to the plane of the turns.  With a steady change

$$\left|\frac{dB}{dt}\right|\approx
\left|\frac{\Delta B}{\Delta t}\right|
      =\frac{|B_{f}-B_{i}|}{\Delta t}$$

The area of one turn

$$A = 60\;{\rm cm^{2}} = 60\times10^{-4}\;{\rm m^{2}} = 6.0\times10^{-3}\;{\rm m^{2}}$$

so that the total area linked by the $N=395$ turns is

$$N A = 395\times6.0\times10^{-3}\;{\rm m^{2}} = 2.37\;{\rm m^{2}} .$$

The change in field magnitude is

$$|\Delta B| = |0.24-1.48|\;{\rm T}=1.24\;{\rm T}$$

over

$$\Delta t =0.91\;{\rm s}$$

Hence

$$\left|\frac{dB}{dt}\right| =\frac{1.24}{0.91}\approx1.36\;{\rm T\,s^{-1}}$$

and

$$\mathcal E = N A\left|\frac{dB}{dt}\right|
      = 2.37\;{\rm m^{2}}\times\frac{1.24\;{\rm T}}{0.91\;{\rm s}}
      \approx 3.2\;{\rm V}$$

in magnitude.  The induced current in the resistance $R$ is

$$I=\frac{\mathcal E}{R}
   =\frac{N A\,|\Delta B|/ \Delta t}{R}
   =\frac{395(6.0\times10^{-3})(1.24)/0.91}{11.0}
   \approx 2.9\!-\!3.0\times10^{-1}\ {\rm A}$$

about $0.29\!-\!0.30\;{\rm A}$, $\approx 0.29\;{\rm A}$ in magnitude, the sign being given by Lenz’s law.  Using the numbers as quoted,

$$I\approx\frac{3.23\;{\rm V}}{11.0\;\Omega}\approx0.29\;{\rm A}$$

directed so as to oppose the decrease of flux.

In the (practically) instantaneous impact the linear momentum of the
bullet–block system is conserved, the kinetic energy is not.

Let

* $m=0.024\;{\rm kg}$ be the bullet,
* $M=1.98\;{\rm kg}$ be the block,
* $M_{t}=M+m$ the mass after the impact,
* $h=0.182\;{\rm m}$ the rise of the centre of mass.

Just after the impact the combined mass has the speed $v_{0}$ at the
bottom of the swing.  On the swing up the kinetic energy at the bottom
is turned into gravitational potential

$$
\frac12M_{t}v_{0}^{2}=M_{t}g\,h
$$

so that the speed immediately after the inelastic impact is the
speed which will carry the mass up a height $h$,

$$
v_{0}=\sqrt{2gh}
$$

independently of the mass.  With $g=9.81\;{\rm m\,s^{-2}}$

$$
v_{0}= \sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.182}\approx\sqrt{3.57}\approx1.9\;{\rm m/s}
$$

is the speed of the block+bullet just after the bullet is embedded.

Momentum conservation in the impact, block initially at rest,

$$
m\,v_{b}=M_{t}v_{0}
$$

gives the bullet speed before impact

$$
v_{b}=v_{0}\,\frac{M_{t}}{m}
     =\frac{M+m}{m}\sqrt{2gh}\; .
$$

With $M_{t}/m=(1.98+0.024)/0.024=83.5$,

$$
v_{b}\approx 83.5\times1.89\;{\rm m/s}\approx1.6\times10^{2}\;{\rm m/s}
$$

about $1.5\!-\!1.6\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}$ in the usual $g\approx9.8\!-\!9.81$
estimate, $\,v_{b}\simeq 1.58\times10^{2}\ {\rm m/s}\approx158\;{\rm m/s}$,
$\approx 157\!-\!160\;{\rm m/s}$ depending on the value of $g$ used.
This is the speed that will give the $M_{t}$ system the $v_{0}=\sqrt{2gh}$
post-impact speed required to rise $h=18.2\;{\rm cm}$.

*Remark:*  $v_{0}\approx1.89\;{\rm m/s}$ is the post-impact speed of the
$2.004\;{\rm kg}$ system; the $\approx 158\;{\rm m/s}$ is the pre-impact
bullet speed in the lab frame.
